->TO THE ROYAL MAJESTY,<-

->A MOST PRUDENT COUNSELOR.<-

<note>An ornamental initial 'N' depicts a figure, perhaps a scholar or a magistrate, seated at a desk or lectern, emphasizing the themes of study and governance.</note> **N**either the dignity of your eminent honor, nor the brilliance of your high place or office—which are but momentary and depend upon the pleasure of the Prince—nor your piety and humanity toward the poor who plead for justice; nor that unexpected duty in public administration <note>original: "politiae munus." John Williams was unique in his time for holding both high church office and the highest legal office in the land.</note> (so fitting for a man of this rank, as the surest pillar and support of the realm); nor, finally, that divine virtue of Justice, which is held in perfect balance by you, and is generously dispensed with just scales to each according to their right (injury having been banished into exile) and distributed with a straight measure—none, I say, of these gifts granted to you by God (Most Reverend Father, a President most experienced in the loftiest affairs) is the reason for this dedication of mine.

Indeed, these qualities ought to be present in any excellent Chancellor, Keeper of the Great Seal, and protector of the state by virtue of their office—though this does not always happen. Rather, two virtues especially closer to your heart and nature urge me, and persuade me to insist on dedicating these works and my most cherished nighttime labors <note>The term "lucubrationes" refers to scholarly works produced by the light of a lamp late at night.</note>—born of much toil—to your lordship and dignity before all others, and to bestow them most willingly.

The first of these in order is your soul-nourishing charity in the advancement and exaltation of the sciences, and your voluntary, unforced love toward scholars. This love we can never sufficiently describe or explain, even with the sharpest wit of a pen resting on the wings of truth, while storing your happy deeds and actions in the memory of eternal posterity. This zeal of yours toward all learned men has already produced two children <note>The "two children" or "offspring" likely refers to the libraries or collegiate foundations Williams famously supported at St. John's College, Cambridge, and Westminster.</note>...

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal dedication to John Williams, Bishop of Lincoln. Having previously praised the Bishop's general virtues of justice and piety, Fludd now turns to specific acts of patronage—namely, the Bishop’s support of libraries at Cambridge and Westminster—and highlights their shared familial or "spiritual" connection as the primary motivation for this dedication.</meta>

*DEDICATORY EPISTLE.*

...brought to light two characters <note>original: "characteres." In this context, Fludd refers to distinct expressions or monuments of the Bishop's legacy.</note> which, in nature and condition, were not at all different from one another. One of these rendered that illustrious and world-renowned Academy of Cambridge richer through the tools of study and science, more adorned with a magnificent building, and more pleasant and accessible to those eager for learning. Furthermore, there is that magnificent sanctuary of select books, a vast structural undertaking destined for the use of a Library—a gift pleasing to all literate men, profitable to anyone seeking utility, and abundantly pouring forth (as if it were sweet milk from the breasts of Minerva <note>Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom; her "milk" represents the nourishing quality of knowledge provided by the library.</note>) upon the thirsty, liberally raining down its contents. 

The other offspring, or "character," of your fruitful charity is that distinguished Library in the Monastery among the Londoners (most famous for the monuments and tombs of Kings, and called Westminster), erected at no small expense to your Dignity. It is furnished and adorned with every necessary refinement, and especially with rare books of the highest estimation. This library is celebrated and trumpeted throughout nearly all of Britain for the beauty of its structure and arrangement, as well as the excellence of the books contained within. It daily depicts and carves the praises of its noble founder and patron into eternal monuments of fame. Thus, it is clearly shown by this sweet and voluntary goodness of yours that your honor and dignity were born not for yourself alone, but for others, and that you are naturally inclined and devoted to doing good. 

Finally, the latter order—and the reason more immediate to me—which has cautiously led my respect and prompted my mature consideration to celebrate your name and honor through this dedication of my works, is that close proximity of our spirits and the firm bond of our shared lineage <note>original: "consanguinitate nexus." Fludd is highlighting a blood relation or a shared Welsh heritage with John Williams.</note>. By virtue of this, though our bodies are otherwise separate, they are nonetheless joined, bound, and united by the strongest ties and by a certain magnetic glue of nature. 

Therefore, since these works are offered to your Lordship and Dignity with a sincere heart and mind, may you (Reverend Father, a President most worthy of so great a place and office) deign to receive them with a serene brow and a peaceful countenance. I beseech you to follow me—who am most devoted to your Lordship in every duty of diligence and obedience—with favor and benevolence. Meanwhile, for my part, I humbly and from the very center of my soul pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that you may live long and happily, that you may be guided by a favorable and propitious divinity throughout your life, and that you may finally remain forever in the duty of holy goodness toward all.

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the schematic overview provided on the previous page into the formal prose introduction of the treatise. Having outlined the "principles" of meteorological phenomena, Fludd now establishes his ideological stance: that true natural philosophy must be based on Divine Revelation (the Bible and Moses) rather than the "vanity" of ancient Greek and Arabian thinkers.</meta>

1

<note>A decorative headpiece featuring intricate scrollwork sits at the top of the page, common in 17th-century printing to denote the start of a major section.</note>

->### PREFACE: IN WHICH IT IS DECLARED<-
->THAT THE LEADERS OF THE **PAGAN PHILOSOPHERS**<-
->arrogated to themselves the foundations of their philosophy by **stealthy means** from the Priest **Moses**, and upon them constructed the building of their philosophy poorly; and in this also the gross and palpable error of **Christian Philosophers** is pointed out as if with a finger—those who, having neglected the **Holy Bible** and rejected the Teachers of hidden **Theosophy**, flee to the vain doctrine of the **Pagans**.<-

<note>The text begins with a large decorative initial letter 'Q' set in a square woodcut border.</note> **HOW** varied and differing among themselves are the opinions of philosophers, both ancient and modern, concerning the essence, origin, and effects of meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, clouds, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>; how unstable their assertions are, cannot remain hidden from those who have devoted themselves with a little more accuracy to the reading of the books and volumes of Philosophy. Indeed, the reason for this matter is usually obvious to men endowed with sharpness of mind; for where the foundations of the palace of Philosophy are found to be mythical, there the structure must be expected to be weak—not unlike the shadows of a Chimera—and consequently stuffed and swollen with the wings of probability and doubt. What of indubitable truth is to be drawn from a spurious philosophy, produced by the inept labors of the Pagans? For to them, it was by no means granted by the central light of nature—that is, the Creator of nature and natural things—to truly penetrate the fountain of Christian Philosophy or the spring of the sacred scriptures.

What is the doctrine of Aristotle, what of Plato, what of Pythagoras? What, finally, is the doctrine of the Greeks, Hippocrates and Galen, and what of Avicenna and the rest of the Arabs—whether Philosophical or medical—if we look upon the marrow of the most Holy Bible correctly and in a mystical manner, or with the eyes of a Lynx? <note>A "Lynceus" or "eyes of a Lynx" refers to someone with extraordinarily keen sight, a common metaphor for deep intellectual or spiritual insight.</note> Certainly, it is a merely deceptive vapor or a vanishing smoke, and a plainly empty fiction. Hence it is that St. Paul <note>original: "D. Paulus"</note> exerted himself to the utmost to draw us away from vain Philosophy, inasmuch as in it nothing is to be elicited but trifles and things scarcely probable, rather than any matter as it truly is. Do we not gather from the excellent teaching of the Prophet how impious and profane it is, having left the way of truth, to imitate the doctrine of the Pagans? By this we are taught that the fountain of all wisdom must by no means be abandoned to seek art, science, and understanding in foreign regions, as the Agarenes <note>The Agarenes (descendants of Hagar) are referenced here, likely following Baruch 3:23, as symbols of those who seek wisdom in human reason rather than divine revelation.</note> used to do.

<summary>Fludd introduces his treatise by arguing that classical Greek and Arabian philosophy is a "vanishing smoke" compared to the "marrow" of the Bible. He asserts that true scientific knowledge was stolen from Moses and that Christians err by following Pagan authorities like Aristotle instead of sacred scripture.</summary>

<keywords>Mosaic philosophy, biblical authority, pagan errors, meteorology, St. Paul, Theosophy, Aristotle, Plato, Avicenna</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the sentence from the previous page, moving from the "shadows of a Chimera" to the "imaginations" of the pagan philosophers. Fludd is arguing that because the ancient Greeks did not know the God of the Bible, their scientific theories about the weather and the world are fundamentally flawed and lead to idolatry.</meta>

PREFACE.

with their own imaginations. From this it happened that they attributed the efficacy of such great miracles and the glory of their effects not to God, the sole Creator, but to created Nature and the elements, which were brought forth and produced from the womb of that same Nature. From here came the origin of Idolatry; namely, the veneration of the Sun and Moon, the cult of Osiris and Isis, the worship of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, the sacrifices to the Sky, Ceres, Vesta, Proserpina, Vulcan, Pluto, and Neptune, and infinite other errors by which ignorant men are persuaded to wander away and depart from the contemplation of the true **GOD JEHOVAH**, rather than approaching a perfect knowledge of their Creator. The cause of this error, however, was an ignorance of the operation and property of the Divine Word and the Holy Spirit, and a neglect of the Holy Bible—the fountain and origin of all science and wisdom. But the Sacred Scriptures contain the secrets of the most holy Philosophy, revealed to us Christians, through which the miracles of the Word are manifested to us by the mediation of worldly Nature: just as it is explained in those writings: *This Word was in the beginning (John 1) with God, and in God, and was God himself, and it was the light of the world, in which was life, and through this Word all things were made, and without it, nothing was made.* <note>original: "Hoc verbum fuisse in principio (Ioan. 1.) cum Deo, & in Deo & ipsum Deum, & quod fuerit mundi lux, in quo erat vita, & quod ab hoc verbo omnia sint facta, & sine eo nihil."</note> Therefore, through true knowledge of the Word, we understand the nature of the Speaker <note>Referring to God the Father as the "Speaker" who utters the "Word" (Christ).</note>, since the Son has a relationship to the Father. When these two are known, the Spirit of holy discipline immediately follows, as the revelation proceeding from both. Therefore, he who does not know the Word of **GOD** knows nothing, *since by the Word, God made all things (Wisdom 9:1)* <note>original: "quoniam verbo Deus fecit omnia Sap. 9. 1."</note>; and he who does not understand it cannot understand the truth, because Christ is the only truth, the true **GOD**, and eternal life—or, as the Apostle intends in *1 Corinthians 1, the power and wisdom of GOD.* From this it follows that those who do not know Him cannot centrally <note>To know something "centrally" in alchemical thought means to know its inner essence or divine core, rather than just its outward appearance.</note> know the things created by Him, nor their essences. *From Him, in Him, and through Him are all things (as the Apostle says); to whom be praise and honor.*

How great, then, is the madness in us Christians to venerate those pagan authors of philosophy and Medicine as if they were deities? Indeed, to cite their authorities so stably and firmly in our writings and disputes, as if they had been poured out and distilled onto the earth divinely from the heavens and immediately from **GOD** himself? For the sacred scriptures testify that Christ is the only truth, and every truth of things is from Him—the power and wisdom of **GOD** teaching all things. Who, then, of all the Philosophers, can demonstrate the nature or a natural thing by primary reasoning, if he is ignorant of the true and primary cause of things? Are we not also taught that there is no truth of science outside of the true gift of the Holy Spirit, seeing as He is the only Teacher of true doctrine and science? This can be gathered from many places in the sacred writings (Exodus 28:3; Exodus 31:2; and 35:30). Hence, that Royal Psalmist says in *Psalm 119:99* with exultation: *I have been made more intelligent than all my Teachers, because the testimonies of GOD are my meditation.* <note>original: "Omnibus Doctoribus meis intelligentior sum factus, quoniam testimonia DEI mea meditatio sunt."</note> What then of that Aristotelian "Nature"? Surely it is either vain, or an attempt to explain the unknown by something even more unknown, since Aristotle himself was ignorant of the **Cupid** <note>In Fludd's philosophy, "Cupid" or "Eros" represents the animating Spirit of Love and Desire that holds the universe together—a Christianized version of a Neoplatonic concept.</note>, who is the true and shining spirit of all wisdom, the light of the world, the glory of the truly wise, the life of creatures, the mind of souls, and the prince of reason, governing in the very center of natural things. Aristotle, Plato, Pythagoras, and Hippocrates undoubtedly perceived a great light in nature from afar, as they were instructed by the Ethiopians, Egyptians, Hebrews, and certain peoples of Armenia and the Arabs after long and tedious travels; but they then changed the names of the three principles of **Moses** and falsely attributed them to themselves. According to the smallness of my talent, I will strive to reveal and publish them to the world, having girt my loins with the belt of truth, with the favor of a fortunate and propitious divinity.

# THE FIRST CHAPTER OF THE FIRST BOOK
# CONCERNING THE PRIMARY PRINCIPLES OF
# METEORS, FROM THE FOURTH PORTION
# OF THE FIRST SECTION OF THE FIRST PART.

### *In which various opinions of philosophers, both ancient and modern,*
### *concerning the name and essence of the Meteor are treated.*

<note>Decorative initial Q</note> Although I have spoken quite extensively throughout the entire seventh book of our treatise on physics concerning the various natures of meteors, both physical and metaphysical—and also throughout the thread of the *History of the Preternatural Events of Both Worlds* <note>original: "De præternaturali vtriusque mundi historia"</note> in the second portion of the first section of the third part—nevertheless, in this place, a profound contemplation of the subject currently at hand and the necessity of our project compels me to penetrate into their centers with a somewhat more accurate investigation. For whoever desires to reach the very heart <note>original: "meditullia," referring to the innermost core</note> of meteors, and does not attempt to lead such a business to a happy conclusion, will indeed confess that he has not reached the smallest secret of GOD and nature. First, therefore, before I descend into the depths of a work of such great difficulty, I shall briefly and clearly explain what the Philosophers, both Ancient and modern, have thought regarding the general naming, essence, and origin of the meteor.

The Greeks assigned the name "meteor" <note>original: "meteori," from the Greek *meteoros*, meaning "raised up" or "suspended in the air"</note> because of the sublimity of its position in the region of the air. But among our own people, meteors are called "impressions" <note>original: "impressiones"; in early modern science, atmospheric phenomena were thought of as "stamped" or "impressed" upon the air</note> because they are mostly seen to be impressed and formed on high, that is, in the upper regions of the air. Yet truly, this kind of naming is attributed to them not from their essence or constitution, but rather from their location. With respect to their consistency, however, philosophers call them "imperfectly composed" and "imperfectly mixed" <note>original: "corpora imperfecte composita & imperfecte mista"</note> bodies; or (as some wish) they are so called because of their sudden generation, seeing as they are observed to be formed in an instant or a moment of time. Others maintain that they are called "imperfectly composed" bodies because their composition does not seem to occur according to a change of substance, but rather through an alteration of qualities. Certain others call them "imperfectly mixed" insofar as they are compared to animate and perfectly mixed bodies. Finally, there are others who assertively say that these impressions are called "imperfect mixtures" because a "perfect form" is not acquired in them, nor is a great alteration of parts found in such a composition; rather, the parts of things only lightly altered are confounded amongst themselves. And this is the reason why the parts of such an imperfect mixture are so easily dissipated from one another and dissolved into their primary elements, from which they were previously coagulated without any perfect mixing or transmutation having taken place.

Regarding the existence of these impressions, everyone agrees that two things are required for it: One, namely, that *in which* they are made, which is the air—serving as the medium or the lowest spirit of the world, which is the <term>matrix</term> <note>The "matrix" here refers to a womb-like environment where things are generated or nurtured.</note> of all meteors; the other, that *from which* they are made, and they conclude that this is vapor or, as others prefer, smoke <note>original: "fumum"</note>, fundamentally rising from either the earth or the water. In this upward motion, they identify celestial heat as the more principal and primary agent, and the air as the secondary agent. Then, they believe that this matter, thus raised upward, is united and given form through the nature of a <term>coagulum</term> <note>A "coagulum" is an agent that causes liquid to thicken or curdle; here it refers to the force that turns gas/vapor into a visible atmospheric event.</note> that is partly celestial and partly elementary.

However, some seem to disagree regarding the material cause. While one scholar chooses only vapor as the universal matter of meteors, others assert that vapor and exhalation are their material subjects. They say that vapor is hot and moist, and thus they believe that "aqueous meteors" <note>such as rain or snow</note> proceed from its substance. On the other hand, they wish for "ignited impressions" <note>such as lightning or comets</note> to arise from exhalation, because it is hot and dry according to the nature of fire. For this reason, they have made smoke the common matter of meteors instead of vapor, since smoke, because it participates in the nature of every element, is sometimes hot and dry, and sometimes hot and moist; thus its matter is as fit for the procreation of aquatic impressions as it is for fiery ones. But truly, Robert of Lincoln <note>original: "Robertus Lincolniensis," referring to the medieval English philosopher Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253).</note>, supported by the authority of Aristotle, seems to include "exhalation" under the dimension of "vapor," since, according to the opinion of the said Aristotle, he established that vapor is threefold: namely, hot and dry; hot and moist; and cold and moist. He asserted that the first is extracted materially from the earth or earthy things, the last from water or watery things, and the middle one from both, but with the watery part dominating. Hence, it followed that he defined vapor as a subtle substance from any one or two of the lower elements—

**On the Primary Principles of Meteors. 5**

derived or exhaled from the lower regions, refined by celestial action, and raised to one of the three regions of the air. Those who proposed that a general smoke was the matter of such impressions claimed it arose from water or earth; for this reason, they conceived of two kinds of smoke: namely, **Vapor** and **Exhalation**. They described the former as a warm and moist smoke, watery and non-flammable, arising from earth and water; the latter they described as a warm and dry smoke, terrestrial, flammable, and drawn out from the earth. Therefore, they called earth and water the "remote material causes," while vapor and exhalation were the "proximate causes."

But indeed, as we come to the opinions of the philosophers concerning the efficient causes of meteors, we shall find no small discrepancy among them. Some have been of the opinion that the efficient causes of these impressions are heat and cold. They made this heat twofold: namely, that of the place and that of the sun. Furthermore, they distinguished the heat of the sun into that which "calls forth," which draws out and elevates the smokes extracted from the earth or water, and that which is "scorching," which burns the elevated smokes according to the direct or indirect path of the solar rays. They also imagined cold to be of two conditions: namely, that of the place and that which is external. Again, they made the external cold either "constricting" or "prohibiting." By constricting, they mean the pores and surface of the earth are tightened so that the solar rays approaching from afar cannot extract smokes; they assert this is the reason why there are few fiery meteors in the winter time, but many more and more abundant watery ones (such as rain and snow). Others, making no mention of cold, proposed that the heavens, the light of the sun and the other stars—and especially the hidden influences of the planets—were the efficient causes of meteors. They argued that according to their various positions, relationships, and conjunctions, they produce different and diverse impressions in a hidden manner. Some supposed a hidden warmth of the air worked together with that celestial heat to produce such "imperfect mixtures" <note>original: "mista imperfecta," a standard term for atmospheric phenomena which were seen as less stable than minerals or animals</note>. Thus, various men have produced various efficient causes of meteors according to their differing fantasies. We shall bring the opinions of all these to the Lydian stone <note>original: "examen Lydium," a touchstone used to test the purity of gold</note> or to a trial by fire, with the assistance of the divine power, in its proper place.

They recognized the formal cause of these impressions—by which some are adorned with different shapes and others with different ones—to be varied according to the diversity of the place, the motion of the matter, and the acting heat.

Even in their opinions regarding the final cause <note>The "final cause" refers to the ultimate purpose or end goal of a thing's existence.</note> of meteors, those well-versed in natural philosophy are quite anxious and uncertain. Nevertheless, all of them, taught by outcome and experience, recognize a twofold effect of meteors in nature: namely, the good and healthy, and the evil and unhealthy. For they have learned by observation that the final effect of these tends toward the universal health of living plants and other bodies, as well as the convenience of each particular thing. They confess themselves to have experienced that every one of them has its own manifest and hidden virtue; for instance, the office of rain is to irrigate and fatten the earth, while the office of **Comets** is to consume the corrupt and poisonous smokes of the air, and so on. That they sometimes result in the worst and most mournful effects is taught to us not only by the more skilled Astrologers but also by those immersed in the mud of common philosophy. Daily practice has instructed them on how heavy floods are produced by immoderate rains, and how much terror of war, famine, and plague a Comet portends—which must also be judged of the other meteors, both watery and fiery, according to the disposition of their mass and quality. Indeed, on the testimony of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and geographer whose works were foundational to Renaissance science.</note>, meteors have more obscure significations regarding both the benefit and the harm of the lower world and its creatures than the stars themselves; nonetheless, he confesses that these can be soberly observed and judged in some way by men endowed with prudence.

Such, therefore, are the opinions of the Philosophers, both ancient and modern, regarding the general Being and existence of Meteors. If we compare these with the sense of the Sacred Page <note>original: "sacræ paginæ," referring to the Bible</note> through diligent observation, we shall clearly perceive—or it will be very easily brought into the light—whether there is any relationship between that Scripture and these opinions or not. For whatever is seen to be out of harmony with the fountain of all truth is false and deceptive.

**On the Primary Principles of Meteors.** 7

Having already clearly explained these matters in our physical history of the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole</note>, and later in Book 9, Tract 1, Chapter 9 of the **Natural History of the Microcosm** <note>The "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>; and finally in the first and fifth chapters of the first book of the first section of the first part of the second volume, concerning the **Cabalistic and Physiological Discourse of Both Worlds**—where the primary elements of Nature are discussed—and also in Chapter 1 of the same discourse where the triple principles of the Macrocosm and Microcosm are debated; it is my purpose in this place to briefly review and recount those same things for the sake of fresh memory and a more certain method.

We say, therefore, according to the doctrine of the High Priest **Moses**, that there are three primary principles of all things, and consequently of meteors: namely, **Darkness**, **Light**, and the **Intermediate Spirit** which participates in both. For its sublunary part <note>the region below the moon</note> is more familiar with the earth and darkness, which is why it is subject to constant alterations. Its empyrean <note>the highest, fiery heaven</note> and super-celestial part, however, is observed to have a greater fellowship with the source of light, as it was the receptacle for the light created on the first day, and it is that over which the **Spirit of God** is said to have moved. Finally, its middle portion participates equally in both extremes; for this reason, the "sphere of equality"—which is the solar orbit, or rather the path through which the Sun passes daily—is said by the Platonists, not without reason, to be drawn in its very center. From this, it is called **Ether**.

Moses called this worldly spirit **"the waters,"** the subject of which is the **"second matter"** arising from the depths of the formless darkness (which is the first or potential matter of the spirit itself). The procreator or beneficial midwife of this birth was that fiery power emanating from the Spirit of the Lord; this was that **igniting love** <note>original: "amor ignens"</note> by means of which potential matter—lurking in the depths of formless chaos or **Hyle** <term>Hyle: a Greek term for "prime matter," the raw, unformed substance of the universe</term>—was brought into the actual state of waters.

Therefore, **Water** is the daughter of the latent God (the darkness), while **Light** is the offspring of the divine power or splendor (the manifest God). The midwife of both is the **Word** or the **Divine Spirit**. Hence the wise man said: *God created the world out of formless* or (as Jerome has it) *invisible matter*, Wisdom 11:18. And Saint Peter says: *the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and through water by the word of God*, 2 Peter 3:5. From this it is clear that the first matter of the world was formless matter, which Moses called **Darkness** or the **Dark Abyss**, and its second matter was **Water**, from which the heavens and earth were later made. The worker or operator of all these miracles was the **Word** with the **Spirit of the Lord**, as in Psalm 33:6. And hence the royal Psalmist sings: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth.*

Here, therefore, we have confirmed from Holy Scripture:
1. The **Potential or Privative Principle**: namely, darkness or formless and invisible matter (wherefore it is said that the earth was empty and void).
2. The **Positive Principle**: namely, **Light**, or the effect of divine power, by whose presence the invisible, formless, and potential matter was made visible and active.
3. The **Intermediate Subject or Object**: namely, **Water**, from which the heavens and the earth were fashioned by means of **Form**.

For this reason, natural philosophers, when describing the breadth of all beings, place at the summit **Pure Act** without matter, and at the bottom **Matter without Form** (namely, darkness). They demonstrate that all intermediate things are mixed from form and matter—specifically, water mixed with vivifying light. This is the same reason we conceived the origin of our formal and material **Pyramids** <note>Fludd often used diagrams of intersecting pyramids of Light and Darkness to explain the composition of reality</note>.

From these things, it is clear that:
*   **Earth** is nothing other than thick water and the dregs of the spirit remaining after its extraction from the formless chaos.
*   The **Universal Air** is thin and subtle water, or the invisible spirit extracted from chaos.
*   **Visible Water** (sea, spring, river) is the intermediate substance participating in both extremes. In that it is thicker, slower in motion, and heavier than air, it appears to have commerce with the earth; yet, insofar as it is clear, mobile, and not as heavy as earth, it seems to taste of the nature of air and stand apart from the laws of earth.

When Saint Peter said the heaven and earth consist of water and through water by the Word of God, he understood "heaven" to mean the universal air (whose base is visible water), and by "earth" he seems to imply everything dark, opaque, and dense. The order of these principles is also best denoted by the **Regular Bodies of Geometry** <note>The Platonic Solids</note>, where the **Cube** is defined as the most extreme and ample body, because it is first-born and contains the ratio of the whole.

This body [the Cube] is regarded by the more occult philosophers as **Chaos** or **Hyle**, or opaque, dark, and formless matter, from whose bosom or womb both light and water emerged—that is, the formal and material principle of all things. This is **PAN**, or universal nature, produced from the formless chaos by a **Virgin birth**. And when the philosophers said that the **Tetrahedron** <note>A four-faced pyramid, representing the element of Fire</note> was the first-born from the cube, they understood that **Fire** (or primary lucid form) emerged from the immense darkness as if from a most massive and opaque body. For then, formal light immediately appeared in the moist nature; then, I say, the Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters, imparting fiery vigor to them. This was followed by the completion of the first day of creation. Thus, according to the words of the wise man: *Wisdom was created before all things*, Ecclesiasticus 1; that is, divine light shone out of the darkness before any other creature. King Solomon also seems to confirm this in these words: *Jehovah possessed Wisdom in the beginning of his way, before his works, before any time; before the beginning of the earth. When there were no depths, I was brought forth* (says Wisdom), *when there were no fountains; when God strengthened the clouds above, when he prepared the heavens, I was there; when he set a compass upon the face of the deep...*

Then, from the bowels of the Tetrahedron—or the illuminated spirit—the **Dodecahedron** <note>A twelve-faced solid, representing the heavens or the universe as a whole.</note> is extracted. For when the bright spirit was created on the first day, the Heaven or the Expansion was created from its womb or matrix on the second day of creation, as Moses testifies. This Dodecahedron is formed from pentagonal surfaces, and for this reason (as I believe) heaven is called the **fifth essence** <note>The "quintessence," a refined substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>, arguing from this that the fifth element is distinct from those four sublunary elements. The work of the third day, however, is the gathering of the thick or sensible waters into a place destined for them by God; their symbol is the **Icosahedron** <note>A twenty-faced solid representing the element of water.</note>, from whose belly the air immediately flew forth, whose symbol is the **Octahedron** <note>An eight-faced solid representing the element of air.</note>; for water became air through thinning. The remainder of the dark Cube, however, settled into the earth, and thus it now obtained the name of "fertile earth," which was previously called "void earth" by Moses. Therefore, in the image of these three principles—namely, darkness, waters, and light—the entire spirit of the world is divided into three elements, differing from one another in nature and disposition: namely, into **Earth**, into the **Sphere of Moisture**, and into **Fire**, just as has been more than sufficiently explained in the second book of our *History of the Macrocosm*.

From these things explained here, there arose so much discrepancy among the leading ancient philosophers concerning the principles of natural things, though their opinions do not seem to differ much from one another if we consider the matter a little more accurately. For **Thales of Miletus** placed **Water** as the principle of all things; **Anaximenes** said that infinite air was the cause of the existence of things, whence **Anaximander** even made air **God**. But **Zoroaster** thought all things were made by fire or light, and the **Pythagoreans** said fire was the unique thing throughout the whole.

And certainly, as has been said, if we consider the matter well, we will find these men did not wander far from the path. For fire, first emerging from the darkness, revealed the unseen waters by its sudden splendor; the vast, subtle part of these waters is the airy spirit, whence both Thales and Anaximenes seem to agree in a certain way. But indeed, both of these explained only the material or passive principle. But Zoroaster, preferring fire above the rest, quite rightly called it the primary principle, inasmuch as it preceded the moist matter, no differently than action precedes passion, or an act precedes the thing to be produced into action. And yet he himself erred in a way, because an active principle cannot exist except insofar as it relates to a passive principle.

Hence St. Peter said the heaven and earth were made from water and through water by means of the Word—that is, the agent, or the first act. Therefore, with more mature speech, **Diogenes** spoke of the principles of things, saying that **air** endowed with divine reason is the principle of things: that is, air or the created moist nature, and the divine light; as if he wished to say with Moses that the Spirit of the Lord, carried over the waters, was the principle of created things along with the waters. And **Zeno the Stoic**, more cautious in his opinion, attempting to make his sentiment on the principle firmer, says that the substance of **Fire** converted through air into water is the principle of all things. And **Empedocles**, proceeding in a coarser manner, established the **four elements** as the principles of all things. Finally, the error of all these in their judgment of principles was immense, because they did not notice that the divine power or the most holy Word was the more ancient beginning of all these things. If they had understood this with more mature meditation, they would say with Zoroaster, instructed by primary reasons, that the **divine light** was the **Monad** <note>The "Unit" or "The One," representing the ultimate source of all being.</note> or primary author of all things, since it is the source and origin of acts and forms; by the revelation of which the number **Dyad** <note>The number "Two," representing duality or the emergence of a second principle from the first.</note> was produced—namely, the dark Monad which was water along with the bright Monad.

### CHAPTER IV.

In these, substances mixed both imperfectly and perfectly are gathered in a homogeneous way, digested, matured, fixed, and led to the goal of perfection; and likewise, heterogeneous things are cut, scattered, dissipated, driven away, and reverberated. This duty is indeed completed by **heat**, insofar as it is from the most noble and subtle spirit...

### **CHAPTER V.**

#### **On the progression in Nature which occurred from these primary principles toward the fabric of the three Elements: which are the secondary principles of Natural things.**

Thus, once these simple qualities—and those derived from them—were produced from the aforementioned principles of Nature, the movement of nature then immediately tended toward the generation of secondary principles, which are called elements. In this state of simplicity, Nature seems to rest in its absolute construction of the world, so that in such a condition it would remain without any evident change or alteration until the very end. However, those things that follow these in the order of nature, pertaining both to the generation of a perfectly mixed body and to its corruption in this sublunary world <note>The "sublunary world" refers to the region below the moon, which in ancient science was the realm of change, decay, and death, unlike the "unchanging" heavens.</note>, are subject to daily changes and alterations and can never rest in the same state for long. These are called **meteors** or imperfect mixtures, which we have not unwisely designated as tertiary principles, as was declared in its place in Part 1, Section 1, Portion 1, regarding the physiological discourse of both worlds, and will be explained more copiously below. Concerning these principles subject to change, as well as those simple ones—meaning the simple, least corruptible elements—the Wise Man <note>A common title for King Solomon, the traditional author of Ecclesiastes.</note> understood this when he spoke these words: *Generation passes away, and generation arrives, but the earth stands forever* <note>original: "Generatio præterit, & generatio aduenit, terra autem in æternum ſtat." This is a quote from Ecclesiastes 1:4.</note>, arguing from this that the elements are immutable (meaning they are not to be resolved back into their primary principles), but that all "Generable" things, such as meteors and things procreated from them, are subject to alterations.

Just as three principles offered themselves at the first moment of the world's creation—namely, darkness (or Chaos), Light, and Water—so also in the production of these secondary principles, three parts of the universal water, distinct from one another in nature and quality, are seen to concur. Each of these has a very close relationship to one of the aforementioned primary principles. Of these portions of the moist sublunary nature, the highest is benevolently set aflame by the act of light and its heat. Since heat is excited by the vehement motion of light (for light is more mobile than all other things, as you will find abundantly in Chapter 1, Book 1 of our *History of the Macrocosm*), and since its nature is to thin and disperse the moist nature, it drives the humidity of the waters of that place downward from its region. From this, it happens that that place becomes very dry.

Furthermore, that moist vapor, having been driven downward toward the dark place of the earth, is naturally denied the ability to tend there because it participates in the heat of the light, which is in every way contrary to the terrestrial darkness and the cold inherent to it. Thus it happened that between these two extremes, a vast sphere of moisture was gathered, participating in both to some degree. Because of its commerce and proximity to the earth, the base of this sphere becomes thickened and rendered visible, borrowing its cold disposition from the earth. Hence, that portion of this sphere is called "cold and moist," just as, conversely, the part nearer to the luminous or fiery orb is the thinnest, and not as moist as the middle portion of the same, which is nonetheless called "moist and hot" along with the whole invisible portion. 

And this is why Philosophers, both ancient and modern, have divided that sphere into two distinct elements, which they made Water and Air. However, my purpose in this discourse carries me to consider these two as nothing other than a single "moist element," which we call the **Sphere of Moisture**. In this way, we may better arrange these three principles according to the norm and order of those three prior ones. For Moses did not say: *He divided the air from the water*; but rather *He divided the waters from the waters*, etc. We therefore assign this sphere of moisture to the created waters. And just as in the first creation, the spirit of the Lord (or fiery love) was carried over the waters, so also the luminous orb (or fire) is carried over this sphere. Finally, the Earth, which is the lowest of the secondary principles, is compared to darkness—indeed, it is the gathering of darkness itself into the center of the universe. From this, cold keeps its offspring ready within its bowels to attack any invasion of the son of hot light.

Thus far, then, we have arrived at the completion of the fabric of the Macrocosm: namely, from the circumference of the shapeless shadows divided from the infinite darkness (from which the moist or aqueous matter of the world emerged) all the way to the center of the periphery, in which all the darkness resided.

But lest you think these things are fictions of mine or invented by my own brain—what we have put forward concerning the production of the first principles, the procreation of the primordial qualities (which serve the principles as handmaidens), and also the origin of the three Elements from them as secondary principles—I wish for you to observe with a diligent gaze and a somewhat more accurate speculation how these assertions of mine are defended by the consensus of Holy Scripture as well as those skilled in **Theosophy** and the mysteries of the **Cabala** <note>original: "Cabala." Refers to Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that influenced many Renaissance thinkers.</note>, and how they seem to be supported by shoulders like those of Atlas.

->**CHAPTER I.**<-

**Concerning mixed principles or meteors: where they originate, and where they naturally tend.**

**J**ust as we expressed a twofold type of principles within that category of simple substances—namely, that they are either absolutely simple, which we called "primary," or simple things [derived] from those [absolute] simples, which we made into "elements"—so too, in a similar respect, we had asserted that among the mixed principles, some are primary. These, according to the intention of the Philosophers, are **vapor** and **exhalation**. Others, however, are secondary—specifically, those constituted either from vapor, or exhalation, or both joined together simultaneously. These are called **meteors** <term>Meteors: In this era, "meteors" refer to any atmospheric phenomenon like rain, wind, or clouds, not just falling stars.</term> or <note>original: *corpora imperfecte mista*</note> **imperfectly mixed bodies**. And so it is necessary that, according to the intentions of the philosophers, the last of the simple principles—namely, the "simples from simples"—are the proximate principles of smoke, or vapors and exhalations. According to their intentions, these are likewise the closer beginnings of meteors. And just as these are imperfectly mixed bodies, so in the same progression of nature, they follow toward the procreation of all composite bodies—that is, the **perfectly mixed** ones.

From this it happened that, in the circuit of nature, from darkness, water, and light (as if from primary principles), the three elements were immediately born: namely, the **earth**, the **sphere of moisture** (both the visible kind which they call "water" and the invisible or aerial nature), and **Fire**. Thus, up to this point, the progression toward the complete production of the material and formal world has been made; its framework, due to the simplicity of its substance, will remain firm and unchanged in the same state until the last day of judgment.

Hence it happens that elements of this kind are the "simple principles" from which (as a starting point <note>original: *terminus à quo*</note>) nature proceeds into the generation of any composite or mixed creature. And again, they are the endpoint <note>original: *terminus ad quem*</note> toward which nature itself tends in its progression from generation to corruption. The middle path, however, is the **meteor**: it is either "waxing" (like the Moon) in generation, or "waning" and scattering the parts of the composite in corruption. Thus, the starting point in generation is the "point of the elements," while the endpoint is the **perfectly mixed body**, such as the human body, which we are primarily concerned with in this place.

Therefore, it is necessary that in the corruption of a composite body, the starting point is, conversely, that perfectly mixed body. Likewise, the point toward which nature leans in the act of corrupting is the simple element, from which the progression toward both perfect and imperfect mixtures began. Beyond that point, there is no further progression of corruption, owing to the simplicity of the subjects or principles. The middle point, or the "path through which" <note>original: *terminus per quem*</note> it passes, is the meteor.

Since it is impossible for any progression to occur from one extreme to another without an intervening medium, it is necessary that an "imperfect mixture" (called a meteor after the place of its procreation, whether in the heavens or the earth) should come between the simple natures, where there is no mixture, and the composite bodies, where the mixture is perfect. Consequently, it follows that both **life and death**, as well as **health and disease**, are perfected by the mediation of meteors. Just as a meteor is the middle point between the point of perfect generation and that of complete corruption, so too **disease** in a creature is a withdrawal of the creature’s health toward the goal of corruption or dissolution (which is found in the elements). Thus, disease is, as it were, the reduction of a healthy, generated thing back toward the nature of a meteor—that is, toward the "middle way" in dissolution.

Therefore, that healthy nature which was of a "perfect mixture" has now become "imperfectly mixed," since its nature is morbid and, as it were, in the middle way between the point of complete generation and that of absolute destruction. Thus, the nature of a mortal creature is just as capable, in this middle station, of retreating toward the point of health from which it withdrew, as it is of proceeding toward the extreme boundary of destruction, which is to return to the nature of the elements (especially the air) from which it first arose. Therefore, the more nature tends in its motion beyond the middle point toward simplicity, the more the composite creature gradually approaches its end; but by taking the contrary path, it begins to grow stronger and stronger.

And in this place, we ought to observe diligently that the conjunction of a **wicked meteor** (that is, a dissolving and destructive nature) with the middle nature of a thing reduced to a complete composition is the cause of death or destruction, unless it receives aid from a **salutary meteor**, by the intervention of divine assistance, as will be explained more broadly and clearly below. But that this is the motion of meteorological nature in a composite body is clearly declared by its effects within the bosom of the macrocosm's sphere of moisture. For just as meteors, both healthy and poisonous or ill-omened, are frequently produced in the aerial spirit of the Great World, so it is certain beyond all doubt that meteors of both conditions are sometimes generated in the spirit of any perfectly mixed thing... # On the Material Cause of Meteors. 17

...it is necessary: but no meteor can be procreated unless it be within an aerial matrix, for the air, by virtue of its spiritual humidity, is said to act as a mirror. As such, it most easily either receives or mimics forms, and readily represents and accepts the likenesses of all figures and colors; indeed, the air is the life and essence of "impressions" <note>In 17th-century science, an "impression" referred to any phenomenon or "mark" left by nature in the atmosphere, such as a rainbow or a storm.</note>—whether visible or invisible. Indeed, everything present in a meteor, whether it brings health or disease, is drawn and brought forth from the air itself, as if from a storehouse of the hidden **spirit of the world** <note>original: *spiritus mundi*</note>; or, to speak in the language of the Sacred Scriptures, from the secret and divine **Ark** or **perfume-cabinet** <note>original: *myrothecio*; a chest for storing precious ointments or spices, used here as a metaphor for the atmosphere's richness.</note> of GOD. Air, therefore, is the material cause of meteors, yet other causes are also required for their generation. Hence, in this strict inquiry of ours into these meteorological principles, we shall take care to consider four of their causes first and above all: the first is that *from which* they are made, namely the **material** cause, as the substantial part of their composition; the second is that *through which* they are made, namely the **formal** cause, as the peculiar essence by which one meteorological species is accustomed to differ from another in sight or effect; then follows that *by which* or *through which* it is led to the completion of its species, as if by an immediate **mover** or **operator** <note>The "efficient cause."</note>; and finally, that *for the sake of which* this mixed principle is led to its end by the efficient cause, namely the **final** cause. Regarding these causes of meteors, then—so that we may arrive at a more exact understanding of their formation and their effects, both morbid and healthful—we shall discourse in an orderly and methodical way; and in the first place, we shall deal with the material cause of the meteor throughout this entire treatise of the book.

### CHAPTER II.

**Concerning the material or substantial cause of meteors: What the Author's opinion is on the matter, and how it is seen to differ from the judgment of the ancient philosophers.**

The material of Meteors (says Aristotle, along with the other Philosophers of that same sect) consists plainly of fumes rising from the water or the earth. They claim these fumes are of a twofold nature: either **vapor** or **exhalation**. They assertively call the former "warm and moist," being watery and non-inflammable, arising from earth and water; while the latter they call "warm and dry," being earthy, inflammable, and summoned forth from the earth. For they seem to show, by the following reasoning, why the remaining elements—namely fire and air—do not yield such thick fumes as those that make up the substance of meteors: because those superior elements are much more subtle in their substance than fumes, and therefore they think such air and fire cannot produce fumes of that kind. So they say: But it shall be our task to destroy these arguments of theirs using their own mouths. For every one of them acknowledges in his writings that air, through **condensation**, becomes water, and even more so, **Vapor**, which stands in nature and constitution between pure air and visible water. Furthermore, they themselves acknowledge—and we have experienced—that this same water is reduced back into earth through **thickening**. Does not Aristotle even refute himself with his own mouth in Book 4 <note>Likely referring to *De Caelo* (On the Heavens).</note>, where he says, *The stellar body is the denser part of its own orb*; that is, a visible substance fashioned out of condensed, invisible ethereal spirit? From this, he seems to imply the possibility that a comet, a cloud, or any other meteor can be produced from the condensation of the air.

Therefore, this assertion of the ancients is invalid: that air cannot be the proximate cause of vapors because it is more subtle than vapor. For in Book 7 of my *Physics of the History of the Macrocosm*, where the generation of clouds is discussed, we have demonstrated by infallible arguments that clouds are made immediately from the composition and condensation of air by opposing winds. Consequently, that cloud, as a middle substance between water and air, takes its origin not from the watery extreme, but from the aerial one as its primary principle. From this we say that the air brings forth the matter of the cloud from its own "womb," and administers it centrally to the world—by the operation of the divine power—by way of rain, snow, or hail. We also gather this from these passages of the Holy Bible as the fountain of all truth (neglecting the writings of the **Heathens** <note>original: *Ethnicorum*; meaning the pagan Greek and Roman philosophers like Aristotle.</note> in this matter). For in the Pentateuch of Moses we find these things written: *Jehovah shall open to thee his good treasure, the heavens, to give the rain unto thy land in his season.* <note>original: *Deut. 28. 12*</note> And GOD himself, speaking to Job, says: *Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail?* <note>original: *Ibid. 38 22*</note> and a little later He continues: *Who is the father of the rain? or who hath begotten the drops of dew? out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?* <note>original: *Ibid. 28*</note> From these things, therefore, it is clear to the diligent observer that the sanctuary of GOD in which He hides His meteorological treasures is the **heavens**, and "heaven" in this place is taken to mean the **air**; for meteors are not birthed in the regions above the moon. Moreover, the instruments which GOD uses for the production of such meteors are His **winds**—the angelic winds of Jehovah, I say. Hence Job says in chapter 37:9: *By the breath of GOD frost is given: and the breadth of the waters is straitened.* And in Exodus we have: *By a parching...*

From these passages of the sacred font, we gather that aqueous meteors <term>meteora aquea</term> <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and wind, not just falling stars.</note>—such as clouds, rain, snow, hail, and other such things—are brought forth from the **Ark of heaven**, or the storehouse and sanctuary of the mundane spirit or air. This occurs by divine will, through the winds acting as instruments ordained for this task. Thus, the meteors seem to vary according to the different dispositions of the winds blowing from various regions of the world: when the North Wind <note>original: *Borea*</note> blows, snow, hail, and frost are produced; from the South Wind <note>original: *Austro*</note>, clouds and rain; from the East Wind <note>original: *Euro*</note>, heat and lightning; and from the West Wind <note>original: *Favonio*</note>, thin clouds. All these meteors are procreated from the substance of the air by those winds blowing in opposing ways and differing from one another according to the winds' disposition, as will be clearly declared in its proper place.

As for the origin of "ignited" <note>fiery</note> meteors, which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed lightning was caused by "dry exhalations" from the earth catching fire.</note> believed was caused by an exhalation sent up from the earth: certainly, if we consider the sacred writings of the Bible, we shall observe that their origin is far more hidden and abstruse than the common philosophers have dreamed. For first, we read in Leviticus that a fire or flash of light "going out from the presence of Jehovah consumed the burnt offering on that altar," Leviticus 9:24. And in the following chapter: "Fire going out from the presence of Jehovah killed the sons of Aaron," verse 2. Indeed, God himself is called a "consuming fire," and elsewhere we read that "flaming fire" is called his minister, Deuteronomy 4:24. Hence it was said that the fire sent by Jehovah consumed those 250 men, etc., Numbers 16. And elsewhere, the "fire of GOD" falling from heaven by the power of Elijah's spirit consumed the Captain and his fifty men. And in Job we find: "Can you send forth lightnings, that they may go, and say to you, 'Here we are'?" Job 38:35. Finally, in another place, it is excellently denoted that the source and origin of ignited meteors arises from that very Author, where it is written: "By God’s sneezings light shines," and indeed like the "eyelids of the morning," with "torches proceeding from his mouth, and sparks of fire leaping out. So smoke comes out of his nostrils, as if from a boiling pot; his breath kindles coals, and a flame comes out of his mouth," Job 41:18, where he refers to lightning. And elsewhere: "By what way is the light distributed, and by what path is the East wind scattered upon the earth?" Job 38:19.

By these biblical testimonies, we are taught first of all that the beginning and origin of light and flashing—and consequently of all luminous meteors—is deeply secret and abstruse. It is as far distant from the conceptions of the Ancient Philosophers (who believed their birth was from the earth) as day is from night, or light from darkness. For who among the philosophers will deny that an empty medium <note>likely referring to the atmosphere or "vacuum" of the sky</note> takes its beginning from its principle <note>its source</note> rather than its end? Furthermore, since the beginnings of mixed things are simple, why should the most essential meteors of all be derived from a corrupted and mixed earth, from an opaque body, or from that which comes after—rather than from the first principle, the fire or luminous source corresponding to their own nature? And by what means could that which is hot be procreated by a natural birth from that which is cold? Since like delights in like, and like is usually procreated by its like. Indeed, we may boldly pronounce that if humid meteors are usually formed by the compression of the thin substance of the middle air (or the middle sphere of humidity) by the mediation of two winds, much more are ignited meteors materially elicited from the compression of the highest substance of that same element by the winds gently meeting there. For a portion of the highest sphere of humidity is nothing other than dissolved and expanded fire, or "fiery air." This air, through condensation, appears in the form of an ignited meteor, such as comets, fiery columns, and all those meteors observed to be born in the highest region of the air. Their matter is air contracted by the blast of Jehovah's winds, but their luminous form is fiery light, in the center of which dwells the power of Jehovah—no differently than how He appeared to Moses in the midst of the burning bush, or in the pillar of fire that went before the Israelites at night in the desert. For GOD "clothes himself with light as with a garment" (as the Psalmist testifies), and according to Moses, "He spoke to the Israelites from the fiery flame." Hence elsewhere He is called a "consuming fire." Therefore, it is a very difficult labor, and the greatest of Herculean tasks, to discern the spring and source of these meteors unless it be detected by revelation. And for this reason, that patient man <note>Job</note> said: "By what way is the light distributed, and by what path is the East wind scattered upon the earth? Where is the way where light dwells?" Job 38. And as Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino (1470–1541), a famous Hebraist and Bible translator.</note> interprets it: "Do you know where the way is by which the exhalation is divided, which scatters the wind over the earth?"

If, therefore, the fiery form of meteors comes forth secretly from the presence of Jehovah, as we have said above; if by the "sneezings of GOD" the lightning or flash or light shines; if from His mouth "flames like torches" proceed and "sparks of fire"; if "smoke comes from his nostrils as if from a boiling pot"; if His "breath kindles coals" (Job 41:18); certainly these things are far more occult than to proceed from simple "warm and dry smoke" exhaled from the bowels of the earth. What Christian, even moderately versed in the nature of things, could be so mad as to attribute the immense force of thunder, the admirable power of lightning and the thunderbolt—which is known to melt a sword while leaving the scabbard untouched, and to snatch away the life of animals in the blink of an eye while leaving the body unmarked—to a thing of such little consequence as a terrestrial exhalation? For what more did that fire do which went out from the presence of Jehovah, by the power of which both the sons of Aaron and the 250 others were killed and deprived of life...

**On the Material Cause of Meteors. 19**

...have they not been deprived of life? Suddenly, she was struck by a lightning bolt, and the very limb she had offered in contempt was miserably torn apart in every direction. How do the wretched philosophers of this world respond to these things? Do you believe that this creature, so possessed of a divine reason, received her life from terrestrial and watery smoke? Is it not said everywhere in the holy scriptures that thunder is the voice of GOD? <note>original: *tonitru vox DEI*</note> Psalm 103:4. <note>In modern Bibles, this reference to the "voice of the Lord" over the waters and the winds as messengers is typically found in Psalm 104 or Psalm 29.</note> Are not the Angels of Jehovah called winds that do his pleasure? What then? Is it to be thought that such wonders of GOD consist of the accidental generation of watery vapor and earthly exhalation? Far be it from a Christian man, aware of the divine mind, to believe this.

But to approach somewhat more closely the empty trifles of the vain philosophers, we shall examine their opinions a little more strictly: first regarding the origin of the winds, then the generation of clouds, then the procreation of ignited meteors <term>meteora ignita</term> <note>At this time, "ignited meteors" included phenomena like comets, shooting stars, and lightning.</note> in the highest region of the air, and finally the beginnings of hail, snow, and ice.

### CHAPTER III.

### In which the trifling vanity and improbability of the ancient philosophers' opinions regarding the origin of meteors is discussed.

To begin with the opinion of the ancient philosophers regarding the origin of winds, they seem in some way to hesitate and disagree among themselves. Those who embrace the Peripatetic <note>The Peripatetic school refers to the followers of Aristotle.</note> sect and uphold Aristotle’s view on this matter define wind as a hot and dry exhalation, difficult to ignite, raised up to the middle region of the air. From there, it is driven downward by the coldness of that place, and then, striving upward again by the inclination of its own nature, it is moved laterally across the earth in the lowest region of the air—partly due to its own lightness and partly because of other exhalations encountered from below. This wind agitates and fans the air so that it does not rot from a kind of perpetual laziness; or so they say. Others (among whom I name Vitruvius) maintain that wind is a "wave of air" <note>original: *aeris unda*</note> with an uncertain abundance of motion (Vitruvius, Book 1, Chapter 6), occurring when heat meets moisture, and the onset of the heat turns the force of the blowing spirit into a gust. Those first ones, therefore, who support the Aristotelian sect, say that a breath, smoke, or a hot and dry exhalation—having no "fatness" <note>original: *pinguedinis*; meaning oily or combustible matter</note> in it by which it could be set on fire—is the material cause of wind. Because it lacks this fatness, it can neither be ignited nor reduced into a mist by condensation, much less thickened into a cloud; and they said this emerges from the earth, although Pliny says some winds breathe out from the waters.

But let us now ask what these Peripatetics (who seem to so excel in the inspection of nature) think about the origin of a Comet? They say that this arises from terrestrial smoke or exhalation that is thick, fatty, and viscous, and made of densely compacted parts. By the power of the stars, it is raised from the bowels of the earth into the highest region of the air, and there it is spread out, set on fire, and ignited. Thus, the difference between the "windy" exhalation and this "mother of the comet" is this: the former is light, hot, and dry, and difficult to ignite because it contains no fatness; whereas the latter is terrestrial, thick, fatty, and viscous, made of densely compacted and easily flammable parts.

These Peripatetics thus fall into Scylla while wishing to avoid Charybdis <note>A classical metaphor for trying to avoid one danger only to fall into a worse one.</note> because, in their description of the generation of both "meteors," they show that both explanations of the matter are false and not at all true. For what is the reason that one exhalation, since it is not fit for ignition and consequently less opposed to cold, and since it is lighter in its substance than the other, is nevertheless hindered in its ascent by the force of the cold in the middle region of the air and beaten back down to the place from which it rose? Yet, meanwhile, the other exhalation—which is thick, fatty, and flammable, and consequently most opposed to the cold of the middle region, and less suited for upward motion due to its heavy thickness—has a path through the middle region into the highest region without any opposition from the cold? How poorly these things agree, and how adverse they are to the laws of philosophy! Namely, that heavy and more compact things should ascend more easily by natural appetite and tend upward by their nature than those things which are light; and further, that those things further removed from ignition by their nature should be more infested and attacked by cold than those which are flammable and of a purely fiery disposition? From this it is clear that when they say the coldness of the middle region of the air is the cause of the hindrance to the ascent of the windy exhalation (since it is hot and dry but not flammable), it is in every way...

## CAP. IV.

*Where the admirable nature and disposition of the air*
*are clearly treated.*

[Large decorative initial S] **I**f, therefore, it is asked by the curious: what is the material origin of meteors—or rather of all things, whether perfectly or imperfectly mixed—or what is the proximate cause from simple things? We say it is the substance of the air itself, altered from its simplicity. For this reason, Anaximenes <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 585 – c. 528 BC) who believed air was the primary substance of all things.</note>—and not without foresight—did not blush to boldly assert that air was the cause of all things. Indeed, the principle of air is so ancient that Anaximander <note>Another Pre-Socratic philosopher; the author critiques him here for mistaking the creation (air) for the Creator (God).</note> did not hesitate to estimate it as God, though quite inconsiderately in this regard. Therefore, the vast dimension of this our history and its abstruse depth compel me to treat and discourse upon its nature and occult properties in this place.

Regarding the essence and consistency of the air, it is called **RUACH** <note>Hebrew: רוּחַ (Ruach), meaning spirit, wind, or breath.</note> by the Hebrews, by which name spirit or wind is also understood. Whence these three do not seem to differ from one another at all in respect to the word *Ruach*, which denotes them in many places of the Holy Scriptures: seeing as they all agree in the same essence. Therefore, *Ruach*, or Air, is that great spirit occupying the vast cavity of the world with its mass, which encompasses heaven and earth in its embrace and fills all things that are in the world; for it is in angels, stars, men, beasts, plants, the earth, the water, and stones, permeating all things. In its substance, it is not double or manifold, but uniform; not divided, but a single spirit, and as it were, the one sole perfect life and "Spirit of the World" <note>original: "spiritus mundi" — a central concept in Hermetic philosophy suggesting the world is a living organism.</note>. In its existence, it is thin, slender, subtle, invisible, incomprehensible, impalpable, and spiritual: and in its essence, it is not inaptly compared to the spirit and soul of man. For just as the human soul or spirit (which is also derived from the air) is the tabernacle of the spirit of God, and even of other spirits of God (whence it is called the temple of the Holy Spirit by the holy writings), so also the Air is the habitation of the Holy Spirit of God, and also of other spirits. For we are taught here and there in the Holy Bible that thick clouds are His hut, and that He is carried upon the wings of the wind, and that His spirits or Angels are winds and His ministers a flaming fire. From this, it is clear that the Principle of this world dwells in the air. Therefore, from the air and through the air, all creatures live, grow, and move, by means of the Word; for they are first constituted by the air and filled by the air, which rejoices in its own likeness. Hence, those more skilled in Philosophy maintain that air is a spirit of incomprehensible nature and the most ancient foundation of things, which occupies the vast cavity of the universal world and is observed to perpetually circulate through all things contained under heaven—visiting, cultivating, inspiring, transmuting, binding, retaining in vigor, nourishing, and miraculously sustaining them. Hence, the Hebrews did not count it in the number of the elements, but rather made it the firm bond and the nexus of all superior things with the inferior. And the opinion of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed in the mathematical and musical harmony of the universe.</note> is not far from these, for they considered the air to be a certain great divine organ or instrument that perpetually resounds both on earth and in the heavens, and retains the superior with the inferior in union and concord. Thus far his words. From this he concludes that it is the matrix of all impressions, since it is the medium whether in its own region or in the bowels and depths of water and earth; it is also the very matter of meteors, both healthful and unhealthful. Indeed, and what is more, it retains within itself invisible and imperceptible impressions and meteors, which are the effigies <note>In the philosophy of this period, "effigies" or "species" were thought to be thin films or spiritual images shed by objects that allow them to be perceived or to act at a distance.</note> of manifest and visible things. Similarly, through such occult impressions in the air, various dreams and multiform impressions are procreated in the human spirit through the "icons" of idols, or likenesses, or species.
