The majesty of God is all-powerful and renews all things, insofar as He remains within Himself. However, as to how and by what reasoning this spirit acts more particularly to produce the consistency of any given cloud, we shall discuss clearly in our treatise on the *Final Causes of Meteors*.

### CHAPTER VII.

*On the difference of clouds, according to the testimony of Philosophers, Pagans,*
*and Christian followers themselves, as well as*
*the Holy Scriptures.*

Those who were well-versed in Aristotelian Philosophy established many differences between clouds. Foremost, they distinguished some from others by a general difference—namely, by **substance** and **quality**. Then, they divided each of these categories into their own species. For they categorized their **substance** into "dense" and "rare," insofar as dense, thick clouds or thin, subtle clouds are procreated in and from the spiritual medium of the lower world. They claim that the former are composed and fashioned from many thick, earthy "fumes," <note>In the science of this period, "fumes" or "exhalations" were thought to be dry and earthy, while "vapors" were moist and watery.</note> while the latter come from a subtler and far less dense vapor. In this opinion, regarding the difference of clouds in density and thinness, they did not err at all, as they were familiar with the varying consistency of clouds through common experience. 

However, they are entirely deceived in thinking that the "material cause" of a cloud's density is a thick and earthy fume. In truth, the consistency of a cloud, whether in its rarity or density, is **homogeneous air**, accumulated in a greater or lesser mass and bound together in a more compact order. For do we not see that the rainwater from the blackest and densest cloud has the same homogeneity and clarity as that from a thinner, whitish cloud? Therefore, an earthy disposition of "fume" is not the cause of a cloud's density or darkness; rather, it is the density of the air itself, or more precisely, the gathering of its vaporous consistency into a deep mass. For in a mist, we see that the matter of the mist is the same—namely, condensed air—but its diversity lies in the depth of its composition and its compact union. 

But let us proceed. They were also accustomed to distinguish clouds according to their **colored quality**. Thus, they said black clouds arose from earthy fume, or from air that is compressed and compact. We, however, admit they arise from air that is strongly and deeply thickened. They said that reddish or yellowish clouds mixed with blackness arose partly from starlight or fiery exhalations, and partly from thick, earthy fume. We, on the contrary, affirm that they are made by the various "spirit of the winds" compressing the air along with "luminous or fiery seeds" <note>These "seeds" (*seminaria*) refer to the vital, light-bearing principles the author believes are scattered throughout the atmosphere.</note> expanded everywhere through the air, without any exhalation from the earth. Furthermore, they say that red clouds which turn green with blackness are procreated from exhalations mixed with thick and copious vapor, along with a great quantity of water and moisture. We assert that these are generated from various vapor or air gathered into a single mass according to the different winds blowing from the <term>four quarters of the world</term> <note>The four cardinal directions: North, South, East, and West.</note> to produce them. From this, we see that opposing winds tend to produce clouds and lightnings of various colors. Finally, they say white clouds are made from a scarcity of vapor; thus it happens that, because the subject matter is so thin, starlight very easily penetrates the mass and makes it bright.

They also have another distinction for clouds, as they make some "void" and almost empty—specifically those which are dispersed through the sky like flakes of wool <note>Likely referring to cirrus clouds, often called "mare's tails" or "wool-pack" clouds.</note>. The Aristotelians claim these are fashioned more from hot and dry exhalations than from moist vapors or those drenched in wetness. We, however, following the Holy Scriptures, say that **luminous clouds** are those cleansed of their liquid substance by a passing wind. For the Holy Page speaks of them thus: *And now men do not look upon the light when it is bright in the higher clouds, which the passing wind has cleansed.* <note>original: "Iam vero non respiciunt homines lucem, cum nitida est in superioribus nubibus, quas ventus transiens purgauit." Job 37:21.</note> From this passage, Aristotle’s opinion on winds (mentioned above) is refuted—namely, his idea that the matter of winds, which he calls "exhalation," does not penetrate the <term>middle region of the air</term>. <note>Ancient and medieval science divided the atmosphere into three regions; Aristotle believed the middle region was too cold for the dry "exhalations" that caused wind.</note> Yet, by this testimony, the wind seems to blow in the highest part of the middle air, specifically where the "higher clouds" have their positions. Other clouds, however, are overflowing with water—those that dissolve into rainy matter. 

But we, following in the footsteps of the Holy Bible, divide clouds first by their different positions into **higher** and **lower**. Hence it is said: *Men do not look upon the light when it is bright in the higher clouds.* <note>Job 37:21.</note> And elsewhere: *The higher clouds gave forth a sound.* <note>original: "sonum ediderunt superiores nubes." Psalm 77:17.</note> And elsewhere: *He commanded the higher clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven.* <note>Psalm 78:23.</note> And elsewhere: *The higher clouds were strengthened from above.* <note>Proverbs 8:28.</note> And in many other places. By this, it is signified that there are also **lower clouds** which are thicker and denser in their substance.

Furthermore, clouds appear to be distinguished from one another by Sacred Authority in respect to their substance—namely, into **dense** and **thin**. For just as the world was created by God out of dark nothingness and divided into heaven and earth by the mediation of the Spirit of God (which moved over the waters), and is distinguished into four elements, and finally, by the inspiration of that universally breathing and acting Spirit, meteors of every condition are procreated in both heaven and earth—similarly, man was formed by God from the dust of the earth in the image of the world (and consequently of God Himself). He is inspired by the Creator and divided into "heaven" and "earth"—that is, into spirit and body. # On the Formal Cause of Meteors. 73

## CHAPTER VIII.

### On the Halo, the Mist, and the Cloud.

Since air is the medium in which watery meteors are procreated—both in the heavenly macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the great world or the universe at large.</note> and everywhere within its earth—it is necessary that such meteors are also procreated in every part of the human air, whether solid or fluid; specifically, every degree of "cloud" may be found there. However, since the eyes in the highest heaven (the head of the Microcosm) <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note> are strictly related to the two luminaries of the greater world <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>—inasmuch as the rays of the human spirit emit their glances through them—every species of cloud, such as the **Halo**, the **mist**, the **small cloud**, etc., can be very easily discerned by their effects within the eyes.

For just as in the greater world we see a Halo or a very thin mist sometimes interposed between our eye and the sun or moon—sometimes thicker, and sometimes very dense, becoming a cloud barely penetrable by solar rays—so too in the medium of the eye, namely in the humors as well as in the tunics <note>A "tunic" in historical anatomy refers to a membrane or layer of tissue covering an organ.</note> or between the tunics of the eye itself, we sometimes see such meteors intermixed between the visual rays and the objects seen. These are called **mists**, **white spots**, and **suffusions** or **cataracts**. 

Mists in the eye are said to be thin and superficial whitenesses or "darknesses" of both membranes of the eye. Such a disease is called a **little cloud** <note>original: "nubecula"</note> because a certain thin humor exists there, much like a thin and tiny cloud impressed in the air, adhering to the corneal membrane. Because of this, the sufferer believes they see all things through a mist, vapor, or smoke. 

But indeed, if this humor or vapor thickens even further, it coalesces into the "second degree of cloud" and is then called **Albugo** <term>Albugo: a white opacity or spot on the cornea of the eye</term>, in which all clear sight is dazzled and things are seen as if in an obscure shadow—just as in the densest mist of the greater world, we see the image of an object previously visible completely removed from our sight. Furthermore, sometimes due to the excessive density of the corneal tunic, vision is rendered dark; hence such an occurrence is called **caligo** <note>original: "caligo," meaning fog, gloom, or dimness of sight.</note>. 

There is also another species of cloud created in a deeper place, namely in the **crystalloid** <note>The lens of the eye.</note> or **vitreous humor**, by reason of which that humor is changed into a bluish-gray or dark color. People affected by this believe they see through smoke or mist, and such an alteration of vision is called **Glaucoma**. Finally, we have another species of these meteors which produces that effect in the eye called a **suffusion** or **cataract**. This is created from a "misty hardening" of the air, either in the seat of the pupil, or between the **rhagoid tunic** <term>rhagoid tunic: an old anatomical term for the uvea or iris, named for its resemblance to a grape skin</term> and the crystalline humor. This happens gradually and little by little, so that at the beginning it can scarcely be discerned. 

Thus, in the creation of a celestial cloud, we observe various degrees: a progression from air into a scarcely perceptible vapor, then into a very thin mist, then into a thicker one, which finally hardens into a dense cloud. Furthermore, when the air is condensed into the first degree, and the area around the circumference of the pupil remains untouched (or obscured by only the thinnest smoke at the center), it is observed to take on the appearance of a **Halo**. 

Whatever the case may be, we see here that the process of air converting into thin and thick mists, and eventually into the consistency of a cloud, follows the same reasoning as it does in the mundane air. Indeed, we have observed that the watery humor of the eye is nourished and preserved by such air, which compacts into a dense vapor and hardens into a "dew." That this vaporous substance was previously air is proven in two ways: first, because it proceeds step-by-step from invisibility to visibility; and second, because it could not penetrate through the spongy and porous substance of the optic nerve unless it were in an airy and spiritual condition. 

The cause why such an airy substance sometimes hardens in these places is due to the nature of the air penetrating that seat—specifically, its "central force" which can be changed into various states by a "constricting wind." Through this wind, the air gradually contracts into a mass. Conversely, air influenced by a wind of the opposite nature remains dissolved, the better to perform the duties of the watery humor according to the laws of Nature.

In the ventricles <note>The cavities or chambers within the brain.</note> of the brain, whirlwinds of air, vapors, mists, and clouds are also generated, either by natural paths or against the laws of nature. For just as in the cells of the brain, vapors of air drawn in through the nostrils—prompted by the good and healthy spirit of nature—harden into a sweet and natural mist by circulating. By condensing slightly, they are dispersed partly into the dewy moisture of the anterior ventricles and partly into the invisible **animal spirits** <note>In Fludd's time, "animal spirits" were thought to be a refined substance that traveled through the nerves to produce movement and sensation.</note> through the passages of the **choroid plexus**. Their superfluous part is contracted into a thick water, which is excreted through the "funnel" <note>The infundibulum of the brain.</note> and the **pituitary gland**, and finally through the openings of the sphenoid bone, distilling into the palate. 

In the same way, air filled with the "seeds" of unnatural meteors—drawn in and out through the **mammillary processes** <note>The olfactory bulbs, which Fludd identifies as the site of "internal weather" creation.</note>—is sometimes observed to be reduced by unnatural means into a misty or cloudy substance. From this, **Catarrh**, **Scotomia** <term>Scotomia: a condition of dizziness accompanied by the appearance of dark spots or "clouds" before the eyes</term>, **Vertigo**, and other such effects of "internal meteors" are created in the ventricles of the brain. These afflictions correspond to the airy substance and the qualities of the winds predominating within them, as well as the specific location where they are formed.

**CHAPTER IX.**

***On the dark, thick meteors of the macrocosm, of a watery consistency in general.***

<note>A schematic diagram (labeled O) categorizes watery meteors of thick consistency. It branches into three origins: 
1. Those descending from heaven (referencing section P).

**CHAPTER X.**

***On watery meteors descending from heaven. And first, concerning those of a more liquid consistency.***

<note>A schematic diagram (labeled P) categorizes watery meteors descending from heaven. They are divided into:
1. Liquid forms: Dew and Rain.
2. Frozen forms: Referencing section S.</note>

Those watery meteors, which possess a thick and more compact consistency than those that are either cloudy or misty, differ from one another according to the place or "seat" from which they arise. Some descend from heaven, some rise from the bosom of the earth, and others draw their origin and growth from the sanctuary of both—that is, from both heaven and earth.

Those which descend from heaven are observed to differ evidently in their consistency. Some take on a liquid and flowing form, while others are frozen by the Northern cold and become, as it were, fixed and not at all fluid. Those which fall from heaven in a fluid and liquid form are Dew and Rain, which we propose to treat primarily in this section. Therefore, we will first express the opinion of Aristotle and the Peripatetic sect <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while teaching; Fludd often contrasts their "pagan" logic with "sacred" Biblical philosophy.</note> regarding the arrangement of these two meteors; afterward, we shall briefly declare the opinion of the Holy Scriptures concerning them.

According to the opinion of the Peripatetics, therefore, Dew <note>original: *Ros*</note> is defined as a vapor, mixed with a small amount of earthy matter, condensed in the lowest region of the air <note>In traditional meteorology, the atmosphere was divided into three regions; the "lowest" was warmed by reflected sunlight, while the "middle" was perpetually cold.</note>; they assert that it is dissolved into water as soon as it settles. Or they define it thus:

Dew is a vapor which, in the spring and autumn seasons, is attracted on high by the power of the sun during the day; but because it does not reach the middle region of the air, it is condensed by the nightly cold in the lowest region of the air and is forced to descend in the form of drops of water. Or thus: It is that which is generated from a weakly warm, thick, and moist vapor, not raised far from the earth in the lowest part of the air, condensed by the nocturnal cold and resolved into water. Rain <note>original: *Pluvia*</note>, however, they define as a liquefied cloud, resolved into water, dripping down drop by drop. Or alternatively: Rain (they say) is a warm, smoky, and thick vapor, elevated from moist bodies by the heat of the sun and other stars up to the middle region of the air. By the cold of that region, it is condensed and converted into a cloud; this cloud is again liquefied and resolved into water falling to the earth for the health of living and growing things.

Rain falling more copiously and with great force they call a Heavy Shower <note>original: *Imbrem*; specifically a downpour or storm-rain.</note>.

From these definitions of Dew, the Aristotelians seem to place no difference between the matter of a cloud and that of dew. For the composition of both, they assign a warm, moist, and sufficiently compact vapor, rising from earth and water and attracted upward by the force of solar heat; hence they have not hesitated to attribute the same "agent" to both. They placed the entire difference between the two in the diversity of their locations—namely, in the varying disposition of cold found there. For if that vapor had been raised into the middle region of the air, it would follow from their doctrine that, by the intense cold of that place, it would [reach] the consistency of a cloud...
K 3 <note>This "K 3" is a signature mark used by early printers to help binders assemble the book's pages in the correct order.</note>

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s discussion on the nature of watery "meteors," specifically focusing on the origins and essence of dew. Having previously categorized meteors by their seat of origin, Fludd now contrasts the traditional Aristotelian (Peripatetic) view with his own more mystical, "central" philosophy and biblical interpretation.</meta>

78 Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member II.

<note>original: "frigore condensaretur..."</note> ...it would be condensed by the cold; but in truth, since it is not raised above the peak of the middle region of the air, it is elevated by the slight cold of that place and of the nighttime only through a gentle constriction. Then, falling downward little by little by its own weight, it is transformed into drops clinging to the herbs. Hence, they <note>Referring to the Peripatetic philosophers.</note> have defined dew as nothing other than a small rain, but without clouds.

Certainly, they assign a very beautiful and, at first glance, quite probable description of the meteor of dew. But indeed, if we look into the matter a little more deeply, we shall perceive it to be otherwise, and as far removed from their opinion as possible. For first, we look back at what was said concerning the origin of clouds, and then we shall discern that the entire origin set forth by the Philosophers is closer to external probability than to the **central truth**. Furthermore, we add in this place that the cause of dew is not originally from the earth, but from heaven or the lowest part of the air. If any air or vapor is exhaled from the earth, it is solely by way of expiration, following the inspiration of the common air. It does not follow, however, that the air expired by a living creature must be condensed into a dewy substance by the nightly cold, although this may sometimes happen by a chilly or northern blast. By the same reasoning, we affirm that although vapor exhaling from the bowels of the earth is sometimes congealed into dewy drops, it does not follow from this that all dew is created from vapors rising out of the earth.

For as air is accustomed to penetrate everywhere, even to the very center of the earth—seeing as it provides life and spirit—so it is necessary that, since it is homogeneous with the air of the universal world, it has the capacity to be condensed or subtilized by that "aerial sea." Indeed, we may boldly affirm that the treasury-chest of dewy substance is the universal sea of air. Thus, there is no need for it to be expired of necessity from the cavities of the earth, since the greater contains the lesser within itself, as you will find confirmed below by the testimony of the **Sacred Font** <note>A reference to Holy Scripture.</note>. The reason for its condensation is the will of **Wisdom**, moving and contracting from the center. At her command, the winds—namely the Northern and Southern—blow most sweetly and lightly, the latter more strongly and the former more weakly, easily condensing the night air by a slight compression. This condensed air, drawn by inspiration through the pores of the earth, adheres to herbs and grasses and appears in the form of little drops.

Does it not seem that Aristotle, contrary to the goal of his own description of dew, acknowledges a great power—albeit hidden—existing in the blowing of the South winds that concurs in the constitution of dew? For there, being taught by experience, he says that there is no dew unless the South wind is blowing. Upon these words of the Philosopher, **Bartholomew** <note>Likely Bartholomaeus Anglicus (Bartholomew the Englishman), a 13th-century encyclopedist.</note> concludes thus: *Since* (he says) *dew is a tiny rain, and rain is a great dew*, in this respect he concludes that the southern wind generates dew because of its humidity, just as, conversely, the northern wind licks up and consumes dew with its dryness, or condenses and freezes its substance by means of its cold. Furthermore, regarding this doubtful resolution—namely, what is the origin of dew?—many have written many things and for contrary reasons. For **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose of Milan.</note> attributes the generation of dew upon the damp earth to the constitution of the moon, *because* (he says) *the Moon is the mother of dew.* In these things, one may see that the Philosophers are by no means consistent with themselves regarding the procreation of dew, as various men have spoken of it in various ways.

What the Holy Scriptures think of dew and its origin we shall now show in a few words. We find the Holy Scriptures speaking thus of dew in general, in the person of **GOD** addressing man: *Gird up now your loins like a man* (says **Jehovah** to Job out of the whirlwind) *and what I ask of you, make known to me, etc. Is there a father of rain? Or who begot the drops of dew? Out of whose womb did the ice come forth? Or who begot the frost of heaven?* <note>Job 38:28-29</note>. By this it is argued that it is beyond human grasp to explain such mysteries without the revelation of the divine spirit. And yet, the Peripatetics nevertheless seem to respond boldly to Jehovah’s objection, asserting that the "womb" or matrix of dew is the earth with its water, and its "begetter" is the solar rays, mediated by the nighttime cold and humidity.

But we shall approach a more particular explanation of this matter. From a twofold consideration of the Holy Letters, we have observed that there is a twofold difference of dew in the world. Namely, we gather that there is one kind springing from the earth, whence it is said: *No vapor had ascended from the earth to water the whole surface of the earth, Gen. 2.* <note>Genesis 2:6. Fludd uses the term "vapor" here, though the Vulgate often uses "fons" (fountain/mist).</note> But **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> has: *A fountain ascended from the earth which watered the entire surface of the earth.* Let the exposition of the text be made in the following manner: we say (as in the preceding pages) that meteors are generated in the spirit or air enclosed within the earth no differently than in the open air. We have also said that **Wisdom** is everywhere—in heaven, on earth, in the depths of the sea, etc. And we say that the earth, at the command of that **Terrestrial Wisdom** (which is a single and simple spirit, existing everywhere through the world, enclosed nowhere), has its expirations and inspirations, which we call vapors.

However, that vapors of this kind are condensed into dew is a mystical and secret work of Divine Wisdom, not that it requires matter from the earth; for in His hands are the spirit of the universal world and all bodies that are animated by it. Whence it is said: *GOD of the soul and the body, the strong GOD of spirits, the GOD of all flesh, Num. 16:22.* But since at His command and breath the air, both celestial and terrestrial, is changed into this or that disposition, we say that heaven is the father of the earth, as it was procreated from it from the beginning. Whence it is said that *GOD created heaven and earth* and not earth and heaven; arguing from this that after the perfection of the Heavens, the earth was created. But truly, as GOD is said to be in heaven, so we acknowledge Him to be on earth, and consequently it is certain that heaven is found in the dark earth, which is also the tabernacle of God. We conclude, therefore, that the matter of dew is principally from the **celestial spirit**, although that spirit is also inspired and expired by the earth for its quickening. Therefore, the air is the treasury-chest of God...

...will be explained more copiously in the treatise on the supernatural efficient cause of meteors. We conclude, therefore, from the doctrine and testimony of Holy Scripture, that hail is to be described in this manner:

**Hail** is a certain hard and icy impression, the matter of which the mighty God Jehovah draws from His treasures or His treasury—namely, from the hidden bosom of the air—shaping and gathering it in the heavens into infinite watery stones by His cold spirit or breath, separately freezing and compressing them; these He finally drives and casts down upon the earth to fulfill His will, either by themselves or accompanied by lightning and rain.

In this definition, there first presents itself the source <note>original: *miniera* — literally "mine" or "ore-source," referring to the origin point of the substance.</note> of its matter or substance, which, as sacred scripture testifies, is drawn from His treasures, which we have explained above to be the heavens or the air. From this, it is clear that the substance of air is the matter not only of hail, but of all other meteors. Secondly, it is explained that its form is received from the divine breath or inspiration, acting as the efficient cause <term>efficient cause: the primary source of change or rest; the "agent" that brings something into being.</term>; for it is said, *that the mighty God brings forth ice by His breath, and the frost is congealed by God standing there. Job 37:10.* And elsewhere, *He casts down ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? Psalm 147:17.* <note>The Latin text cites Psalm 147:16, but this verse is 147:17 in most English Bibles.</note> Here, by "morsels of ice," hailstones can be understood, and consequently, it is confirmed that such hailstones are formed from the cold of Jehovah’s breath in the shape of watery pebbles. This extraction of the matter of hail and ice from the dewy bosom of the air is elsewhere verified: *The ice came out from the womb of the dew, and like the stone of water they are hidden, and the surface of the deep is frozen.* <note>Reference to Job 38:29-30.</note> This can be understood both regarding the ice in the clouds of the middle region of the air, and the surface of terrestrial waters, since those clouds are called "the deep" elsewhere in the Bible, *Job 38:28.* Finally, the final cause <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or "end" for which a thing is created.</term> is explained there, namely to fulfill the divine will. Hence it is said elsewhere, *Cold, ice, hoarfrost, clouds, lightning—whatever God has commanded these to do on the surface of the earth, whether for a scourge or for mercy, they immediately perform it. Job 37.* Furthermore, God sent or brought forth hail from heaven to strike and destroy the men, cattle, herbs, and trees of the Egyptians. *Exodus 9.* <note>The OCR reads "Exod. 19," but the plague of hail is described in Exodus 9.</note> Likewise, *Jehovah sent down great hailstones from heaven, with which He slew the enemies of the Israelites. Joshua 10:11.* Wherefore, we conclude from our description that the material cause <term>material cause: the physical substance from which a thing is made.</term> of hail is drawn from the air; for in its substance it is nothing other than air, coagulated into a cloudy consistency by contrary winds. Next, we have the formal cause in that it is reduced into the form of watery pebbles, either of a round or angular shape; hence Joshua says, *Jehovah sends great hailstones from the heavens.* From this it is also clear that the place where the dense air is reduced into such an image by the medium of the divine breath is the heaven or the air. Furthermore, the efficient cause is the cold, freezing, and hardening breath of God. Finally, the final cause is for the most part punishment and a scourge or penalty: for the earth is rendered far more fertile by rain than by hail, whose nature is rather to harm fruits, trees, and crops than to bring them any benefit or profit.

But now we have reached the third species of these solid meteors, namely **Hoarfrost**, which does not seem to differ much from the others regarding its efficient cause, as it is the cold breath or respiration of Jehovah.

Aristotle, along with the Christians of his sect, defines this as a certain impression from a moist and cold vapor, rising from the element of water and not gathered into the bulk of a cloud, which impression is frozen in the middle region of the air by the coldness of the place (where no heat is present) and the time, and is led into the form of hoarfrost.

Others (among whom I name Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735 AD), an influential English monk and scholar.</note>) hold that such an impression is nothing other than frozen dew, which in its descent toward the earth drinks in and receives into itself the nocturnal coldness, by means of which it takes on that white, hard, and cold appearance that is hoarfrost.

We turn then to that Aristotelian description, and we say that if its first part were true—namely, that the matter of hoarfrost was a cold and moist vapor of that kind, springing and exhaling from the nourishment of water and earth—it would follow that it would diminish and decrease more and more daily. This is because, in a storm of hoarfrost, the gates of the earth are closed by the freezing cold, so that neither plowshares nor other iron instruments can penetrate it; then, the waters are for the most part shut up by such tight ice that we see fish die in great quantities for lack of penetrating air. But indeed, everyone will admit that air is thinner than vapor. Since this is proven false by its effect, we say that Aristotle's opinion on the substance or matter of hoarfrost is erroneous, as we do not see hoarfrost decreasing daily from its state, but rather we observe it mostly growing stronger from day to day, and we see the earth and trees increasingly donning a "swan's beard" <note>original: *barba cygnea* — a poetic description of the feathery, white appearance of frost.</note>.

The same must also be said about the material cause of hoarfrost explained in the second description—namely, that it is not from the substance of dew, if we conclude it arose and was procreated in the Aristotelian way, namely from vapor exhaled from the waters and the earth. But that opinion of Bede will be probable if he agrees with us that the entire matter of meteors consists in the power of the air.

But we proceed to the efficient cause of both, which Aristotle believes to be the cold of the middle air, in which he recognizes no heat; but Bede says the coldness of the night is the cause of both the freezing and its white form.

...and let it be granted that it is multiplied. Yet it does not necessarily follow that where air is contained within the cold earth, vapors and springs must also be produced there. For beyond all controversy, it is certain that there is no pore or cavity of the earth that is not filled with air; so subtle and penetrating is air, as it is the life and spirit of every thing. Indeed, even in water, the thickening and constriction of its parts is not so tight that it does not have air disseminated throughout its limbs <note>original: *artus*—a poetic way of describing the internal structure or 'joints' of the water</note> on every side. Furthermore, even if the free passage and succession of air through the pores of the earth were admitted, it would not follow that it would migrate first into vapor, and afterwards into liquid moisture or fluid. We have demonstrated through experience that if a tube of any substance is passed through a jar full of water, the simple air enclosed in the tube is nevertheless not easily observed to convert into vapor, much less into water. Much less would air enclosed in the veins of the earth do so, since the dryness of the earth is more opposed to such a function (namely, the condensation of vapor into fluid water) than water is. But if the cause of vapor migrating into the nature of water in the caverns of the earth were water itself (which is resolved into vapor by the force of heat), then that labor would be in vain; for it is possible that water itself, in its own whole form or nature, without such a reduction, could be raised from the bowels of the earth—which the abyss of the sea usually replenishes anew—into the heights to the location of springs through the veins of the earth. The confirmation of this matter is explained primarily by the two following brilliant demonstrations, and is then supported by the authority of the Sacred Scriptures. As for the first visual experiment, it is found in Hero’s *Pneumatics* <note>original: *Heronis spirital.*—refers to the *Pneumatica* of Hero of Alexandria, a 1st-century engineer</note>, Section 1, where the "bent siphon" is discussed and is illustrated thus:

G.**, such as at **K.**, the water flows, because the part of the balance or arm **K. B.** becomes heavier than that of **B. L.**, it may exit through the orifice **L.**, and thus it will empty that water entirely.

Hence we see that admirable connection and contiguity which exists primarily between water and air: when air is drawn, it is necessary for water to follow, so that a vacuum is not admitted—which is a truly horrible thing in the nature of things. Furthermore, we see that firm continuity which exists between water and water, such that one part included cannot flow, either upward or downward, without the other part closely adhering to it, for the reason of the aforementioned admission of a vacuum.

# Section I, Portion IV, Part II, Book III, Member II.
## Concerning Manna.

Both the Heathens <note>original: *Ethnici*; referring to non-Christian philosophers of antiquity, such as Aristotle or Pliny.</note> and the Christians well-versed in pagan philosophy have admitted that the substance of **Manna** is a certain honey-like dew descending from the sky. However, they also affirm—vainly nursing their own imaginary fantasies—that the origin of this same dew is from the earth and water, specifically from a very rich and viscous vapor. They claim it arises from a mixture of water and earth as soon as the air is exhaled from the interior elements, which then falls back upon plants by congealing like sugar or a very sweet flour. In this opinion of theirs, they always seem to establish the foundations of their philosophy on somewhat erroneous bases, deriving visible things from visible things rather than from the invisible. This is despite the fact that the matter stands quite differently according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, by which we are taught (as has been frequently cited before) that it must be believed through faith that visible things were first made from those that are invisible <note>A reference to Hebrews 11:3: "Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear."</note>. Therefore, we say that **Manna** is a dense species of **Meteor** <term>Meteor: In the 17th century, this term referred to any atmospheric phenomenon (rain, snow, dew, or lightning), not just space rocks.</term>, produced by the thickening of celestial air drenched in moisture. *Does not a certain excellent philosopher say,* he asks, *I pray you, consider a simple cloud of water: Who would ever believe that it contains within itself everything that the world holds—hard stones, salts, air, earth, fire—and yet it appears as simple water?* Thus he spoke. But indeed, in the places previously brought forward, we have sufficiently and clearly proved, by reasons established in the Holy Bible, that vapors, clouds, and their waters are formed from the condensation of simple air and brought forth into the world.

We have therefore deemed it necessary to describe **Manna** according to the laws of holy testimony in this manner:
**Manna** is a fatty substance of the air, which—when the gates of heaven are opened and the divine treasury is revealed—descends from the clouds by divine command in the manner of dew or frost. It grows into a minute appearance, round like a white coriander seed, and falls to the earth to execute the will of the Creator.

Or thus,
**Man** <note>The Hebrew name for Manna.</note> is heavenly bread, the wheat of heaven, spiritual food, the food of angels, and the very word proceeding from the mouth of Jehovah. It descends from the sky and the clouds in the manner of a dewy rain—either together with the celestial dew or upon the dew—onto the surface of the earth by divine power. It appears in a minute and round form, similar to a humped frost or a coriander seed, congealing there into hardness so that it might serve as food, nourishment, and even medicine for men.

In our first description, you have the **material cause** of Manna expressed, insofar as it is described there as being a fatty substance of the air. Next, the **formal cause** is expressed in that it is said to grow into a minute appearance, round like a coriander seed. Then, afterwards, we declared its **efficient cause** to be the divine command—that is, the power and the Word. Finally, we affirm the **final cause** <note>These four "causes"—Material, Formal, Efficient, and Final—are the standard Aristotelian framework used by Renaissance scholars to fully explain the nature of any object or phenomenon.</note> of its descent or generation to be the execution of the Creator’s will. You have all these parts of our description confirmed specifically from the pages of Holy Scripture in this way: For regarding the **material cause**, *God says to the Israelites: Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you (Exodus 16:4).* And elsewhere, *He gave them heavenly bread to eat (John 6:31).* And elsewhere, *He had commanded the clouds from above and opened the doors of heaven, and had rained down Manna upon them.* By these it is clearly enough declared that the matter of Manna itself is of an aerial composition, since by the word "heaven" the air is understood, as it is the place of the clouds which Jehovah commanded. Whence the treasury-chest of Manna, in which it is reserved and from which it is fashioned as a substance, is the air itself. The **form** is also explained by these words: *And in the morning the dew lay round about the host; and when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground (Exodus 16:14).* And elsewhere: *The Manna was as coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.* And elsewhere: *Its taste was as the taste of fresh oil (Numbers 11:7).* Furthermore, the **efficient** or creating **cause** is confirmed by these words: *I (says Jehovah) rain bread from heaven for you (Exodus 16:4).* And elsewhere: *He had commanded the clouds from above and opened the doors of heaven, and had rained down Manna upon them.* Finally, the **end** <note>The "Final Cause" or purpose.</note> of this kind of meteor is explained where it is said: *He fed thee with Manna... that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word, etc. (Deuteronomy 8:3).* And elsewhere: *Thou feddest thine own people with angels' food, and didst send them from heaven bread prepared without their labor, able to content every man's delight, and agreeing to every taste (Wisdom 16:20).* And elsewhere: *He gave them heavenly bread to eat (John 6:31).*

We conclude, therefore, that in addition to all these things, you have the place of generation of this kind of divine nourishment in our said description: namely, that it descends from the clouds when the gates of heaven are opened and the divine treasury is revealed. For it is written: *Behold, I rain bread from heaven for you (Exodus 16).* And elsewhere: *He had commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven, and rained down Manna upon them (Psalm 78:25).*

In the second definition also, you have the four causes of this kind of meteor exactly explained. But that **material cause** is explained in a more hidden way: through the "bread" and "wheat of heaven," through "spiritual food," "angels' food," and indeed even through the "material word." The **efficient cause** of this we establish as Jehovah himself. The place from which it is taken is the heaven and the clouds. The mode of emanation is indicated, and at the same time the **formal cause**: namely, that it descends upon the surface of the earth in the manner of a dewy rain, or together with celestial dew, or upon the dew, congealing into hardness in a minute and round form, like a humped frost or coriander seed. Finally, its **final cause** is explained therein, in that it serves men as both food and nourishment, as well as medicine.

But I know there will be many who will not hesitate to object that the Manna cited from the holy scriptures, by means of which the Israelites were nourished in the desert, was something miraculous and not at all natural, and con—

Wisdom 12.* <note>original: "Spiritus DEI incorruptibilis est in omni re."</note> We say, therefore, that the God Jehovah is both the mediate and the immediate efficient cause of a matter of such great importance, inasmuch as He is the *Alpha and Omega*, between whose prior and posterior acts there is no distinction or separation in essence, since as He is permanent in Himself, so also His actions are permanent. 

But (my good Peripatetics) <note>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who generally sought naturalistic, mechanical explanations for the weather based on the "four qualities" (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> if it were true that the influences of the heavens or the stars were the authors of such a lightning-meteor, I would most gladly know whether there was thunder in the world before the creation of the heavenly hosts or not? And yet we can most easily gather from the sense of the sacred letters—through the passages to be cited by us a little further below where mention of thunder will be made—that **GOD** spoke through thunder even in the beginning of the creation of the world; from which it follows that such an opinion is not well-founded. And although it may be confirmed by the more skillful of the Astrologers, taught by experience, that thunders are heard after certain aspects of some planets, it does not follow that this happens by necessity, because we observe that such effects by no means always follow such planetary aspects. For it is in the power of **GOD**, to whom alone it is given to act according to His will, sometimes using His planetary instruments—namely, by directing His countenance from His solar tabernacle toward this or that planet, or many at once—sometimes by means of His winds, whose duty it is to obey their commander. And we observe this to happen very often with no heavenly cause evidently preceding it, sometimes by means of fiery or watery spirits and demons performing the commands of the creator, and in infinite other hidden ways, which would be impossible for even the most skilled Astrologer to explore. However, in what way and by what means **GOD** operates to produce meteors in the world, we have proposed to speak more clearly below, where the natural efficient cause is treated.

Finally, I would wish you to briefly receive what the thunderstone is according to the intention of the sacred scriptures.

A thunderbolt <note>original: *Telum fulmineum*</note> is a javelin or stony arrow which, like the breath of fiery coals, is ignited from the mouth of Jehovah as if from passing torches, and is sent down from the clouds, either for the public punishment of the impious or for the hidden benefit of those born of the earth.

That the stony javelin, arrow, and weapon of Jehovah exists, we gather from these places: *Jehovah thundered from heaven, and the most High gave his voice; he sent out his arrows, and scattered them; he lightened and consumed them. 2 Samuel 22.* <note>The text cites 2 Reg. 21, following an older numbering system where the books of Samuel and Kings were grouped together.</note> Where it is manifest that he understood thunder-weapons by "arrows," since he speaks afterward of lightning. Similarly elsewhere: *Bow thy heavens, O Jehovah, and come down: touch the mountains, and they shall smoke; cast forth thy lightning, and scatter them: shoot out thine arrows, and destroy them. Psalm 144:5.* Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: *The shafts of lightning go directly from the clouds as if from a well-drawn bow, etc. Wisdom 5:22.* Moreover, elsewhere these are called the little stones of Jehovah. As for its form, where it is said that it is ignited like the breath of fiery coals from the mouth of Jehovah, as if from passing torches, it is confirmed by this testimony: *By his neesings* (says Job) *a light doth shine, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning... his breath kindleth coals, and a flame goeth out of his mouth. Job 41:18.*

Furthermore, it is clear from these things already recited what its efficient cause is: namely, Jehovah Himself through His hot and flashing breath. Finally, its end <term>End: In this context, the "final cause" or purpose for which a thing exists.</term> is explained in such a definition: namely, for the punishment of the rebellious. Whence it is said: *Shoot out thine arrows and destroy them, Psalm 144.* And elsewhere: *He sent out his arrows and scattered them, 2 Samuel, etc.*

But lest anyone should foolishly reply that these words previously cited were brought forth from the sacred page concerning divine thunder and not at all natural thunder, we respond that this can be understood concerning *all* thunder; for without such an efficient cause, no meteor can be produced anew, neither according to the order of nature nor against the laws of nature—indeed, nothing at all in the nature of things—just as we shall make fuller mention in the chapter on thunder and lightning.

**On dust descending from heaven.**

The matter of this kind of meteor <note>In this period, a "meteor" was any atmospheric phenomenon, such as rain, snow, or falling dust, not just a shooting star.</note> differs very little from that of a thunderbolt; however, they are different in form. The substance of the thunderbolt is solid and compact, whereas the dust is dissipated into infinite parts. The efficient cause <term>Efficient cause: The agent or force that brings something into being; here, God is identified as the direct creator of these events.</term> is the same as before, namely the LORD Jehovah, and the final purpose is one of vengeance—specifically, as a punishment for the sins of the rebellious. For this reason, Moses says: *The LORD shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust; from heaven shall it come down upon thee, until thou be destroyed.* Deuteronomy 28:24. <note>The original Latin text cites verse 23: "Efficiet Iehoua ut terra tua sit puluisculus... Deut. 28, 23." In modern Bibles, this is Deuteronomy 28:24.</note>

**On worms, lice, birds, and frogs.**

These monstrous meteors, along with blood, sometimes descend from the clouds because of the sins of men. You will find the Holy Scriptures and other authors are full of accounts of the arrival of such meteors; indeed, you even have these confirmed by experience, though it be rare. From these examples, we can understand clearly enough that the air (which is "invisible water") is capable of being converted into any nature according to the divine disposition: namely into worms, lice, birds, frogs, blood, and so on.

But we also find this confirmed by the Holy Bible, where we read: *In the word was life, and that was the light of men, John 1.* <note>original: "In verbo erat vita, & illa erat lux hominum"</note> And elsewhere: *the holy spirit of discipline fills the circle of the earth,* and again: *the incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing, Wisdom 1.* <note>original: "spiritus DEI incorruptibilis est in omni re"</note> And elsewhere: *Christ is all and in all.* And elsewhere: *he placed his tabernacle in the sun,* <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4, often interpreted by Christian Hermeticists as the divine light residing in the heart of the solar system.</note> and elsewhere: *Christ is the light of the world,* and is the beginning, the word from which all things come and without which there is nothing. By the Cabalists, <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that Fludd integrated into his Christian philosophy.</note> this hidden principle is called the <term>Dark Aleph</term> <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"; the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing the divine potential before it is revealed as light.</note>, but when it manifested itself in the quickening of the world, it was called the <term>Luminous Aleph</term>. <note>original: "Aleph lucidum"</note> Similarly, they called this divine soul, which turns everywhere, the angel Metatron, <note>original: "Mitattron"</note> who is considered by some to be the angel Michael, the leader of souls; to him, the more skilled among the Magi assigned the protection and governance of the solar planet, and not without good reason. Moses describes the appearance of such an Archangel with a fiery face, in whom the name of Jehovah is said to reside. In the Apocalypse, <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> he is described as *having a golden sash girded about his chest, and eyes like flames of fire, holding in his right hand seven stars, whose face shone like the Sun in its full strength, Revelation 1:13.* From this it is argued that this angel is the fountain of light, as he illuminates the seven stars or planets, and he seems to carry the very image of the Sun (whom Plato did not hesitate to call the visible son of God). Similarly, it was said of this angel: *The angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, approaching, rolled back the stone and sat upon it; his appearance was like lightning, Matthew 28:3.* And Ezekiel saw *living creatures present before God, in the likeness of flashing lightning, Ezekiel 1:14.* Is it not also said elsewhere: *Wisdom is brighter than the sun and more precious, Wisdom 7,* and that *when compared to light, she is found to be prior to every arrangement of the stars?* But who is that wisdom? Is it not that uncreated light, the Word or Christ, who is truly the light of the world, the life of creatures, and the soul of the world? So it is also said of the person of the great God Jehovah: *clouds were kindled before the brightness in his presence, 2 Kings 22.* 

And certainly, if we contemplate the sacred scriptures a little more carefully, we will perceive that this universally animating spirit is a soul prone to both corruption and generation and preservation. Hence Jehovah said of this same angel or eternal wisdom: *Behold, I send an angel before you to lead you into that place which I have prepared; take heed of his face and listen to his voice; do not embitter him, for he will not bear your desertion, because my name is in him. Exodus 23:20.* From this we argue that just as that spirit was preserving, nourishing, and guiding the life and steps of men, so it is capable of being turned into a destructive nature to punish the sins of men. Thus it happened that sometimes, in the form of a pillar of fire, he offered comfort to the Israelites and provided them with everything necessary for life, health, and clothing; yet sometimes he punished lethally with the fiery heat of his countenance. Whence it is written in *Leviticus 10:12: Fire coming out from the presence of Jehovah consumed them, and they died.* For this reason, in such a nature, he is called *the Lord God a consuming fire, Deuteronomy 9.* And elsewhere: *the spirit of the power of God winnowing, and justice pursuing the unjust, Wisdom 11:21.* And elsewhere: *The wrath of God is kindled and shaken, and the earth is moved, and the foundations of the mountains are moved and shaken when smoke ascends through his nose and a consuming fire from his mouth, Psalm 18:8.* <note>Fludd cites this as Psalm 21:10, following a different numbering system.</note> As Jehovah thunders in the heavens *and the Most High utters his voice, and casting forth lightnings, he scatters them.* And elsewhere: *The wrath of Jehovah is like a consuming fire.* And so it is in countless other places, where God—by means of a certain flashing and lightning spirit proceeding from him—is accustomed to act for the ruin and destruction of both the members of the Macrocosm <note>The universe as a whole.</note> and of men, on account of the sins of the impious. 

But conversely, for the preservation of pious men, he benevolently sends out his illuminating spirit. Hence David said: *Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me to the mountain of your holiness, Psalm 43:3.* And elsewhere: *Let your face shine upon your servant; save me by your kindness, Psalm 31:17.* Such also was that luminous spirit which descended upon the Apostles in the form of cloven tongues; indeed, such was that God-formed spirit which God breathed into the face of Adam, of which Job also speaks: *the spirit of the mighty God made me, and the breath or inspiration of the Almighty gave me life, Job 33:4.* Truly, such was that Universal Spirit <note>original: "spiritus ille Catholicus"; 'Catholic' here means universal or all-pervading.</note> which in the beginning of creation was carried over the waters, imparting to them fiery vigor and life-like quality. This spirit seems to manifest itself visibly in certain creatures, but only when "clothed" in garments and not in its simple nature—for no one can gaze upon God in his naked essence and live. Specifically, it manifests in the sun, stars, and all clearly luminous <term>meteors</term>, <note>In Fludd's time, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon including lightning, rainbows, and comets.</note> as well as in metals, which are nothing other than an aerial or ethereal spirit animated by divine brightness. 

However, for the most part, the brightness of this divine spirit remains hidden and is recognized only by its effect: namely, in animals and plants, and even in water and air. Thus, clearly flashing meteors—for example, a comet, lightning, a <term>will-o'-the-wisp</term> <note>original: "Ignis fatuus"</note>, etc.—even though they seem to be extinguished and consumed, are not actually consumed or extinguished. Instead, they truly vanish into the air, and their luminous form is made invisible by expansion. And this is the reason why a comet, a burning lance, "leaping goats," <note>original: "capræ saltantes"; a historical term for a type of flickering atmospheric light or meteor.</note> beams, lightning, etc., mostly produce their hidden effects long after their disappearance—namely, plague, famine, war, or fertility—according to the pleasure and inscrutable ordination of the Creator. I would not have you believe there is any extinction or destruction of this divine spirit (whether it flashes hiddenly or openly), for it is in every way free from suffering in itself; for *the word of God will remain forever,* however it may be variously disposed in this world according to the will of the eternal Disposer.

What, therefore, should be thought of that vain opinion of the Pagans, <note>original: "Ethnicorum"; referring primarily to Aristotle and his followers.</note> by which they claimed such a spirit—as well as lightnings, comets, and other fiery impressions—were merely hot and dry exhalations, sublimated from the womb of the earth to either the lowest, middle, or highest region of the air?

We also affirm (as we did previously regarding the rest) that their assertion is unsuitable, because this divine splendor is not absent from the air; for it is nothing other than the **moist fire of nature**, or a **dilated fire**, which by the divine will contracts itself and puts on the moist and dark garment of **Chaos**, becoming a cloud. Or, by manifesting what was hidden, it becomes a luminous mass, as in **Comets**; or a luminous spirit quickly vanishing, like a **flash of lightning**; or penetrating more deeply, like a **thunderbolt**. Let it not seem at all absurd to anyone that I call the flashing, lightning-like, and thundering spirit an **animating and illuminating spirit**. For it is most certain that this kind of spirit—or rather, the central light—is of such excellence and of such profound thought in the nature of things that it claims for itself a place equal to the **internal agent** of an **Angel** dwelling in the innermost part of the human soul. This can be gathered from the words of a certain wise man, well-versed in the mysteries of nature and <term>theosophy</term> <note>Divine wisdom; in Fludd's time, this referred to a mystical insight into the nature of God and the cosmos.</note>, which are as follows: *God created the angels from the spiritual elements of the fire of the **First Matter**, which surpasses and exceeds human grasp and understanding. For this reason, they are much clearer and more splendid than spiritual bodies, which man can hardly admit or comprehend. For that very matter, which is the inner essence of life and consistency for the angelic and human soul and of the lightning-flash, is the very same that informs all things. Thus we see one perfectly mixed creature differ from another, even though the internal or central luminous agent is one and the same, regarding which it is written in *Wisdom 12:1*: *The incorruptible spirit is in every thing.* <note>original: "Spiritus incorruptibilis est in omnire"</note> Regarding this **uncreated wisdom**, the Apostle Paul also speaks: *From Him, and through Him are all things; to Him be praise and honor.* 

The rays of this first emanation from the luminous source were esteemed as gods by **Plato**, **Orpheus**, and other Platonists. Hence they considered all things to be full of gods; however, they referred all these gods to a single **Jupiter**, as their source and origin. In their action, if fiery demons interpose themselves, they produce thunders and lightnings simultaneously according to the will of the Creator. Consequently, the crashes of thunders cannot be produced in that place due to the lack of watery moisture, which ought to resist the impulse of the fiery spirits. Hence it happens that, because of the fiery disposition of the place, instead of dark clouds, fiery meteors are sometimes, though rarely, found there. These are not as massive as the bulk of clouds, since the thinness of the region's consistency cannot produce such a mass in its condensation. Furthermore, the winds are not vehement in that region, but are indeed scarcely sensible, because they find little or almost no resistance there due to the thinness and dryness of the region's consistency. And this is especially to be considered: that fiery spirits always mix themselves with a substance of their own nature and illuminate it, in the manner of that royal spirit who placed his tabernacle in the sun. These lucid spirits receive their splendor from that lucid source reigning everywhere invisibly, and chiefly in his solar tabernacle, from which the lucid power of life is not only flashed forth upon the stars and every other lucid creature, but is even attributed to the angels themselves. It is their office to accommodate the lights received from the source of light to their own proper spheres, from which these lights are then imparted to and poured into the elements. The elemental demons receive and drink in these lights, and according to the divine will, pour them forth into the elements either visibly or invisibly. These outpourings include light, motion, and those "influences" described by Aristotle. These things having been considered, we descend to the general description of comets and of any fiery impressions as follows:

A Comet or *Assub* <term>Assub|An Arabic-derived term used in medieval and Renaissance science to denote a falling star or a specific type of fiery meteor.</term> of the superior order is an aerial body, gathered and condensed in the upper region of the same by angelic breath, animated and inspired by a lucid spirit through the rays of divine wisdom acting via His angelic ministers, ordained by the sacrosanct name of said wisdom according to the will of the Father or Creator to be perfected here in the earth, waters, and air, and finally, after dissolution, expanded invisibly through the common air.

In this description of a fiery impression of the superior order, the material cause of the same is first expressed: namely, that it is drawn from the source of the air and from its very summit and purer part. ...measure? *Job 28:25.* <note>original: "pondus ventis... et aquas in mensura"</note> By these words, he seems to suggest that God sometimes creates winds out of the air by thinning it, and at other times creates water and clouds by condensing it; He establishes the laws for rain, and a path for the lightning of the thunders, and even the dense bodies of fiery impressions. Furthermore, it is written: *Who made the sapphire clouds by wisdom? Job 38:37.* And elsewhere: *the upper clouds by wisdom distil the dew. Psalm 78:14.* Or as we find in the Book of Wisdom: *Wisdom was a covering for the Israelites by day and a starlight by night. Wisdom 10:17.* Indeed, if I were to say that a fiery meteor is the tabernacle of Wisdom, fortified by its fiery ministers—which either looks upon the sins of men with a threatening eye and pursues them in its wrath with threats, or looks kindly in its mercy—you will perceive that this differs very little from the sense of the sacred letters. For it is written: *Wisdom was a covering for the Israelites by day, and a starlight by night. Wisdom 10.* Here, therefore, it looked mercifully upon the Israelites from its tabernacle, which was the Pillar of Fire (one of the primary types of fiery impressions). So also from a tabernacle of this kind—namely, the body of a comet—Wisdom shone forth and by its light directed the Magi or wise men of the East to the place where Christ the Savior of the world was born. But on the other hand, it is written that fire, coming out from the presence of Jehovah—or Wisdom, or the Angel in whom was the name of Jehovah—hidden in the pillar of cloud or fire, killed the sons of Aaron and they died. *Leviticus 10:2.* And elsewhere it is said: *The wrath of Jehovah was greatly kindled, and Fire went out from Jehovah, and consumed those two hundred and fifty men who offered incense, etc. Numbers 16:35.* And hence it is that Jehovah in His wrath is called a consuming fire. *Deuteronomy 4:24.* And so it is certain that GOD is accustomed not only to kill sinners visibly by fire sent forth from a fiery meteor, but also to wound them by dispersing it invisibly and to stir up a foul plague among men by means of His angelic instruments; by such a fiery scourge seventy thousand men of the Israelites died invisibly, by the striking and smiting Angel of GOD. *2 Samuel 24:16.* So also we see that the substance of a comet, being invisibly dissipated through the air, frequently produces plagues, and famine, and drought of the earth, as is declared by the effect. But I would have you understand that there are undoubtedly very many Comets and other fiery impressions in the air which are entirely invisible to men, both in their rising and their effect; these are, beyond all controversy, the causes of various epidemic diseases, as is discussed more copiously in the chapter *On the Invisible Luminous Meteor.* We say, therefore, that GOD, by means of His flaming angelic ministers (among whom we recognize Wisdom as the chief and primary), is the efficient cause not only of every fiery Meteor but also of the watery ones, and every other kind. And although the Peripatetics and many others ascribe such a duty to the stars and the element of fire, and the coldness of the middle region of the air, yet it is the part of a true Christian to attribute such acts to the [First] Act: namely, to give to God what is of God, and by no means to arrogantly claim them for created things. From the lack of such consideration, so great a perversity of Idolatry arose among the Heathens, and the neglect of the worship of the true God; to this error must be attributed the fact that almost every nation of the Barbarians set about inventing and establishing a new God for themselves.

The purpose, moreover, we have established to be for the perfecting of the divine will.

*...light over the ends or borders of the earth. After it a sound roars; He thunders with the voice of His majesty, and He does not restrain them when His voice is heard. God thunders marvelously with His voice, etc. Job 37.* <note>original: *Iob. 37*; referring to Job 37:3-5.</note>
By these things, therefore—contrary to the foolish opinions of the Pagans—it is demonstrated that neither exhalations nor vapors, nor the sun with the stars, nor earth or water, nor the elements, nor created nature itself, but God Himself, who is the worker of all wonders, is the immediate efficient cause <term>efficient cause; the agent or force that actually produces an effect</term> of these marvels. This we also have confirmed by Holy Scripture, lest we falsely attribute to nature, or its elements, or things made of elements, those things which are to be attributed to the Creator first and above all; for in doing so, we might unexpectedly cast ourselves headlong into foul idolatry along with the Pagans.

But I know well that it will be objected by some that thunders of this kind, of which the Holy Scriptures speak, were miraculous and not at all natural. Both modern and ancient philosophers fall into this opinion: namely, that Thunders are sometimes natural and sometimes supernatural. It is as if those things which are perfected in the moist nature of the world are not made immediately by GOD, just as much as those which happen according to the season of the year or the hot intemperance of summer, or those which occur in winter or by other hidden reasons. For it cannot be unknown to a true Christian that GOD is everywhere, and has His dwelling both in the elements themselves and in things made of elements. For in the highest heaven He is clothed with light as with a garment; in the middle of heaven He placed His tabernacle in the Sun; in the lowest region He made the thick cloud His pavilion—indeed, as Job witnesses: *Jehovah answered him out of the whirlwind.* Furthermore, He is also in the earth, *For the earth shall bring forth a Savior.* He speaks in the Prophet and through the mouth of the Prophet; indeed, GOD uses any thing of this world as His instrument <term>organo; literally "organ," meaning a tool or medium through which an agent acts</term>, and speaks in various ways according to the variety of the instrument. In the simple spirit of the world, His voice is neither heard nor understood except by the illuminated or those stirred by the spirit; He speaks in the angels and through the mediation of angelic instruments; but to mortals, He most often speaks terribly in His wrath—that is, in thunder. Whence Job says: *Hear with trembling the voice going out of His mouth under the whole heaven and the light over the ends of the earth. Job 37.* Therefore, those philosophers are of unsound mind who distinguish thunders into "vain and brute"—those which seem to signify nothing—and "prophetic and significant." For thunders should not be called vain, brute, or insignificant simply because the intention of God (who produced nothing in the world in vain) is not revealed to them in their production. O how occult are the mysteries of GOD, and how hidden from the knowledge of profane men! Neither can I praise the skill of Cicero in this matter, who in his book *On Divination* <note>original: *Lib. De Diuinat.*; Marcus Tullius Cicero's *De Divinatione*, a skeptical treatise on Roman religion.</note> seems to deny that any species of divination can arise from the observation of lightnings—and that quite thoughtlessly—but makes it out to be vain and empty. And yet we are taught the opposite by the Holy Bible, where it is found written: *That God is great, surpassing our knowledge; He spreads out the clouds as His tent according to His pleasure, and lightnings flash from His light above; He covers the depths of the sea, for by these He judges the people, and gives food to many mortals; in His hands He hides the light, and commands it to come again, etc. Job 36.* From which it will be right to gather that GOD flashes lightning to execute justice upon mortals, and also turns lightnings into rain for the benefit of mortals. Whence also it is said elsewhere: *When He utters His voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens; He causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth; He makes lightnings for the rain, and brings forth the wind out of His treasures. Jeremiah 51:15.* From this it is clear that there is no thunder unless it be the voice of Jehovah. Whence the royal Psalmist speaks generally of thunder in these words: *The voice of Jehovah is upon the waters; the GOD of glory thunders; the voice of Jehovah is upon many waters; the voice of Jehovah is powerful and in His majesty; the voice of Jehovah is full of beauty; the voice of Jehovah breaks the cedars, even Jehovah breaks the cedars of Lebanon, and makes them skip like a calf, Lebanon and Sirion like a young wild ox; the voice of Jehovah divides the flames of fire; the voice of Jehovah shakes the wilderness; the voice of Jehovah makes the deer to calve and strips the forests bare; but in His temple everyone speaks of His glory, etc. Psalm 29.* Here the King mentions the terrible voice of Jehovah, and that peaceful one.

We conclude, therefore, that it is the greatest folly of any Christian, and indeed an irrecoverable madness, to place such great faith in the vain and lying opinions of the Pagans, who toss about empty words concerning thunder. These men try to persuade people that thunders and lightnings are, as it were, accidental things, arising from the natural intemperance of the heavens and not at all sent by divine power. Thus, looking only at the effect, they delight in falsely taking it for the efficient cause. That is, they wish to attribute to creatures what belongs to God, the Creator of every thing; and so they proceed not only to babble thoughtlessly but to blaspheme impiously, leading men to idolatry, as if one were to attribute the life of a man to his body and not to his soul. Therefore, I would have you know that I have written in this place not at all rashly, but diligently, and supported by good foundations. Other philosophers, deeper in the abstruse mystery of Jehovah, seem to agree with this; for considering the admirable operation of the lightning bolt, they judged it to be not a work of nature, but the immediate effect of the highest GOD.

...[moist] intemperance of the air. I would wish that you listen to this warning of ours, and not reject it as futile or hold it as nothing, if we shall prove that lightning and thunder proceed immediately from God. In performing this duty of mine, I will provide not only solace to you in your tribulation, but also offer glory and honor to God my creator.

Know therefore how the wise of this world—the followers of the Pagan philosophers—rave, have raved, and will continue to rave in their obstinacy. They do not concede that God works all in all, and that His word moves, stirs, and preserves all things. Instead, they ascribe these things to created nature, pretending that God acts out of necessity through means, and indeed through <term>secondary and tertiary causes; the idea that God sets natural laws in motion which then produce effects on their own</term>. Thus erring, they are unwilling to understand further that God works solely through His word, and not through other necessary means; and so, He works by no means through those causes alleged by them, but only in them as if through instruments.

But you, nourished in the Holy Bible and governed by the law of Christ, I advise you to conceive and forever revolve within yourselves that God created the first substance—namely, water—as wet or moist through His word. This very substance remains moist today after the lapse of so many thousands of years. Again, from this water, heaven and earth (as Saint Peter witnesses) were created by means of the word. Furthermore, in heaven He produced light, the sun, moon, and stars, day and night, and all other created things by His said word, and He imposed their services upon them. Therefore, all those things perform their duties according to that word. Where then is the nature of the <term>Peripatetics; the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught</term> which is said to accomplish these things? There is clearly nothing anywhere except the unique and sole word of God, which works these and all other things, according to that saying of the Evangelist: *By the word all things were made, and without it, nothing was made; in it was life, etc. John 1.* <note>original: *Ioan. 1*</note> From which it is clear that without Him nothing can exist or act.

Insofar as the air is part of the celestial substance, it follows that it was made by the word, and swims, so to speak, in the word—as that which encompasses all things—and is moved and governed by the word of God itself. Indeed, even in the air itself, as in God's universal treasure chest, He has His peculiar chambers from which various species of <term>meteors; in the 17th century, this term referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning</term> are produced. These He placed under the protection and governance of various angels and spirits (who were also created from the air and in the air through the word), as is right to gather from various places in Holy Scripture to be cited by us below. By their administration (with the Word moving and working), all meteors are produced in the air, and all storms wonderfully arise which are accustomed to happen to the world. Hence it is said that *He made His angels winds, and His ministers a flaming fire, etc.* 

Thus, at the beginning of the world, God created the angels together with the air, who perform and execute their duty and office in the air concerning the direction of storms, rain, snow, hail, frost, clouds, lightning, thunder, fire, <term>chasms; original: *chasmatum*, referring to openings in the sky or auroral phenomena</term>, thunderbolts, waters, heat, cold, moisture, dryness, and many other things of that kind. And this very thing happens today by His word, all of which will be more clearly declared by us in our following Portion, where the <term>efficient cause; the agent or power that brings something into being</term> of meteors will be treated. This is indeed unknown to Pagan philosophers and their Christian followers, in whose mouths and writings a lying and false spirit has claimed a seat for itself. From this, their ignorance and the vanity of philosophy have arisen; nor is it a wonder, since they knew neither God nor His most holy word. Despising or at least not reading the Holy Scripture, but only leaning on their own ravings, they are accustomed to sew lie upon lie. 

If these Christian disciples of the Pagan Peripatetics had read the Holy Bible with the same zeal as they turned over the false Aristotelian books and volumes, they would have found the truth about the air and storms—that it is not in the way those men wrote in their books filled with imaginations. Rather, for these species already mentioned, God has His peculiar treasure chests in the open air, from which He produces winds and storms, and that the air swims and consists in the word of God, and is led by the angels appointed for this purpose, with the word of God directing, when, where, and how God wills. Whence David said: *The angels of God, most strong in power, doing His word, listening to the voice of His speech, ministers doing His pleasure, Psalm 103:20.* <note>original: *Psal. 103. 20*</note> Do we not also read of the prince having power over the air? <note>A reference to Ephesians 2:2, distinguishing the "prince of the power of the air" from God's holy ministers.</note>

It is vital that the children of God truly and fundamentally know and understand the reason for storms and other operations—not by their own motion, or by chance, nor even in such an imaginary way as the Pagans posit and feign in their writings, but that they proceed from divine providence and the chambers of divine treasures, and are sent down upon this lower world. Thus, if ever dangerous storms arise, they may invoke God, that He might wish to mercifully turn away that danger and in its place grant kind rain, and at the same time defend, protect, and preserve the fruits of the earth along with men and cattle from all evil. By adhering to their testimonies, it is necessary that you depart from the fountain of truth.
