### On the Formal Cause of Meteors. 129

In this description, we make the **material cause** of the **prester** <note>original: *presteris*; a term for a fiery whirlwind or a pillar of lightning.</note> out of fiery or sulfurous rain; however, we establish **Jehovah** himself as the **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings something into being.</note>, as it is He who creates it as if anew from nothing, or brings it forth from the treasury of God, or from the invisible treasury of the air. The **formal cause** <note>The "formal cause" refers to the essential nature or shape of a thing.</note> is explained by the fact that it is called a rain that is not watery, but fiery and sulfurous. Finally, we have expressed its **end** <note>The "final cause" or purpose.</note> in that it is usually brought forth for the punishment and destruction of the wicked.

By the testimony of the Holy Scriptures, we can prove all these causes of the prester in this manner. First, we find these things written by the Royal Psalmist: *Jehovah shall rain upon the wicked coals, fire and sulfur, and a wind joined with various whirlwinds. Psalm 11:6.* <note>original: *Pf. 11. 6.*</note> Here the Prophet expresses the matter as well as the form, and also the efficient cause and the end. He expresses the **matter** in that he says "coals, fire, and sulfur"; and in these words, he also distinguishes the prester from other watery rain by a sufficiently clear **form**. Then afterward, he places the **efficient cause** not as the sun—which is merely a creature—but Jehovah the Creator, who acts immediately in all things. Finally, he establishes the **end**, which is to torment the wicked and affect them with death. Regarding the effect of this kind of meteor, David writes elsewhere: *As fire burns the forest, as a flame sets the mountains ablaze, so pursue them with your tempest, and terrify them with your whirlwind.* Here the Prophet seems to take the prester as a species of whirlwind. Similarly, Moses describes the effect of such a meteor in these express words: *With sulfur and salt the land is so burnt that it can neither be sown nor sprout, nor can any herb grow upon it. Deut. 29:23.* Finally, in Genesis, the parts of our aforementioned description are confirmed in plain and open words: *Jehovah (says the text) sent down from the heavens a rain of sulfur and fire upon the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, which overthrew the cities and the entire plain, and all the inhabitants and the offspring of the earth, because of the wickedness of those dwelling there.*

Therefore, it will appear most clearly to a wise person who diligently considers these things we have brought forward, how vain is the opinion of the **Pagan Philosophers** and their Christian followers in this matter. Moreover, when the text says "from the heavens," it understands the heavens to be the "inner chambers of the air," which we have declared in the preceding sections to be the **treasury-chest of all meteors**. These words of the high priest confirm this: *Jehovah shall open to you his best treasury, the heavens, by giving rain in its season. Deut. 28:12.* And it is said elsewhere: *Have you entered into the treasuries of the snow? Or have you beheld the treasuries of the hail? Job 38:22.* And so it is with the rest; where it is certain that God has His own treasury-chests for every species of meteor, and that they are brought forth from hidden power into manifest action according to the pleasure of the Creator. Certainly, this our disputation concerning the investigation of this kind of meteor ought not to seem irrelevant to the wise, in which, contrary to the opinion of the philosophers of this age, we attribute its generation to the Best and Greatest God, Jehovah, and not to accidental causes in nature, or created things such as the sun and stars, etc.

For since it is certain, and confirmed by the sacred text, that on the day of the last judgment the world will be deprived of its present form, destroyed, and purified by means of such a fiery flood, we think it must be diligently considered among the learned of the Christians that the error of such Pagan philosophers should be driven into exile from the Christian state, beyond the **Hyperborean mountains** <note>In classical mythology, the far northern "land beyond the north wind"; here used to mean extreme banishment.</note>, and handed over to the perpetual oblivion of good men. Specifically, the error that the cause of such a meteor (by means of which the world is to perish in the end, that is, to be changed and purged from its prior form through purification) usually arises from the earth by means of the heat of the sun and stars, and not from God, the Father of all wonders, to whom be praise and glory. Was it not for this reason that it was said *that the Son of Man shall come from the east to the west, in the manner of lightning and a consuming fire? Matthew 24.* So also Jehovah is called a *consuming fire, before whose sight nothing can endure, for the mountains melt like wax, etc. Deut. 4.* And yet the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> and the Christians who follow them wish for such power to arise solely from imaginary exhalations—but to the point.

Since the matter of the **whirlwind** or **Typhon** <note>original: *Typhonis*; a violent, smoky storm named after the Greek mythological giant of chaos.</note> is the same as that of the Prester, although it is observed to be sent forth from the heavens in a different form and smaller quantity, we therefore attribute the following description to it as well, by the consensus of the Holy Bible. First, we divide it into the **fiery or inflamed whirlwind**, and the **non-fiery** whirlwind, which rotates dust, straw, and sometimes larger things in a circle.

We describe the inflamed whirlwind from holy testimony as follows:

-> **The inflamed whirlwind is a fiery wind, rolled into a globe or wheel, which, proceeding by divine power from its inner chamber, as much from the Northern region as the Southern, and also the Southwest, is sometimes made into the vehicle of Jehovah.** <-

From this whirlwind, as if from a tabernacle, it pleases Him to appear to the saints, to speak to them, and sometimes even to snatch them up to Himself into heaven, and most often to send forth His vengeance upon the wicked. In this, the **material cause** is wind or fiery air; the **formal cause** is that inflamed air rolled into a wheel; the **place** is its inner chamber—that is, the cloud appropriated for its generation; the **efficient cause** is the power of Jehovah, by means of which it is brought out from His own treasuries; the **end** is that it may be the seat of the divine essence, and as it were a tent, from which He is accustomed to speak with His saints at times, and frequently to pour out punishments upon the wicked. We have also expressed the regions of the world from which it usually proceeds. And all these things we defend by the authority of the sacred context.

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors. 131

We, however, disagreeing greatly from those others <note>The author likely refers to Aristotelian natural philosophers who sought purely physical explanations for weather.</note>, say that the **material cause** is drawn from the treasury of God—that is, from the heavens or the air. We call the internal agent a certain <term>angelic spirit</term> <note>In this context, an angelic spirit refers to a non-physical intelligence or force acting as God's instrument in nature.</note> which the Spirit of Jehovah animates and is accustomed to stir in the waves to fulfill His will. Therefore, we describe a **sea storm** in this manner from the authority of Holy Scripture:

A **sea storm** is a disturbance of the sea caused by a whirlwind spirit (which Jehovah agitates by His word to fulfill His will in the waters). This consists of its waves being exalted even unto the heavens and then immediately depressed into the abyss, by means of which the soul of the sailor melts in distress, and all his wisdom is swallowed up; at last, unless Jehovah in His mercy causes the whirlwind to stand still in silence, he is swallowed by the surging waters, and thus perishes because of his sins.

In this description, we perceive that the **material cause** of the storm is the seawater, and the **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of the change or action; here, the author identifies God as the ultimate actor using the wind as a tool.</note> is Jehovah Himself, who disturbs the waters by means of His minister—namely, the whirlwind. The **form** of such a storm is depicted by the fact that the surges or waves are sometimes lifted up as if to the sky and soon cast down to the lowest depths. Finally, the **purpose** <note>The "final cause" or *finis*, explaining the moral or theological reason for the event.</note> of such an operation is explained: first, that to those who "go down to the sea in ships," it shows that the vigor of the human soul or the power of worldly wisdom is confounded and brought to ruin when the spirit of divine power opposes itself; secondly, that it is in God's hands either to impose silence upon that turbulent spirit and return it to rest along with the waves (when it pleases Him to have mercy on the sailors) or to continue to agitate and animate it until the ungodly are submerged. And we have this confirmed by the testimony of the royal Psalmist <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>, from whom we receive this discourse:

*Those who go down to the sea in ships see the works of Jehovah and His wonders in the deep. For He speaks, and He makes the spirit of the whirlwind stand forth, and it lifts up the waves of the sea; they mount up to the heaven, they go down to the abyss, so that their soul melts because of trouble; they are tossed and stagger like a drunken man, so that o—* <note>original: "Deſcendentes ad mare nauibus ipſi vident opera Iehouæ & mirabilia eius in profundo, dicitque, Et ſtare facit ſpiritum turbinis, & exaltat fluctus maris, aſcendunt vſque ad cœlum, deſcendunt vſque ad voraginem, ita vt anima eorum in malo liqueſcat, iactantur & nutant ſicut ebrii, ita vt o-" This is a Latin translation of Psalm 107:23–27.</note>

### CHAPTER XVI.

### First Part.

### On the Rainbow, or the heavenly arch.

By the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, which dominated medieval and early modern science.</note>, the Rainbow <note>original: "Iris"</note> is said to be an arc of varied color in a dewy, opaque, and concave cloud, appearing to the eyes of onlookers from the reflection of the rays of the sun positioned opposite it. They say that this phenomenon cannot be otherwise than arched or semicircular in its figure, although it is certain, and proven by experience, that an arc of this kind—according to the testimony of Holy Scripture—sometimes encircles the sky in a complete circuit, just as is demonstrated to the eye in our meteorographic mirror. <note>The author refers to a "meteorographic mirror," likely a specific diagram or optical demonstration found elsewhere in his work to prove the rainbow can form a full circle.</note>

In this description of theirs, therefore, they establish the **material cause** <note>The physical substance of a thing.</note> from which (or in which) it is made as the dewy, opaque, and concave cloud; they explain the **Formal cause** <note>The essential nature or shape that defines a thing.</note> by saying it is an arc of varied color; and they make the **Efficient cause** <note>The primary agent or force that produces an effect.</note> the solar rays, from whose reflection it becomes visible to the eyes of those watching.

We, however, gather from the text of the Holy Scriptures that the Rainbow can be described by a **Christian Philosopher** in this manner:

The Rainbow is the circle or arc of GOD, exceedingly glorious in its splendor, which the hand of the Most High has so extended and placed in the clouds on a day of rain, that it might be a sign of the covenant <note>A reference to the biblical account in Genesis 9, where the rainbow serves as a promise from God to Noah.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the study of the rainbow, contrasting the Aristotelian definition (based on reflection in clouds) with a theological definition that views the rainbow as a "glorious circle of God" and a sign of the divine covenant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Rainbow, moving from the definitions provided on the previous page to a direct rebuttal of Aristotle's physical theories, arguing instead for a more spiritual and experimental understanding of light and color.</meta>

136 Section I. Part IV. Book III. Member III.

...yielding; which is why, contrary to the opinions of the Peripatetic philosophers <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of thought.</note>, it is not required that the rainbow be formed in the concavity of an opaque cloud. Indeed, it is very often observed to appear in air that is sufficiently dense yet diaphanous <note>original: "diaphano," meaning semi-transparent or translucent</note> and transparent, <margin>1</margin> through which and by means of which it is possible to discern a mountain or a forest. It is concerning this misty air that the Sacred Text seems to speak, where it is said by the wise man in *Ecclesiasticus 50:8*: *A rainbow shining among the clouds of glory.* Other testimonies of Holy Scripture also seem to speak of such a cloud—namely, misty air. It appears, therefore, that the Rainbow appears among dense clouds, and the eye perceives it in misty or dewy air. 

And although some philosophers, and indeed experts in optics, wish to discuss and debate the variety of the Rainbow's colors in their own way—saying that the diversity of colors arises as much from the variation of the cloud as from the light, and that thin water in a dewy cloud, otherwise bright air, and dark clouds must all concur for the procreation of different colors—they claim that all these things, when irradiated by the sun, provide different colors: namely, scarlet, green, yellow, lemon-yellow, red, sea-grey, or blue. (Aristotle seems to treat these matters in the 3rd book of his *Meteorology*). 

Nevertheless, if we wish to consider the matter a little more accurately, we see that it is otherwise than they have supposed. The colors of the rainbow are often produced without these specific mediums and in a different subject entirely, as **Roger Bacon** <note>A 13th-century English friar and philosopher known for his early emphasis on empiricism and optics.</note> teaches in his book on experimental science, and as common experience also shows. For in many lower things, colors of this kind are observed to appear: if we take hexagonal stones from India or Ireland <note>Likely referring to quartz crystals or basalt formations</note> and hold them against the rays of the sun penetrating through a window or some hole, we will perceive in the shadow (or the shadowy air) all the colors of the rainbow in the same order as they are arranged in the heavenly arch. 

Therefore, it is certain that colors of this kind can be produced without the aforementioned conditions; thus, it does not seem to follow that these colors are brought into light solely because of the reflection of solar rays into a concave and opaque dewy cloud. Nor does it follow of necessity that the solar rays striking immediately are the cause effecting such a great variety of colors. For if, according to the testimony of Roger Bacon, an operator takes the said hexagonal stone and turns himself toward a somewhat darker place, and applies the stone to his half-closed eye, he will immediately discern the said colors of the rainbow in the air. 

There are, therefore, some who believe that colors of this kind are procreated from the property of that stone. But truly, this is false, because both with a crystal or a well-polished glass body shaped into a triangular form, colors of this kind appear in both shadowy and luminous air. Furthermore, on the oars of a boat wet with dew and dripping with droplets, such colors sometimes appear upon being lifted from the water; the same happens when water is violently thrown against the rays of the sun. Yet, as has been said, it is not necessary that we have the presence of the sun in such an appearance, since it often happens that even at night, in the absence of the sun, these colors are observed appearing around a candle. However, we admit that some light must be present, without which we cannot discern anything colored, much less colors that cannot be seen without a colored object. But as pertains to the subject in which these colors are conspicuous, we say it can be the air itself imbued with light; for I remember lying in bed in the morning and clearly perceiving the colors of the rainbow in and near the solar rays for a long time.

Therefore, without a doubt, the **efficient cause** <note>The agent or force that produces an effect.</note> of these miraculous colors is more occult <note>hidden or secret</note> and concealed than can be easily comprehended by the Pagan <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note> philosophers, or even by those Christian followers of theirs in this age. For GOD, who is all and in all, and who fills the worldly spirits everywhere with His own brilliance (albeit invisible), is the cause of such a wondrous thing in nature: He who is accustomed to reveal Himself to men through signs, through colors, through lightnings, and infinite other ways. 

In moist nature, this light is called by Hermes Trismegistus in the *Pimander*, Chapter 1, the "Voice of Light," or the **Word** <note>original: "verbum"</note>, which, standing by moist nature, nourished it. And another, immersing himself deeply in the mysteries of nature (*On the Art of Chemistry*, ch. 9), says that this hidden nature is a certain infinite force, procreating like from like, increasing and nourishing all things, and for this reason possessing the names of all things in itself—having no color, yet participating in and effecting all colors, the fertile mother of all qualities and things. From this he concludes that this nature is GOD, and GOD is that uncreated nature—moist, created, creating, and nourishing—which the Platonists recognize as the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "mundi animam"</note>, existing in its whole and in every part, though invisibly within itself, in the manner of the human soul in its body. 

Zoroaster (with whom Heraclitus of Ephesus also seems to agree) calls this the **invisible fire**, from which all things are born. And others among the Hebrew Doctors hold that it is that fiery vigor which the Spirit of **Elohim** <note>A Hebrew name for God.</note>—which is the fiery love that was carried over the waters—brought forth in them, and consequently is dispersed everywhere in the world, though invisibly. For according to the testimony of St. Peter, *The heavens and the earth were of old from water, and through water consisting by the word of GOD (2 Peter 3)*; that is, by the primary emanation from the throne of divinity, by means of which *all things were made, and without it nothing (John 1).* 

Does not the wise man also speak clearly concerning the nature of this spiritual sun or invisible light when he breaks out into these words: *Wisdom is a spirit having all virtues in itself, simple and yet manifold, looking forth upon all things, containing all intelligible spirits, more mobile than all mobile things, and reaching everywhere because of her purity, inasmuch as she is a certain emanation of the clarity of almighty GOD, sincere, more beautiful than the sun, and compared to the light she is found prior to every disposition of the stars, etc. (Wisdom of Solomon 7).* From this it is clear that the operation of the rainbow, as well as of all other meteors, should be attributed to this spiritual sun and light instead.

<summary>This page critiques Aristotle's physical explanation of the rainbow, arguing instead that colors can be produced through prisms and crystals without clouds. It concludes that the rainbow is a spiritual phenomenon caused by the "invisible fire" or World Soul, identifying God as the true efficient cause.</summary>

### The Four Elements and their Qualities
<note>The "sublunary" world—everything below the Moon—is composed of four elements. Their interactions create the "meteors" or weather events we witness.</note>

*   **Fire:** Hot and Dry. It rises to the highest region, near the sphere of the Moon, creating lightning and comets.
*   **Air:** Hot and Moist. It fills the middle space and is the medium through which winds and clouds travel.
*   **Water:** Cold and Moist. It gathers in the hollows of the Earth and is drawn upward by the Sun to form rain.
*   **Earth:** Cold and Dry. The heavy center of the world, providing the material base for all physical manifestations.

142                                  **A Clear Exposition**

We believe that the upper region is vast and exceedingly spacious; the region situated between the two, or the middle region, we consider to be moderate in its dimensions between those extremes. Within these designated regions are included the primary subjects of our intention (as has been said); and we have thought it most important for you to consider and place before your eyes this arrangement, particularly regarding the various seats and positions of the **meteors**. <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, rainbows, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>

In the upper region, we have set forth the divine act and the instruments or ministers in and through whom all things in these lower parts—and indeed in the heavens above—are perfected, to be distinguished according to the strength of our understanding. Regarding these ministers, who are the beginnings of all things, whether perfectly or imperfectly mixed, we shall speak here with light and brief words, descending from the peak of the mirror down to its base, since mention has been made of them abundantly in both the preceding and following sections, to the honor of GOD the creator of all, and the instruction of man, who is the end and perfection of all things.

Since all things created in the world—whether they be simple or arisen from simples (such as Angels, being an "otherness" and forged from two; the stars; and also, among sublunary things, especially those bodies imperfectly mixed, which are composed in and from the air; and finally the perfectly mixed things, such as animals, vegetables, and minerals)—are composed of a **luminous form** (whether apparent or hidden) and **matter** as the subject from which they are made. Of these, the nature of matter is to suffer <note>To be acted upon; passive.</note> and the nature of form is to act. Without these qualities, nothing in the world could exist or reach the goal of perfection toward which all things tend. Thus, in the first place, we must especially consider what the source and beginning of motion is in this continuous action, from which various acts flow and are sown everywhere throughout the world. Then, we must consider what the immediate ministers or instruments of the primary Actor are, through which and in which He acts, or pours out the acts of His emanation. Finally, we think it must be considered with diligent intuition what the primary subjects in the world are—both in the ethereal heaven and in the air—where all kinds of meteors (with which we are chiefly concerned here) are accustomed to be procreated; and lastly in the water and the earth, where the aforementioned acts of God are observed to work and dwell.

In the first or highest place, we find God Himself in the immense and infinite dimension of His divinity, described as it were by letters, since He can never be depicted by an image nor comprehended in His infinity by the human mind. It pleases us to signify or express Him there by the term *Infinity* <note>original: "Ensoph." In Kabbalah, Ein Sof represents the Godhead prior to any self-manifestation.</note> with the Kabbalists and more secret Theologians. This signifies the Boundless, which they asserted to be the unique fountain of divine life and essence—an infinity, namely, without which nothing lives and nothing is, for all things proceed from the One. This unique fountain (into whose secrets it is impossible to penetrate) they not unwisely divide into a double spring, namely the natural and the spiritual, from which the living waters proceed. These descend by way of emanation, first through a stream into the bright paternal gate called the *Supreme Crown* <note>original: "Elion Cheter," referring to Keter, the highest of the Sephirot.</note>, and then into the Son, *Wisdom* <note>original: "Hochma."</note>. Hence the royal Psalmist says, *with thee is the fountain of life.* From this, it was right to gather that GOD in His innermost essence is outside all things and beyond the cavity of the world, nor can He be grasped by the sharp edge of the mind. Nevertheless, through various breathing-holes, which are the *Sephirotic* <note>original: "Sephiroticae."</note> numerations or bright gates, He disperses and sows various bright emanations downward everywhere through the cavity of the world, distinct from one another in their properties. These emanations, taking on a worldly spirit, are accustomed to take on the names and properties of Angels. The first three of these from the number of ten are ordered for the forging of the world's regions, heavens, and elements: the first, the Crown, is ascribed to the Father; the second, called Wisdom, to the Son; and Prudence <note>Often referring to Binah/Understanding.</note> to the Holy Spirit. This the royal Prophet also seems to prove in this discourse: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit from his mouth.* Where the Lord is the Father, emitting the Word or Wisdom, by means of which heaven and earth were created out of the waters (as St. Peter testifies), and by the Spirit from both of them comes all power in them. However, seven other emanations are received and, as it were, imbibed by the seven remaining Angelic spirits, by means of which the said Angels are shaped, and they act and work according to the property of the Divine name by which they are filled, into those worldly subjects disposed everywhere through the spacious world. And these are those angels who are said to preside over the Seven Planets, of whom more will be said below.

Regarding these angelic or spiritual receptacles or instruments, which are ordained by God to receive the types of divine influxes, we shall explain them in a few words for the better understanding of the readers, along with the channels of the influxes, the orders of angels who receive them first, and finally to which orbits of the celestial region they lead them by virtue of their office.

First, therefore, it must be known and observed with diligent intellect that from the infinite fountain of immense divinity, called *The Infinite* <note>original: "Ensoph"</note>, ten bright emanations (according to the intentions of the Kabbalists) flow through as many channels differing in property. These are poured out and emanate everywhere into the world according to the will of God, primarily into ten various orders of Angels and saints. From these, ten Archangels (counting the Soul of the Messiah among them) created by GOD for this business, each receive any of those emanations as bright influxes from any order. The **Sixth Emanation** is called **ELOAH**; and this one, most full of every luminous virtue, has as its channel **Tiphereth**, which signifies grace, beauty, and brightness. This influence directs its power into the lowest order of the middle hierarchy, which is the **Powers** <note>original: "Potestatum," the angelic rank responsible for maintaining order and restraining demons.</note>, whose duty it is to subject wicked angels or spirits to themselves, and this by force and power, as Gregory says. By its presence and virtue, good influences, pleasing to the human race, are scattered everywhere through the sublunary air, water, and earth. Hence it is also that this planet, namely Venus, is called by astrologers the "Lesser Fortune." <note>original: "Fortunium minus." Mercury is (according to the opinion of the Poets) the great messenger of Jupiter. From there, the influence is later sent out into the sublunary region, where it sometimes creates rapid winds in the air, which are not infrequently associated with heavy showers and rain. The **Ninth** is called **SADAI**, whose bright gate is **Iesod** <note>Yesod.</note>, through which it descends and passes into the order of **Angels**. Finally, the **Tenth** is called **ADONAI**, that is, Lord, whose channel is **Malchut**, that is, Kingdom. From here this emanation descends into the sphere of souls (as the Kabbalists maintain) under the leadership of the soul of the **Messiah**, which is finally carried down by it into the elements, where for the most part, severe effects are produced on account of man's disobedience.

But here, in passing, I would have you know, according to the intentions of the Magi and Kabbalists, that each of the aforesaid angels is a great Prince, having the power of much liberty to dispose these gifts of GOD, or these His properties, according to His will—either mercifully or severely—among the creatures of this sublunary world. Their powers seem to increase more according to their common and natural or accustomed disposition in the annual course, in the dominion of their planets and signs, and consequently in their ordained times, namely years, months, days, and hours, and in the elements and parts of the world, and the winds appropriated to them. And certainly, to speak more truly, the dominion belongs neither to the signs nor to the planets, but in respect to the more abundant divine efflux, which comes to it more at one time than another, according to the divine will. Consequently, the Angel or Intelligence of a planet or star is like its internal spirit moving it, whose central soul is that very emanation of divinity, by which it is constantly intoxicated as if with divine nectar. Therefore, it is poorly said by those skilled in Magic that the Angels act in the dominion of a sign or planet, but rather that the sign and planet are stronger or more powerful according to the greater or lesser strength of their Intelligence in the divine emanation which it receives. Furthermore, it is also to be understood that every one of these powerful Angels (of whom seven are said to stand before the face of God) rules over many legions, with which they are accustomed to act both in heaven and in the elementary region.

   But now we have arrived at the subject at hand: namely, the exposition and explanation of the forms, locations, and qualities depicted in our **Meteorographic Mirror**. As far as their location is concerned, we find it to be either common or specific. We call the "common" location the entire space of air between the ethereal heaven and the earth. However, we establish three specific regions within this entire common air. We see the **upper region** filled with comets of various kinds and differing shapes, along with the **chasm** <note>original: *chasmate*; a "gaping" opening in the clouds or an auroral display.</note> and the **burning beam** <note>original: *trabe*; a long, horizontal streak of light or fire in the sky.</note>, about which we speak only a word here, as they are treated more fully elsewhere.
   Just as there are various species of comets, the Philosophers have assigned names to them according to their matching appearances.
   The first species they called the **Lance**, as it is stretched out in length.
   The **Xiphias** <note>from the Greek *xiphos* for sword.</note> is a shorter lance, and this species of comet is tapered to a sharp point.
   The **Mercurial** is a comet that is somewhat bluish from its heat, small in size, having a tiny and long tail.
   The **Soldier** <note>original: *Miles*.</note> is so called because it has a Martial color <note>A reddish hue associated with the planet Mars.</note>, and this comet is also tailed, just as you have it drawn in the Mirror.
   The **Aurora** has the appearance of a star, but it excels every star in its clarity and splendor.
   The **Rose** is a comet large in size and round, which seems to display and carry a human face.
   The **Tenaculum** <note>Literally "a holder" or "pincers."</note> is a comet which, standing as if upon a fiery base, is tailed in a wondrous manner.
   The **Black** <note>original: *Niger*.</note> is a comet of a dark color, endowed with a short and brief tail, and it appears to be adorned in a certain way with very little hair <note>original: *capillamento*; the "coma" or hazy envelope of a comet.</note>.
   The **Ceratias** <note>from the Greek *keras* for horn.</note> is a comet which, from the appearance of its heat or the shape of its fire, is called "horned."
   There are also other ignited meteors <note>In the 17th century, the term "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including weather and lights, not just falling rocks.</note> which are sometimes visible in this region, which we nevertheless do not call comets at all. While comets are set on fire in such a way that they are not quickly extinguished, these other apparitions—such as the **Chasm**, the **Beam**, and **flying sparks**—last less time, as they arise from a substance or spirit that is less firm and more inconstant. But since we have spoken of these before and have also explained their forms in our Mirror, we have decided not to make a longer discourse in this place.
   Regarding the other meteors, both luminous and dark, I judge that for the sake of brevity you should be referred primarily to an inspection of our Mirror for their forms and locations, and to the aforementioned table or classification for their order, without further explanation in this place.

   **On Meteors which are seen and are not what they appear to be.**

   Now, however, we come to those meteors which show a certain shape or image in the air, and yet they are not what they seem. But truly, since this will appear hard and difficult to consider at first glance for those who are unlearned and least skilled in the science of optics, we have expressed the reasoning of those appearances in the perspective manner in our **Meteorographic Mirror**. We have done this with proper and consistent demonstrations, so that you might reach a certain knowledge of such visions in the air more easily and without great exhaustion. In this task of demonstrating, I confess that I follow and imitate the doctrine of **Witelo** <note>original: *Vitellionis*; a 13th-century friar and scientist whose work on optics was a standard textbook for centuries.</note> regarding the manner of seeing. By this doctrine we are taught that we see through the action of a visible form upon the eye, and the "passion" (or receiving) of the sight by such a form. 
   Meteors of this kind, the reasoning for which we gather solely from the science of optics—since they are not what they appear—are the **Parhelia**. These occur at the rising or setting of the sun from an oblique angle, in the lower part of a cloud, and this happens in the lowest part of the air region. They are images or likenesses of the Sun or Moon which are represented in a dewy cloud, not otherwise than how an object is seen in water or a mirror. We show the reasoning of the vision through **pyramidal lines** <note>The "cone of vision" extending from the eye to the object.</note> from the place of sight to the objects of the Sun and Moon in the lower part of the cloud, just as is demonstrated in our Mirror.

### Of the Meteorographic Mirror. 147

   Similarly, the **heavenly arc** <note>The rainbow.</note> is most often seen at either sunrise or sunset, but rarely at midday, except occasionally during the winter. This occurs by divine power as it is drawn from the moist air into our sight. For our vision is not reflected by lighter substances; rather, objects with brighter colors stir and move our sight. 
   
   But now, contrary to the common opinion of philosophers <note>The author is challenging the traditional Aristotelian view that rainbows are reflections off distant, solid clouds.</note>, we believe it must first be understood that the rainbow does not form in a cloud, but in the lower part of the lowest region of the air, as we have stated previously. Indeed, it is observed to be not far from the eye—specifically, no further than **three hundred paces** <note>original: *trecentesimum passum*; a "pace" is roughly five feet, meaning the author believes the rainbow is within 1,500 feet of the observer.</note> away. We have proven this by the fact that we can see the rainbow shining with its **four colors** <note>In the 16th and 17th centuries, many scholars identified only four primary colors in the rainbow (often red, yellow, green, and blue) before Isaac Newton later defined the seven-color spectrum.</note> positioned between the eye and a nearby mountain or forest. Nay, we have even seen the rainbow descending upon the grass itself by means of a dewy rain. 
   
   If you wish to know the clear explanation for this matter, you must pay diligent attention and correctly understand what is about to be said, setting aside the vain opinions of many philosophers which are buried in mists and darkness. In a thick, clear medium (such as water), a small, round image of the sun is reflected; in a thinner medium, a large round image is reflected. When the medium is thinned even further, the image becomes larger, though everything around the center of the image appears empty because the scattered rays are not brought to a single point. Instead, they are scattered there in the lighter air, much like how we are accustomed to using **burning glasses** <note>original: *vitris... congregare*; magnifying lenses used to concentrate sunlight to start fires.</note> to gather rays. This has great significance for that sudden constriction of the air. When the air is further thinned and changed into a humid, droplet-filled, and vaporous state, the largest [arc] is not...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Efficient Cause" of the universe. Having previously discussed how God uses physical elements like fire and clouds as instruments, the author now pivots to a deeper metaphysical and mystical description of God's essence, drawing on Scripture, Hermetic philosophy, and the Jewish Cabala.</meta>

150 Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

Although it is permitted for us to perceive God through His "garments" <note>A metaphor for the visible natural world as a covering for the invisible Divine.</note>, nevertheless, to search out His magnitude is beyond the capacity of human intellect, since *it is not* (as the Prophet testifies) *to be grasped, Psalm 145:3.* Furthermore, His pure essence is even less granted to be seen by human and fleshy eyes, according to that saying of the Prophet and the Evangelist: *No one has ever seen God. Jeremiah 1. John 4.* <note>The author refers to John 1:18 and potentially a thematic parallel in Jeremiah regarding the invisibility or unsearchability of the Divine.</note>

We shall therefore follow, in this description of God, partly the doctrine of the most excellent philosophers, and partly that of the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of the Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that explores the nature of the divine and the universe.</note> in those matters where they agree with the Holy Bible; and finally, we shall declare in a few words what is to be gathered from the Word of God toward a living description of God.

We gather therefore from the testimonies of divine writers that God has a twofold nature in relation to us: namely, the *latent* <note>hidden</note> and the *patent* <note>revealed or manifest</note>. The **latent** nature is surely that in which, before the creation of the world, He seemed to the human mind to rest in infinite darkness and to do, as it were, nothing. Instead, He reflected His ardor and virtue back into Himself, and did not apply the rays of His light to the creation of the world at all. This same thing must also be said concerning His rays or essence as they rest and are hidden within the opaque and shadowy things of the world; He is described in such a form by <term>Mercurius Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus, supposed author of the Hermetic Corpus, which blended philosophy, alchemy, and magic.</note> in these words: *The Monad (he says) begat the monad before the creation of the world, and reflected its own ardor into itself; that is, it shone back, as it were, onto itself.* <note>original: "Monas ante mundi creationem monadem genuit, & in seipsam reflexit ardorem suum..."</note> By these words he seems to imply that the divine nature—that luminous fountain, the act of all active things, the origin of life, and the ocean of form—reflected the rays of its fiery and purely formal nature back into itself. 

From this it happened that before there was any will in Him to create the world, an infinite abyss was overwhelmed with shapeless darkness and was empty. Indeed, the aforementioned Philosopher seems to imply this in another place: *There was (he says) an infinite shadow in the abyss.* In this discourse, he seems to agree with Moses, who says that *darkness was upon the face of the deep.* And this was that matter "in potentiality" of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who taught that before things are physically created, they exist as "potential" in prime matter.</note>, which they called the "first matter"; hence, this type of hidden nature is called "divine power" by some, as will be declared below. Just as the Philosophers considered that divine nature—hidden in shadows and gloom and not at all dilating itself—mathematically, so indeed they called it **Arithmetical Unity**, and sometimes the **Geometrical Point**. I call it a Unity because it is simple in itself, without any regard to number; and a Point because it has no relation to a circumference. Rather, as they are considered in either art, they are in their own nature simple, indivisible, of no quantity, quality, or substance, and yet they are the principle of all these things—inasmuch as once it is dilated, it is everything that is, or everything that can be understood in the ten <term>predicaments</term> <note>Aristotle’s ten categories of being (substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.) used to classify everything that exists.</note>, as will be more broadly declared in the description of the manifest God. In that manifest state, it will be shown how this most simple Unity is fortified by its peripheral numbers, just as a point is by its circumference.

In the art of the Cabalists, the more skilled have called this divine power, when so hidden, the **Dark Aleph**, just as they called it the **Luminous Aleph** when it is manifested and shining forth from the darkness. But truly, they understand by the *Dark Aleph* the numbering according to the Cabalistic system, namely **Hochma** <note>original: "Hochma seu sapientiam"; the Sephira of Wisdom.</note> or Wisdom, or that Monad which the Monad begat before any creation, the ardor of which it reflected back into itself. This divine wisdom, emanating from the Father and soon returning into the Father’s bosom before the act of creation, the wise called the "Principle" or "Beginning," concerning which it is written in the book *Bahir*: *Nothing is the beginning except Wisdom.* <note>original: "Nihil est principium nisi sapientia"</note> Reuchlin <note>Johann Reuchlin, a famous Renaissance humanist and scholar of the Cabala.</note> says in Book 3 of *The Cabalistic Art*: *In the Infinite itself, the most absolute essence of the three highest numerations of the Cabalistic tree (which we Christians call the three Persons in the Divine)... since it is retracted and remaining in the abyss of darkness, as if idle, or as they say, looking toward nothing, it is therefore called **Ein**, that is, Nothing, or Non-being, and "No-End" [Infinite], because we, with such thin poverty of intellect regarding divine matters...* <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the thought that human intellect is too poor to describe the infinite nature of God.</note>

### CHAPTER IV.

### What this all-creating divine spirit is, and how it is sometimes called the Word, and occasionally Wisdom.

That this spirit of immense power is **GOD** himself—since it is no more to be divided from the divine essence or the "luminous fountain" than the rays of the sun are from the solar body—we have already demonstrated in the preceding sections using the opinions of both Holy Scripture and the philosophers. We shall now explain how, by its emanation from the darkness, the darkness or the abyss was overwhelmed and illuminated, and how the waters, both thin and thick, were animated and produced from nothing (as it were) into action and being. We have already spoken of this quite clearly; for it is written: *The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters*, imparting vigor to them. These waters, before this liquid spirit went forth from the luminous fountain or the "bosom of the Father," were called the **Abyss**, upon whose face there was darkness, as it is held in the sacred text. Finally, we are taught by many passages in the sacred context that this spirit is the **Alpha and Omega**, the beginning and the end of all things, as it is the one from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. *I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord* (Revelation 1). And elsewhere: *I am the first, I am the last; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens; I will call them and they shall stand together* (Isaiah 48). It is established that *in God himself we live, move, and have our being* (Acts 17), which is also to be understood regarding every created thing, because the *incorruptible spirit of God is said to be in every thing* (Wisdom 12:1). For this reason, and by virtue of this spirit, it was said by the Apostle that *God works all in all* (1 Corinthians 12). From this, the said Apostle concludes elsewhere that God is the father of all, whom he says is *above all, and through all, and in us all* (Ephesians 4:6). And elsewhere he says: *God gives life to all things* (1 Timothy 6). This also seems to be verified by the Evangelist, affirming that *by the Word all things were made, and without it nothing was made that was made, and that in it was life* (John 1). Elsewhere we are taught by the Apostle that *from Christ and through Christ are all things* (Romans 11). And in another place he says: *Christ fills all things* (Ephesians 4:8). And elsewhere: *from him, in him, and through him are all things, to whom be praise and honor*. In the same epistle, he acknowledges that *God created all things through Jesus Christ* (Ephesians 3:9). 

Furthermore, this name **Jesus** is said by the <term>Cabbalists</term> <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that explores the relationship between the infinite (Ein Sof) and the finite universe, often through the symbolism of Hebrew letters and divine names.</note> to contain all the names of God within its power—indeed, even that most essential name of God, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter unpronounceable name of God in Hebrew (YHWH), often rendered as Jehovah or Yahweh.</note> or **Jehovah**. For at that name—namely, **Jesus**—*every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth* (Philippians 2). Thus it happens that everything ascribed to the ineffable name *Jehovah* in the Old Testament is transferred to the name *Jesus* in the New. Hence Job says (understanding this regarding the creating spirit and speaking of its efficacy): *Jehovah stretches out the North over the empty place, and hangs the earth upon nothing; He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, so that the clouds are not torn under them; He covers the face of his throne and spreads his cloud upon it. He has circled the face of the waters with a boundary, until light and darkness come to an end. By his power he breaks the sea, and by his understanding he strikes through the storm; by his spirit he has adorned the heavens,* etc. (Job 26:7). From this it is clear that the work in creation which is ascribed to **GOD** is assigned to **Jehovah** in the Old Testament and to **Jesus Christ** in the New.

In him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it,* etc. *He was the true light, he was in the world, and the world was made through him,* etc. (John 1). By these words, he argues: first, the most excellent lineage of this divine spirit, namely that it is of Divine and Deiform birth; next, that the place from which it went forth was the darkness, which nevertheless the darkness did not comprehend. Hence it was said: *Even the darkness cannot be so darkened but that you foresee, for the night shines for you as the day, and darkness is to GOD as light itself* (Psalm 139:11). Furthermore, its essence and pure formality are indicated by the fact that it is the light of the world and the light shining in the darkness—indeed, the light not only of the world but of man himself. Finally, its office is explained in that all things were made by it; and the reason is that the life of every thing is within it. Hence it is written elsewhere: *IN GOD himself we live and move and have our being* (Acts 17). And elsewhere: *God gives life to all things* (1 Timothy 6). ### CHAPTER VII.

->On the First Mover, the First Movable, and the Divine Will.<-

We have said that the first mover of all things is **Wisdom** herself, inasmuch as she was created before all things and, by her own property (as the wise man testifies in Wisdom of Solomon 7), is "more mobile than all mobile things," reaching everywhere because of her purity. For emanation from GOD is the most vital act of all, and the origin and fountain of all actions. This Wisdom, indeed—having driven back the darkness to the region of the earth—immediately exercised its primary moving power in that first heaven which is called the **Primum Mobile** <note>Latin for "the first moved." In traditional cosmology, this was the outermost sphere of the universe that imparted motion to all the inner planetary spheres.</note>. For this reason, it is called the "first movable," because all the other spheres of the world take their movements from east to west according to its motion. Hence we find it written that the most powerful GOD, who is truth, "turns the heaven in a circle into its place in one day" (3 Esdras 4:34). From this, it is clear that divine Wisdom is, as it were, the **will of GOD**, emanating immediately from the **Word**, being continuous with it and not at all divided from it (Ecclesiasticus 1).

From this, therefore, as the Word is, so is the will of GOD, and such is Wisdom. "The Word of our GOD," says the Prophet, "remains forever" (Isaiah 40:8). And the wise man says, "the will of the Lord shall remain forever" (Proverbs 19:21). The will of GOD is the word **FIAT** <note>Latin for "Let it be done," referring to the creative command in the Book of Genesis.</note>. And elsewhere it is said, "not my will, but thine be done." ### The Sun as the Secondary Efficient Cause

->**On the Heart of the Macrocosm**<-

While the Divine Will is the absolute first cause, we must also recognize the Sun as the heart of the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: the "great world" or the universe, viewed as a large-scale reflection of the human body (the microcosm).</term>. We believe, therefore, that the Divine Will—the **motive act** <term>Motive act (actus motivus): the active, initiating force of a being's will that leads to movement or creation.</term> of the divine Word or Wisdom emanating from the essence of GOD—is never to be separated from its own ray. It is eternal with the Word and its emanation, and no more divisible from it than heat is from fire or light is from the sun. We hold this same Will to be the proper and God-formed parent of the divine ray in man, which is the "first act" in the human will. For when God said, *“Let us make man in our image,”* this word *“Let there be”* <note>original: "Fiat"</note>—the motive power of the Word—was the Will of God, or the living signature of His will. From this root, the human will arose; for immediately following the Word itself, there followed an act not only of life, but an act of will joined with that life.

What follows then? Shall we conclude that the will of man is the will of God? By no means. Just as we say that the life and the sublime mind of man are not separated from the essence of God—since they are the "breaths" from God <note>A reference to the *spiraculum vitae* (breath of life) from Genesis 2:7.</note> and consequently not to be divided from His emanation, for the divine essence is indivisible—so we say that the will of man issues from the divine. However, that Will of God was intended for the shaping of the human species, and for its continuation, governance, and direction in this life toward good things, and for the avoidance of foul things which are abominable to God and human nature. This is according to the words of the Wise Man: *“GOD sends wisdom from the holy heavens to man, so that she may be present and labor with him, and that he may know what is pleasing to Him”* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:10</note>. And elsewhere: *“That he may direct man in his way.”* 

Yet this **spark of divinity** <note>original: "scintilla hæc diuinitatis"; a common mystical term for the indestructible bit of the divine within the human soul.</note>, on account of the perverse error and sin of Adam, has been so obscured and overshadowed by darkness in our successors that, although this spark always tends toward the good in its own movement, its impressions are nonetheless poorly received because of the dark disposition of the body. The Wise Man seems to acknowledge this in these words: *“Who among men can know the counsel of GOD? Or who can know what GOD wills? For the thoughts of mortals are timid and our providence is uncertain; for the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things. We struggle to grasp the things that are on earth, but who shall search out the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your counsel, unless you give wisdom and send your most holy spirit from the highest? Thus were the paths of those on earth corrected, and men learned the things that please you”* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:13–18</note>.

By these words, as if by a third thread, he seems to argue that the heaviness and darkness of the corruptible body is the cause of the uncertainty of the human way. However, we gather that GOD immediately infused the ray of life and intelligence into man from these passages: *“There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding”* <note>Job 32:8; the OCR incorrectly cites Job 9.</note>. And elsewhere: *“The spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.”* From these, it is clear that the origin of both human reason and life is the divine spirit or breath. Similarly, we understand that this ray of life and intelligence is the very spirit of wisdom from the speech of the Wise Man: *“GOD made man by his wisdom, that he might have dominion over the creatures made by Him”* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:2</note>. And from this it is said, *“GOD made man in his own image”* <note>Genesis 1:27; OCR cites Genesis 5:1.</note>. Whence it is certain that Wisdom itself (whose act is the effect of the divine will) is the fountain and origin of the human will no differently than it is of the divine.

But the darkness and corruption of the human body, brought upon it by the sin of Adam through the craft and malice of the Devil, are the occasion for error in life and the cause of the depraved effects of the divine will in man. For God, in the first creation of man, gave him the Holy Spirit to rule him, lead him in his paths, and defend him from corruption; hence it was said, *“Man is the temple of the Holy Spirit.”* This we confirm from the sayings of the Wise Man: *“GOD created man to be immortal, and made him in the image of his own likeness; but through the envy of the Devil, death entered into the world”* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 2:23–24</note>. And elsewhere: *“Do not seek death in the error of your life, nor pull down destruction by the works of your hands; for GOD did not make death, nor does He rejoice in the destruction of the living. For He created all things that they might exist, and He made the nations of the world healthy”* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 1:12–14; OCR cites 1:16.</note>. 

By these, he indicates that the gift given to man was an act of health, prudence, and happiness, and that it is overshadowed by the vice of man, procreated by the malice of the devil. Thus man errs in his life unless those shadows are illuminated by the influx of divine wisdom sent from the highest heavens—that is, unless the ray is increased by rays, all corporeal and diabolical obscurity is removed, and so **nature will rejoice in nature** <note>original: "natura naturâ lætabitur"; a famous Hermetic aphorism suggesting that like-elements are drawn to and perfected by one another.</note>. 

For this reason, there is a difference between the human will and the divine will. It is not because they differ in essence, but because the divine is never occupied with vain effects, whereas the human will—though always good in itself and possessing the most certain knowledge—sometimes has its good operations converted into evil and vicious effects by the foul and vile flesh. This is just as the pleasant rays of the sun are converted into a violent, burning heat by the reflection of a **burning mirror** <note>original: "speculi vstorii"; a parabolic or concave mirror used to focus sunlight to start fires. The author uses this as a metaphor for how the physical body "refracts" divine intent into sin.</note>. It is not that the mirror (or the flesh) receives evil impressions from that divine act, but that by receiving its good acts poorly, the flesh is accustomed to sinning—turning the direct motion of the rays into an oblique path away from truth itself through rebellious reflection. Thus, this perverse and oblique will makes man err through the perverse reception of his own flesh.

And Christ himself, having overcome the narrowness of his flesh by first praying that God would turn away that cup, said nevertheless, “yet not my will but yours be done,” Luke 22; according to that in John 5: “I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.” But if the human will is united with that Divine Will, then it is accustomed to bring that same will to perfection; and it is of this state that John speaks: “He who does the will of God remains forever,” 1 John 2. That is to say, he has been made one with God. Indeed, so that this might be accomplished in the Royal Prophet <note>original: "Propheta regio"; referring to King David, traditional author of the Psalms.</note>, he himself speaks thus when praying to God: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God,” Psalm 143:10. It is as if he had said: let your face shine upon your servant, and in your light I shall see light; or as he says elsewhere, “You, the Sun giving life and glory, and illuminating my lamp, shall make my darkness shine bright,” so that I may enter upon the right path to execute your will, Psalms 18:29 and 84:12. From these things, therefore, one may see that the **lamp of man** does not differ in essence from the **spiritual sun**—which gives grace, glory, and salvation—except in this: that the lamp resides within a created body as a specific ray of that Sun, providing the body with its being and existence, and occupying the place of a creature; whereas the Sun exists in and through itself, attributing life and being to the worldly spirit. It exists so far beyond all things that it is said to fill all things: the Father of all, who is over all and through all, the God who gives life to all, the worker of all in all, Ephesians 4:6, Timothy 6. He is the center of every thing whose circumference is nowhere <note>A famous Hermetic definition of God, often attributed to the *Book of the Twenty-four Philosophers*.</note>, the unity of unities, the father of fathers, the principle of principles, the fountain of fountains, the root of roots, the star of stars (as Synesius says in his *Hymns*), the good of goods, the idea of ideas, immense beauty, the hidden seed of things; the father of ages, the father of the intelligible worlds; the spirit of Ambrose instilling life, floating upon the mass of the body, which now awakens the world; Jupiter or Jehovah from whom all lower Gods depend, as Orpheus and the Pythagoreans would have it. Finally, He is everything that truly exists, in which definition we exclude from Him all things empty, deceptive, and fantastical—those children of darkness which seem to be and yet are not, as will appear in the final examination when all things must be reduced to the one light <note>original: "ad vnam lunae"; likely a typo in the OCR for "ad unam lucem" (to the one light) or "ad unam lineam" (to one line/limit).</note>.

We conclude, therefore, that God acts voluntarily and not out of necessity (as the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who argued that the universe and its Prime Mover acted according to fixed, logical necessity rather than a personal, choosing will.</note> maintain), and that nothing has been made in the heavens or on the earth that did not receive the motion of its origin from the Divine Will. If a spark within a creature does not produce the desired effects that would be pleasing to God and good men, this does not happen because of the incorruptible spirit acting at the center, but because of the deceptive mass of darkness—subject to all manner of change—which receives the acts of the Divine Mind poorly. Thus, they obscure the rays of such great light, and the darkness in the creature does not comprehend that light dwelling within the darkness; according to that saying of Saint John: “In the Word was life, and that life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” We can most aptly compare this light, or the spirit of wisdom, to the nature of the **Sun**. In itself, the Sun is simple and always uniform in its action, yet it is manifold in respect to the variety of operations which its rays are accustomed to produce in the world. This does not happen because of any varied action of the Sun, but because its impressions are received differently according to the variety of bodies—varying according to their existence or the greater or lesser resistance of those receiving the solar acts. For, as the Wise Man witnesses, God—composing all things by number, weight, and measure—made one thing differ from another by proportion, so that by His unique and simple act He might produce various creatures, both corporeal and spiritual, in this world. Thus we see that by these solar rays, various effects are produced in the world according to the character of the recipients. In one place, the Sun causes grass and herbs to sprout and bloom; at another time, it scorches and dries them up. Sometimes it nourishes and refreshes animals with its beneficial heat, and sometimes it makes the weak and sick languish by its presence; indeed, it compels healthy men to hurry to shaded places to escape the piercing perfection of its burning rays. Again, the rays contracted into the center of a **burning-glass** <term>Burning-glass (speculi vrentis): A lens or curved mirror used to concentrate sunlight to a point, capable of igniting fires.</term> set fire to things, and by such a fire consume cities and reduce royal palaces to nothing; yet the Sun is not observed to act in the same way upon water. It inflames stones and rocks with heat, and at other times it warms them only gently. Sometimes, therefore, the effects of generation are hastened, and sometimes they tend toward corruption—and yet the Sun itself, together with its rays, remains the same: permanent and simple in its act. The entire difference lies in the diversity of the object, which receives the solar acts either well or poorly. The matter is no different regarding the rays of the **invisible and intellectual Sun**, which gives life and being to this worldly sun. And so you have my conceptions regarding the Divine Will and its branches, according to which all things are made in this world, in which it produces various effects according to the variety of those receiving the divine rays—varying by number, weight, and measure. As for the act of the human will, both obscured and enlightened, we have depicted it in this place to the best of my ability for the better understanding of the readers.

C H A P T E R IX.

*That contrary to the opinion of Aristotle and certain other Pagans,
God works and acts in his creation and the continuation of creatures
not out of necessity, but by his own proper will.*

WE call that **necessary** which indeed cannot be otherwise, but truly we call **contingent**—which includes both the voluntary and the fortuitous—that which can be otherwise. However, a very great dispute has arisen among the Pagan philosophers as to whether God created the world and his creatures within it either in this way (namely, **voluntarily**) or in that way (specifically, **out of necessity**). The greater part of these philosophers fell into the opinion that God acts in the world both regarding its creation and the decay <note>original: "corruptionem"; in early modern philosophy, "corruption" refers to the natural breakdown or death of a thing, the opposite of "generation."</note> of things generated within it by necessity and not by will. They speak as if he were driven to such works without his own choosing, through the compulsion and prompting of some nature that was either co-eternal with him, pre-existing, or at least already created by him. How profane this is and how it exceeds the bounds of reason <note>original: "metam"; literally a boundary marker or goal-post.</note> will be made clear from what follows.

For what is more ancient than God, seeing as he exists before all things? What is smaller in measure than a point, or lesser in number than unity? Therefore, it is necessary that God be free and voluntary in his actions, insofar as he is the one who exists through himself and without regard for other things, and was sufficient unto himself before any creation.

### CHAPTER X.

*On the property of Divine numbers and names among the Cabbalists,*
*how the various effects of the divine will depend upon their na-*
*tures, tending toward both benevolence and ma-*
*lediction.*

In our "Mirror of Causes," annexed to the end of this part, you have seen it demonstrated how a different name of GOD presides over each Cabbalistic numeration <note>original: "numerationi Cabalisticae"; referring to the Sephirot, the ten attributes or emanations of God in Jewish mysticism.</note>. This is not because there is any diversity in the essence of GOD, but because His properties in the world are various, according to His good pleasure and will, wherever it seems good to Him. Some of these properties tend toward mercy and benevolence, while others tend toward severity and harm. For a fuller understanding of this matter, it should be known that although many names are attributed to God (according to the opinion of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Rabbi Moysis Aegyptiaci"; referring to Maimonides, the influential 12th-century philosopher.</note>), all of them—except for the unique **Tetragrammaton** <note>The "four-letter name" of God (YHWH), considered too sacred to pronounce in Jewish tradition.</note> which is called the "separated name"—are assigned to Him alone because they signify the substance of the creator in a pure sense, without any participation with creatures. These other names, I say, denote Him through "participation," that is, with respect to created things, and consequently they are derived from His works. It was for this reason that His essential name was never spoken, except in the sanctuary by the holy priests of the Lord, and specifically in the priestly blessing by the high priest on the Day of Atonement. The rank of this name (says Rabbi Moses) is great, and it was not to be uttered rashly by the mouth, since it signified the substance of the creator; through this, God is noted to be above all being, and to have existed before any thing was. But the other names denote God as He is present *within* all being.

For example, when Moses asked, GOD answered: *I.H.V.H.*, that is, "my name for eternity." Therefore, this name alone is the name for eternity—that is, for the Divine essence in its purity. No such name can be composed by a human voice that could equal the nature of divinity; although there are various titles for GOD derived from His works, this is the only name appropriated to Him before any created thing existed. But insofar as the divine essence exists as much within created things as it does outside of all things, the Tetragrammaton is also common and general, acting in every branch of the **Sephirotic tree** <note>The *Arbor Sephirotica* is a symbolic diagram representing the process of creation and the structure of the divine attributes.</note>, so that the other various titles of GOD are merely properties, or offices, or various acts of power of that single and individual essence.

Thus, among the various titles of God inscribed on the Sephirotic tree, *Ehieh* <note>Hebrew for "I Am."</note> signifies the fountain of all creatures, the first source of all clemency, of all graces, sparing all, the father of mercies, and the God of all consolation—whom Christ teaches us to pray to thus: *Our Father, who art in heaven, etc.* And of Him it is said that the Father judges no one; furthermore, this is assigned to the Father as one who is always clement and benevolent toward His children, just as *Psalm 103* teaches how God has mercy on His children. This name, therefore, is assigned as the ruler of the Sephirah <term>Sephirah: a single "emanation" or node on the Cabbalistic Tree of Life</term>, or numeration, or the "Luminous Gate," or the first branch of the Cabbalistic tree, which is called *Cheter* <note>original: "Cheter"; Kether, meaning Crown.</note> or the Crown. For just as *Kether* is, as it were, the root of the tree, so indeed *Ehieh* is the father of all creation. From this it is clear that the reason for this title of God is taken from His property in clemency and mercy, which is occupied with creatures—namely, in giving and granting life, and giving the gift of being or existence to the world and the creatures contained within it.

The second title of GOD in the Sephirotic order is *Iah* <note>Yah</note>: which also tends toward the benign property of GOD, specifically in the formation of the world and the extraction of the waters from the belly of Chaos. The numeration over which it presides is *Hochma* <note>original: "Hochma"; Chokhmah, meaning Wisdom.</note>, that is, Wisdom, concerning which it is written: *He who made a weight for the winds and weighed the waters by measure, when He set a law for the rains, and a way for the sounding storms, then He saw wisdom, etc. Job 28.* And elsewhere: *When He formed the heavens above, when He strengthened the fountains of the deep, when He set a decree for the sea, when He established the foundations of the earth, I, Wisdom, was with Him like a foster child, composing all things. Proverbs 8.* From this benign disposition, He is also said to be mild, kind, and a lover of good; and elsewhere, it is said that Wisdom is given by God to men so that He might show them what His will is. Nevertheless, as it is certain that *Chokhmah* stands in the middle between *Kether* and *Binah*—the latter of which denotes severity, while the former denotes clemency—so the title of God *Iah*, or Wisdom, sometimes punishes, though very rarely. Hence Jehovah said, speaking of the Angel or of Wisdom: *do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him. Exodus 23.*

The third Sephirah or Cabbalistic numeration is *Binah*, that is, Prudence <note>More commonly translated today as "Understanding."</note>, and the title of the Tetragrammaton attributed to this is *Elohim*, that is, terror and dread, since it is through this name that severe punishments and slaughters come; for in this property, GOD exercises His power by punishing the wicked. And in such an office He employs angels, who for this reason are called *Bene Elohim*, that is, sons of *Elohim*. The Doctors of the Cabala also hold that the plague of the world, from which such demons are sent forth...

However, its property in creation is to illuminate and give form to matter, an action in which it is necessary for a privation of the preceding form (if there were any) to intervene.

You see that the effects of these three Names of God, taken from His properties toward His creatures, are varied: namely, the first inclines entirely toward clemency and mercy; the last toward severity; while the middle one participates in both natures, yet is most inclined toward clemency. And to this middle one is assigned the essential name **Jehovah**, because it is also exercised in this world, both in punishment and in beneficence, but it is much more prone to mercy than to punishment; hence it is written: *The LORD <note>original: "DEVS Iehoua"</note> is long-suffering, great in kindness, forgiving iniquity and transgression, who by no means clears the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, etc.* Numbers 14.

But let us proceed to the fourth enumeration <term>Sephirah; a divine emanation</term> which is **Chesed** or Clemency, to which are attributed grace, goodness, and mercy; its presiding Name of God is **El**, whose nature is to cherish all things and succor everyone with the highest piety and clemency; under this property, bodies are said to have received their forms. From this enumeration, therefore, grace and mercy flow into the lower realms through its channel or "bright gate."

But we think it should be noted in passing, as some might ask: what use is this Cabalistic science to us, or how is it to be proved that this or that name of the <term>Tetragrammaton; the four-letter name of God (YHWH)</term> has this or that property, or an inclination toward clemency or severity? To which we respond: it is proved by the effect in the Hebrew text. Hence the property of the name **El** is openly explained by Moses in that he records that he extracted the gift of health from God for his sister Mary <note>Miriam</note> when she was suffering from leprosy in this manner: *El na rapha na la.* **El** means GOD of grace, **rapha** means heal, **na** means I beseech, **la** means her.

Over the fifth enumeration (which is **Geburah**) presides the Name of God **Elohim Gibbor** <note>God the Mighty</note>, in which property God is said to have drawn the elements out of turbid Chaos; and this denotes power, violence, severity, judgment, and the punishment of sinners. This property of God flows into the lower realms—namely into the world—the effects of plague, famine, war, plunder, and desolation; whence it is clear that just as the nature of the Tetragrammaton **El** promised every good to the creatures of the world, so **Elohim Gibbor** seems to announce every evil and turbid outcome, such as occurred in the extraction of the elements from chaos.

The sixth enumeration is **Tiphereth**, which denotes grace and ornament, beauty and delights; the Name of GOD assisting this one is **Eloah**, whence it happens that all those influences poured out from this Channel, or this path, or divine property, give form to the sun, rendering to it clarity, life, and light, and they adorn the heavens according to that passage in Job: *By His spirit He has adorned the heavens,* Job 26:13. And also: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all the host of them by the breath of His mouth,* Psalm 33. From these influences later proceed minerals, of which the prince is gold; vegetables, among which Bread and wine are the princes; and animals, whose head in dignity is man, following the position of the sun in heaven.

The seventh Sephirah is called **Netzach**, namely Triumph or victory. Furthermore, it indicates charity and the love of justice, and from here also follow the influences of multiplication and generation. The Name presiding over this is **Jehovah Sabaoth**, the Lord of Hosts.

The eighth is called **Hod**, namely praise, honor, and beauty. The Name according to its property is **Elohim Sabaoth**, that is, GOD of hosts, yet not for rigor and war, but for piety, justice, and concord.

Over the ninth enumeration presides the Name of GOD **El Chai**, that is, the living GOD, or **Shaddai**, GOD almighty, or self-sufficient; and this enumeration is called **Yesod**, that is, Basis, foundation, redemption, and rest.

The tenth and final Sephirah is called **Malkuth**, that is, kingdom, church, empire, and the temple of GOD; hence the Psalmist says, *for the kingdom is the Lord's,* Psalm 22. The Name of GOD presiding over this is **Adonai**, the Lord, and this enumeration brings severity and servitude to those upon whom it flows.

From these things it can be seen that in all the properties or operations of the divine essence upon the world—whether for punishment and the scourge, or for beneficence—GOD is more prone to clemency and mercy than to severity; for in the property of His first Name, He extends His charity out of the darkness into the world, as a father to a son, whence also **Hermes Trismegistus** calls the world the son of GOD.

In the property of the second, through His wisdom, He is more inclined toward creating things than toward striking the created human race with a plague for their sins, as is explained by the words of GOD to the Israelites: *Behold, I send my angel before thee to keep thee in the way and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared; beware of him,* etc. Exodus 23. But I have shown elsewhere that this angel was Wisdom, which was sent to the Israelites for their preservation, yet with the precaution that they should not commit evil, because He says, *he will not bear your transgressions.* Whence it is clear that God is more inclined in this property toward doing good than toward the scourge. In the property of the third Name, severity and punishment are included, for the name **Elohim** is by its nature terrible; whence it happens that as the name of the first Sephirah, namely **Ehyeh**, related to the Father, is attributed to the Empyrean heaven, the place of the blessed and of rest; and...
