### CHAPTER XI.

### How the Spirit of Wisdom, expanded everywhere in the world and informing and fostering its moist nature, informs, creates, and preserves all creatures within it that are composed of elements, until they finally perish.

...a certain invisible fire, from which they acknowledge all things to have been born. It is as if they understood that Spirit of the Lord (which is a fiery love) when it was carried over the waters, imparting a certain fiery vigor and, as it were, "Being" to them. Hence, for this reason, the world was called a "living animal" by some, whose heart they claimed was the sun; similarly, they called the stars "living animals," and believed that the souls of all particular things in the world were intelligent participants of the divine mind. They announced, not without reason, that these souls were rays or sparks emanating from that entire luminous nature. For this cause, therefore, they recognized that a soul presides over every single thing, and consequently Democritus and Orpheus, along with many of the Pythagoreans, were of the opinion that all things are full of Gods. To these they established divine honors, dedicated sacrifices and prayers, and worshipped them with diverse rituals.

Furthermore, they reduced all such souls to a single "Soul of the World" <note>This concept, known as the *Anima Mundi*, suggests that the entire universe possesses a single underlying soul that connects all living things.</note>, and consequently referred all Gods back to a single Jupiter. From this source, therefore, proceeded all the errors of the pagans in their adoration; from here, I have no doubt, emanated the fictions of the Poets, the diabolical sacrifices, and the sacrilegious offerings. From this, the land of Egypt worshipped and adored certain animals and other monsters and portents. But concerning various types of such Idolatry—where, specifically, the creature is worshipped instead of the creator—the scriptures speak everywhere, namely regarding the profane worship of stars, devils, men, and others of that kind.

In this, therefore, those Philosophers were deceived: they did not distinguish the simple uncreated light (that is, the creative nature) from the "moist" created nature. Instead, they considered only the created light—that is, the whole illuminated moist nature, namely the "angel" or "otherness" (as the Kabbalists <note>The Kabbalists are practitioners of Jewish mysticism; "otherness" here refers to the state of being separate from God's absolute unity.</note> have it)—and not that Unity which preceded it. Hence some of them said fire was God, others air; some made the earth a divinity, others water, and so on.

But indeed, in saying that all things are full of Gods—or rather, animated and filled with sparks of divinity, all of which they referred to a single Jupiter—or that all things are endowed with luminous souls which they taught have a relation to the single soul of the world, they do not seem to differ from the sense of the Hebrew Doctors, or even from Holy Scripture. For *Rabbi Bereshit* <note>Likely referring to the author of a commentary on Genesis (Bereshit).</note> says that the creator daily creates a gathering of angels, whom others call "forms," inasmuch as they are formal substances with which the entire sphere of things that can be born or decay is filled without number. Of these Angelic forms, the *Porta Lucis* <note>original: "Porta lucis"; this refers to *Sha'are Orah* (Gates of Light) by Joseph Gikatilla, a fundamental text of Kabbalah.</note> has this to say: *From the earth even unto the firmament there is no empty place, but everything is full of forms; some of them are pure, some are capable of grace and mercy, and below there are many foul, harmful, and tempting shapes, etc.* From which he seems to imply that all forms, both good and bad, are like angels; but of these we shall speak elsewhere.

Regardless, we see that just as all these forms in the world are like sparks of divinity and rays of one spirit—assigned with various properties and shapes either for the preservation of life or for its destruction, as is sufficiently explained in the divine properties inscribed on the Sephirotic Tree <note>The Sephirotic Tree (or Tree of Life) is a symbolic diagram in Kabbalah representing the ten attributes through which the Infinite reveals Himself and creates the universe.</note>—nevertheless, all these pure forms or rays of divinity are no less to be divided from their fullness of essence than solar rays are from the Sun. And although, by the divine will, they are enclosed in various dark tabernacles (both foul and pure) to execute His various commands, they themselves, as sparks of truth, will ultimately return to the fountain of unity from which they went forth. Concerning this matter, the Apostle speaks thus: *GOD will be all in all, when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father. 1 Corinthians 15.* <note>original: "DEVS erit omne in omnibus, cum Christus patris regnum obtinuerit."</note> Nor do the Holy Scriptures seem to distance themselves from the aforementioned opinion, in which we have it that Christ fills all things. And elsewhere: *GOD, not needing anything, gives to all life and breath and all things, Acts 17.* <note>original: "DEVS non aliquo indigens dat omnibus vitam & inspirationem & omnia."</note> And elsewhere: *In GOD himself we live and move and are, Acts 17:28.* <note>original: "In DEO ipso viuimus & mouemur & sumus."</note> And the wise man gives a reason for this thing, because, he says, *the incorruptible spirit of GOD is in every thing, Wisdom 12:1.* <note>original: "spiritus DEI incorruptibilis est in omni re."</note> which in another place he calls a "pure emanation or flow of the brightness of the almighty GOD" and the "brightness of eternal light," which gives life to all things (*Wisdom 7*).

We conclude, therefore, that it is certain that the life and being of every creature is from GOD, and is like a fiery impression from the "Character" or divine Seal of the Word (which the Kabbalists call *Emeth* <note>Hebrew for "Truth."</note>) or a ray from the shining Word, which is more abundant and flowing in one creature than in another—for example, in the sun of heaven and in the Man of earth. Hence the Evangelist says, *in the word is life, and this life is the light of men.* And of the other it is said, *by his spirit he adorned the heavens.* And for this reason also it is said that GOD saw all things created by Him were *good, Genesis 1.* That is, insofar as they participated in the divine essence, which is alone goodness and truth, as the holy scriptures testify.

## CHAPTER XII.

## On the Void and the Full.

At this point, we believe it to be of no small value to declare to you what that **void** <note>original: "vacuum"</note> is—which is so avoided by nature—and what the **full** <note>original: "plenum"</note> is. The solution to this doubt seems especially relevant and necessary to our current purpose. For the fathers of Philosophy, as well as those who adhere to the sacred scriptures in Theosophy, have said that this **Void** is **Nothing**.

**Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," a legendary Hellenistic figure often credited with ancient wisdom and the founding of alchemy.</note> calls this a **horrendous Shadow**, destitute of all form; the **Kabbalists** <note>Mystics of the Jewish tradition who sought to understand the divine nature through the study of the Hebrew alphabet and numbers.</note> call it the **potential Principle** looking toward nothing. **Plato**, in his *Timaeus*, says it is a thing without sense, barely perceptible, and hardly credible through "spurious reasoning" <note>original: "ratiocinatione spuria." This refers to Plato's difficult concept of "space" or "receptacle" (khora), which is neither physical matter nor pure idea.</note>; he makes it out to be a fear, as if it were a dream. And **Augustine** says: *When I conceive of something formless, I understand "nothing" before I understood what I was thinking; just as by seeing nothing, darkness is seen, and by hearing nothing, silence is heard.* From this, he seems to compare it to **Darkness** and **silence**. **Job** says, *God stretches out the North over the empty place and the void, and hangs the earth upon nothing,* Job 26:7. And elsewhere, *He reveals foundations out of darkness, and brings the shadow of death into the light,* Job 12:22. By these words, he seems to argue that the **Empty**, the **Void**, **Nothing**, **Darkness**, and the **Shadow** are the same thing.

Specifically, it is called **Empty** and **Void** because all fullness comes from **GOD**; but since **GOD**, the parent of light, had not yet shone upon the world, and insofar as the first matter of the world was destitute of all grace and deprived of goodness, it was called **Empty** and **Void**—indeed, it was called darkness and the shadow of death, insofar as it entirely lacked the rays of life. Thus the earth was called empty and void, and it was said that darkness was over the face of the abyss before the Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters. But after the appearance of the said Spirit, it was said: *And God called the dry land Earth, and God saw that it was good, and it produced tender herbs and seed of every kind, and trees bringing forth fruit, etc.* Genesis 1. Wherefore the earth, once empty and void, has now been made full of divine grace; hence it is rendered not empty, but fertile; not void, but completed on all sides by divine fire and incorruptible rays. *The hand of the Almighty created the world from formless matter,* Wisdom 11:12 <note>This refers to the "Hand of God" as the Word or Spirit emanating from His mouth, giving shape to the chaos.</note>. Here, by "hand," he indicates the Word or the Spirit emanating from His mouth. Hence the Apostle **Peter** says, *The heavens were of old, and the earth out of water and through water, by means of the word,* 2 Peter 3; that is, by a holy emanation. By this light (says **John**) the world was made. Indeed, where the rays of that informing divinity <note>In this context, "informing" means giving *form* or essential nature to something, rather than providing information.</note> are absent, there is the **greatest void**—that is, the absence of complete form.

And this is why the **void** seems so horrendous in the kingdom of nature, for every thing, by a natural appetite, greatly desires to be **informed** <note>Given form.</note>; wherefore not only a particular nature, but even that universal parent of all particulars, is accustomed to abhor and avoid deformity above all things. From this, therefore, it is clear that all fullness in nature is from the divine abundance, which fills all things in the world by its power so that, from nothing and emptiness, something actually formal and relatively existing might be made. This gift of existence they received from **Christ**, or **Wisdom**; hence it is written that *Christ fills all things,* Ephesians 4. And elsewhere: *The holy spirit of discipline fills the whole world,* Wisdom 1. Wherefore, unless **GOD** had filled all things in the world, there would be void and nothing in the world; but because He Himself created all things by His presence, it is therefore necessary that nothing in the world exist as a void.

...created the earth in numbers, and this is confirmed by the testimony of the royal prophet <note>referring to King David</note>, from whom we have: *Give thanks to the Lord of lords, who made the heavens in wisdom, for his mercy endures forever; who established the earth above the waters, for his mercy endures forever. Who made the great lights, for his mercy endures forever, the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night, for his mercy endures forever, Psalm 135.* <note>original: "Pfal. 135." This corresponds to Psalm 136 in modern English Bibles.</note>

This is, in its own property, assigned to the first numbering or Sephirotic manifestation, namely **Ehieh** <note>The Hebrew name for God meaning "I Am," associated with the highest point of creation.</note>, which name presides over **Kether** <note>original: "Cheter," meaning "the Crown," the first Sephirah in the Kabbalah.</note> or the Crown, and is attributed to the Father and to Mercy. From this, we have the reason why God, who is free in himself, willed to create the world with its creatures: namely, out of his sheer clemency and mercy toward formless things. That is, from empty things veiled in darkness or lethal shadows, he would procreate good things adorned with divine beauty. He infused every creature with a living soul or a spark from his own luminous fountain, by which it might live and exist in its own being. For this, they first desire to return great thanks to him, and then they proceed to fulfill the duty assigned to each by God and to faithfully carry out the creator's commands. Regarding the giving of thanks, we read in the royal Psalmist: *Praise God from the heavens, praise him all his angels, and all his powers. Praise him Sun and Moon, praise him all stars and light, praise him heaven of heavens, and all waters that are above the heaven, let them praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were created. Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit or wind of storms, which do his word, etc. Psalm 148.* Here he surveys all creatures, both terrestrial and aquatic.

But to declare the office of the stars, we say with the Prophet in the place cited before, that he made the **Sun** to have dominion over the day, and the **Moon** and other stars, both fixed and wandering <note>original: "erraticas," referring to the planets</note>, to have power over the night, and this because of his benevolence. Regarding the substance or consistency of the stars, both fixed and wandering, it seems to be very clean and pure, so that they might better receive their luminous forms from the creator. This also seems to be confirmed by these words: *The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God, much less men, Job 25:5.* From this speech, it appears that they are indeed very pure, though not absolutely pure as they appear in the sight of God. Yet if they were not very pure and polished in their substances, they would be least capable of receiving such splendid forms; for as **Plato** rightly says, form is given by the creator according to the merit of the matter. However, because their substance varies in purity, it is said by the Apostle: *That star differs from star in clarity, 1 Corinthians 15.*

It remains now to discuss briefly the property and influence of the fixed stars, among which we read: *that God alone, stretching out the heavens, made Orion, the Pleiades or Hyades, and the stars of the inner chambers of the South, Job 9:9.* <note>The text cites Job 32:4, but the quote is found in Job 9:9.</note> and elsewhere, mention is made of the *circuit of Arcturus or the belt of Orion, Job 38.* Also the Prophet speaks thus: *It is God who makes Arcturus and Orion, who turns darkness into morning and changes day into night, Yahweh is his name, Amos 5.* All these stars of the firmament are numbered by our great God, great in Virtues, whose wisdom is without number; he counts however many stars there are and has called them by their own names, as **David** testifies in *Psalm 147.* To these he undoubtedly assigned names based on their various properties, thereby declaring that many hidden properties reside in them beyond the common and vulgar one—namely, that they have dominion over the night. For it is not likely that he would have assigned them various shapes in splendor and figure if they did not have other faculties over creatures. Especially since the Prophet adds: *He calls however many there are by name, our great Lord, of many strengths or virtues, whose wisdom is without number.* From this it is argued that he, who is great in virtues and of innumerable wisdom, also assigned various virtues to the innumerable stars of the firmament. This can also be understood through these words: *Do you know the laws of Heaven? Do you set its dominion upon the earth? Job 38:31.* By which the creator seems to indicate that heaven, through its "army" <note>the stars</note>, is accustomed to work in various forms upon the earth. Hence, by some, the heaven is most aptly likened to the husband and the earth to the wife; consequently, every particular star of the heaven or firmament has a particular virtue of influencing particular things, whether animal, vegetable, or mineral. 

For example, it is handed down and confirmed by experience itself that the **Pole Star**, called *Alracuba* <note>An Arabic name for the constellation of the Little Bear or the Pole Star.</note> by the Egyptians, having the nature of **Saturn** and **Venus**, attracts the magnet-stone to itself, as appears in the mariner's needle. And that same magnet attracts iron to itself, provided that a diamond <note>original: "adamas"</note> is not present, for the diamond by its presence hinders the influences of the said star. And **Cecco d'Ascoli** <note>original: "Cichus Eſculanus," a 13th-century astronomer and poet.</note>, writing on the sphere in the place where he speaks of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, affirms that each of the 12 signs receives its particular and special name from the nature and property of some animal of the earth, the nature of one of which seems to symbolize the nature of the other. And **Moses the Arabian** <note>original: "Moſeus Arabicus," referring to Maimonides.</note> says that every living thing claims for itself a peculiar star in heaven, from which at every moment it draws and receives influence to protect and sustain its essence, and he says this is done by divine command and will. Thus the stars in the body of **Aries** in heaven have a relation to such animals on earth, and the **Scorpio** of that place to the scorpion of this, and so in the rest. For this reason, **Diodorus Siculus**, speaking generally, not foolishly confesses that the lower is ruled by the higher, and the lower world is [subject] to that superior one.

We say, therefore, that just as the Angelic world is a type <note>a symbolic model or pattern</note> of that Divine world, so too the celestial world is an image of that Angelic one. Therefore, just as the Angelic world receives influence immediately from the archetypal world and pours it into the celestial world, so also the celestial world is a likeness of the terrestrial world. Consequently, its "army" <note>the stars and planets</note> sends its influences immediately into the creatures of the earth that are most conformed to them in nature and disposition.

We conclude, therefore, with the sacred Priest in 4 Esdras 16, that the stars were founded in the Word or Wisdom of the Lord, who also knows the number of the stars and has imposed upon each of them a name most fitting to its property. We conclude that every one of them, by its own property, has a relationship to terrestrial creatures, through which it continually pours its influences into similar creatures by the direction of the intelligences <note>spiritual beings or angels</note> who preside over them, and who take care of lower things by the divine will and command.

->**On the creation of the wandering stars in general, and especially on the Sun and its creation, dignity, utility, motion, and obedience toward its Creator.**<-

In our discourse on the physical subject of the macrocosm <note>the great world or universe</note>, where I spoke at length regarding the origin of the fixed stars, I proposed a certain doubt: namely, whether the fixed stars were created on the fourth day of creation along with the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, or at least on the second day. We expressed our reasons there, by which we proved it likely that they were established on the second day of creation. Indeed, if we consider the orders of the Sephirot <note>original: "sephirotarum," the ten emanations of God in Kabbalistic thought</note> or "numberings" of the Kabbalists and the reason for their influences, we will perceive that just as the influence of **Kether** <note>original: "Cheter," meaning "The Crown," the first Sephirah</note>—which is the crown or first numbering—flows through the Seraphic order of Angels into the *Primum Mobile* <note>the "First Moved" sphere that carries all others</note>, so **Chokhmah** <note>original: "Hochma," meaning "Wisdom," the second Sephirah</note> flows through the order of Cherubim into the starry heaven. If that heaven were empty and without stars, it would receive those influences from Chokhmah in vain. But we shall now proceed briefly to the production of the planets, or wandering stars, and their creation within their orbits.

It is most certain, and to be granted without controversy, that all stars are created by God himself, as we have confirmed by many testimonies of Holy Scripture. "The Sun," says Moses, "the Moon, the stars, and others, God created for the service of all nations under heaven" (Deuteronomy 4:19). However, how each of these stars has an intelligence presiding over it, which receives influences from the "shining Sephirotic gates," and what the duties of said angels are, both in the ethereal heaven and the elementary region, and who is their Prince—all this we shall discuss copiously in the second member of this part.

In this place, however, we shall primarily hold a discourse concerning the most noble creature of the celestial bodies: the king of stars, the corporeal Emperor of the heavens, the heart of the firmament, and the clearest eye of the world—namely, the visible Sun. So that we may arrive at a better understanding of it, we shall first speak a few words concerning the invisible and uncreated Sun, which is the life and light of this created sun.

            *   With its motion, it carries the spirit of the world along with it.
            *   With its light, it animates and illuminates that spirit, and provides life to composite creatures.
            *   With its heat, it cherishes and preserves all things.
        *   Secondary and from its effect, which:
            *   Generates and corrupts <note>In alchemy and natural philosophy, "corruption" is the necessary breakdown of matter that precedes new growth.</note>.
            *   Multiplies life by its own seed.
            *   Illuminates the bodies of the stars and pours the seed of life into them.
    *   **Dignity** which arises:
        *   From its origin and lineage.
        *   From light and grace.
        *   From the command it holds over the material world.
        *   From its primary and principal or royal office: for it is the house or palace of the archetypal <note>The "archetypal world" refers to the original divine blueprint or the mind of God.</note> king.
    *   **Obedience necessary in:**
        *   Its direct motion according to the ordained laws of nature.
        *   Retrogression <note>The appearance of moving backward in the sky.</note> and Station <note>Appearing to stand still.</note> which occur beyond the common custom of nature.
    *   **Passion and patience in the deprivation of its light and, as it were, its life.** <note>A reference to solar eclipses.</note>
    *   **Transfiguration, exaltation, and resurrection, as it were.**

**CHAPTER XIV.**

**Second Part.**

***Concerning the Uncreated Sun.***

**H**ermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, which explores the relationship between the divine, the cosmos, and humanity.</note> seems to acknowledge that the whole and entire world, constituted from the elements, proceeds and is led by that one who is abundantly full of the fertility of all things, of both one and the other sex, containing in himself every power of generating without any other assistance. Whence he is also called **PAN** <note>Pan, the Greek god of nature, whose name also means "All."</note> by the poets, as if to say the "Whole" and the "Universal." The Arcadians, thinking him to be the sun, worshiped him as the true GOD. Their error seemed to lie in this: that they falsely accepted and worshiped the creature in place of the creator, and the visible and created sun in place of that invisible and uncreated one—that is, the royal palace in place of the King of kings, who built it and inhabited it centrally. Regarding this uncreated and invisible sun, not only the wiser of the Philosophers but also the sacred scriptures have made rich and copious mention. For among those most skilled in Philosophy, Plato—indicating that wonderful consonance which exists between that sun of the world and that of the supreme order—calls the mundane sun the shining son of the supreme Good; not the first son, but the second, through whom we reach the knowledge of the first. Hence says the wise man: *the sun that giveth light looketh upon all things, and his work is full of the glory of the Lord.* <note>original: "sol illuminans per omnia respicit, & gloria Domini plenum est opus eius."</note> *Ecclesiasticus 42.* Which glory is indeed the divine essence itself, covered and veiled in luminous garments; for which reason it was also said by the royal Prophet <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>, *that God is clothed with light as with a garment,* and in another place, *that he hath set his tabernacle in the sun. And the Israelites were commanded to revere [this presence] with every effort: *My angel (says Jehovah) will not bear your defections, because my name is in him, Exodus 23.* <note>original: "Non feret angelus meus (inquit Iehoua) defectiones vestras, quoniam nomen meum est in eo."</note> That is to say: I wish for you to obey his voice, because my Word—which is your creator—is in him. This means, "do this, because I am in him," or "I will be present," whom alone and no other you ought to adore. It is not, therefore, in honor of the physical sun that the wise man speaks these words: *It is necessary to precede the sun for your blessing and to adore you at the rising of the light, Wisdom 16:28.* <note>The source text cites Wisdom 10, but the passage "prevent the sun to give thee thanks" is traditionally Wisdom 16:28.</note> Nor is it because the Prophet Daniel looked toward the eastern region while praying, or because it is the custom and habit of Christians to pour out our prayers with our faces turned toward the east. Rather, it is so that we may worship Him with every effort—He who gave form to so excellent a vessel, and who established his tabernacle in this polished vessel which he chose for his instrument. He did this so that from it, as if from a visible sanctuary of life, he might rain down life, multiplication, and visible light everywhere upon the world and its parts. In this way, the Creator provides solace and joy both to opaque bodies (to which the invisible light is least apparent) and to the soul sustained by invisible light; and also, by this means, he reveals himself and manifests the grace of his essence to both earthly and celestial beings, to both bodies and spirits. Whence he is rightly called the **God of soul and body, the God of all spirits, and the God of all flesh.**

Finally, this sun is called in the highest heaven *Ehieh* <note>The Hebrew name for God, "I AM" (Exodus 3:14).</note> the Father, or God giving grace and glory; in the Empyrean <note>The highest part of heaven, believed by ancient cosmologists to be composed of pure fire or light.</note> he is Wisdom clearer than the sun; and plunging himself more deeply into the matter of the world, he placed his tabernacle in the sun and flashes in the thick clouds and speaks with the voice of thunder. *Revelation 22.* In Christ the man, he is called the **bright morning star**; a star (says the Holy Page) shall rise out of Jacob, *Numbers 24.* And elsewhere, the **Sun of Justice,** *Malachi 4,* who is promised to rise for those who fear his name, with healing in his wings; whence he is also called **Jesus**. Furthermore, Jesus Christ is called in many places of the scriptures the sole fullness of his own light, of life, and of all good things; whence also he is the **Word, the light of the world shining in the darkness, John 1.** But I would like us to arrive at the examination—or the "Lydian stone" <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here used metaphorically as a test of truth.</note>—of these matters. The wise Philosophers say that a thing is usually finished in that which it had its origin. Therefore, if we wish to inquire into and prove the beginning of the mundane sun, we shall perceive it best from its end. For in the holy letters we have this: *Thy sun shall set no more; thy moon shall not be diminished, because the Lord shall be unto thee, Jerusalem, for a light; Isaiah 60.* And with this place agrees that of John: *And the city hath no need of the sun nor of the moon to shine in it; for the clarity of God shall enlighten it, and the lamb is the lamp thereof: and the nations shall walk in his light; and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into it, Revelation 21:23.* By these things it is indicated that in the final days of the world, this celestial sun will cast off its thick and dark garments: and it will appear as it truly is. For there is no truth except in the true light of the world, which reveals all fictions and reduces them to nothing by the Lydian test. For by such an examination, the moon in the final days will have the clarity of the sun by laying aside its created garments; and the truly central and divine Sun, by stripping off its thick and created clothing, will be in its naked and clear nature, providing light to the blessed servants of God in their purification and, as it were, resurrection. This is no different (though in a far more exalted degree) than the common sun or the sun visible in the sky; which indeed we can clearly gather from these words of the Prophet: *The light of the moon (he says) shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, Isaiah 30:26.* That is, seven times as bright. And the Apostle speaks to this sense, saying: *There shall be one clarity of the sun, another of the moon, and another of the stars, 1 Corinthians 15.* From which it is right to gather that in the end, everything that is a fiction shall perish and be abolished, and be thrust down into the vast abyss of Nothingness; but that which is of the simple truth (with which God filled the entire universe), all that shall return into its fountain of unity by being purified through a fiery purification. And the Holy Bibles seem to confirm those things which were said above: for it is said that God fills all things: *That from God and through God are all things, Romans 11.* That *God is the father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all, Ephesians 4:6.* And that *God works all things in all, 1 Corinthians 12.* Whence, since he himself is the only truth, it is necessary that nothing be true unless it is of his essence. Therefore we say finally, that just as God was the beginning of solar beauty—that is, if his glory is the cause of the excellence of the solar creature—once the fiction is laid aside, it will be far more beautiful, just as it was in the beginning. That is, in its first emanation, when it was called *Hochma* <note>The Hebrew word for "Wisdom," often associated with the first manifestation of light in Kabbalistic thought.</note> or divine wisdom, which is the brightness of the light of the Almighty. So it was in the beginning, and its beginning shall be justified by its end, inasmuch as he is the **Alpha and Omega, Revelation 1,** the beginning and the end. Hence the Apostle says: *God shall be all in all when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father, 1 Corinthians 15.* Whence also he said elsewhere: *When I am exalted, I will draw all things to myself,* that is, everything which is of purity and truth; for nothing is to be regarded as nothing in its mere nature, nor as void and empty.

But let us proceed rapidly to the nature of our created sun—that is, the solar creature.

"By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their virtues" <note>original: "virtutes," often translated as "powers" or "hosts"</note> or armies, Psalm 33. And that distinguished priest Esdras denotes this with these express words: "the stars were founded in the word of the Lord," 2 Esdras 16:55. But truly, to treat the specific manner of this creature’s origin, and to immerse oneself in its mysteries, will seem somewhat difficult for a human, unless we look into the Holy Scriptures with <term>lynx-like eyes</term> <note>A common early modern metaphor for sharp, penetrating vision capable of seeing through solid objects or into deep mysteries.</note>. Regarding its matter, then, it is certain that it has the consistency of a very clear, highly polished, and exceedingly spiritual earth, which emerged from the darkness (after the bright rays of divine wisdom were reflected into the center of the world, as has been declared in our Macrocosmic history). By the help of divine rays, it was exalted in the marrow of the heavens like molten metal and illuminated on all sides by the rays of divine grace and beauty. Thus was the body of Adam formed from chosen mud, animated and quickened by the breath of life and the bright spirit of the Almighty, and formed in the image of the Omnipotent. Thus the earth is said to give birth to the Savior; and our Savior, rising from the tomb and emerging from the gape of death or the lethal shadow of darkness like the morning star, ascended into heaven clothed everywhere in celestial spirit. Why then should the created sun refuse the "earth" as the parent of its consistency, seeing as it is the condensed spirit of a celestial nature, in whose marrow the uncreated Light of the World placed its tabernacle, as the royal Psalmist teaches us? Furthermore, we see that just as our Savior rose from the darkness of death and the abyss of the tomb on the third day, so indeed after the third day of creation—and not before—was there any mention made of the creation of the greater light. Before this, the fixation of the earth in the center of the world, or its suspension over nothingness, had been established. From this it is likely that the sun ascended from the earth, having stripped off its dark filth, as if from a tomb—for in the sun is the tabernacle of the invisible and divine Sun, which acts as a most brilliant soul to that highly polished body. But however we read it, that ethereal matter is so involved in a spherical mouth, so pure in its consistency, that it is called by the wise man a "vessel, the admirable work of the Most High," Ecclesiasticus 43:2. And in that it is announced elsewhere, "The Sun, the work of the Lord, is full of his glory," Ecclesiasticus 42:16, and elsewhere, "that he placed his tabernacle in it," it is clear that it is a vessel in nature that is exceedingly clean and polished. For otherwise, it would not be capable of containing a form so pure and simple, since form is usually given according to the merits of the matter. And yet it is impossible, through the entire created spirit, for matter so exquisitely pure to be given that it could merit a form as pure and simple as that divine essence, which is without any stain or impurity. Hence it is written first of the angels and then after of the stars, that in respect to the sincere purity of the divine essence, they are not pure. Regarding these stars, it is written: "The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God," Job 25:5. Of those angels, indeed, we read these words: "Behold, God found wickedness in his angels," etc., Job 4:18 <note>The text cites Job 14:17, but the quote corresponds to Job 4:18 or 15:15.</note>. For it is impossible that a created thing could be equated in its Being to the essence of the Creator. But truly, among all visible bodies, it is certain that the solar substance is the purest; this is declared because the visible glory of God is indicated more to mortals in it than in any other creature of the world. And hence it is said by Augustine, that as much light as something has in itself, so much more of God it seems to claim for itself. Hence also the wise man says of the sun: "The sun illuminating looked upon all things, and his work is full of the glory of the Lord," Ecclesiasticus 42:16. From this it is evident that the presence of that divine glory denotes the purity of the <term>subject</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "subject" is the matter or underlying thing that receives a "form" or quality.</note> into which it enters. For in holy writing we read everywhere that the Holy Spirit does not descend except into a pure spirit or a clean heart—that is, into a purified subject. For such must be the respect between the bridegroom and the bride, between Cupid and Psyche, between Christ and the Church, between the mind and the spirit, or there will be no firm bond or coupling between them.

Hence, therefore, we ought to gather that insofar as the mundane sun is a creature, and like a shadow of the majesty of the archetypal sun, it is in no way to be worshiped as God by mortals who are consistent in themselves and not seized by diabolical madness. For this would be to adore the house instead of the master, just as those twenty-five men did who (as Ezekiel witnesses) between the porch and the altar, with their faces toward the east, adored the rising of the sun, having their backs against the temple of the Lord. Concerning them, God spoke to the Prophet: "Is this a light thing, that they should commit these abominations which they commit here? For they have filled the land with iniquity," etc., Ezekiel 8:16-17. But the sacred page also reproves this in express speech: "Thou shalt not look upon the sun, the moon, or the stars, or any thing of the host of heaven, so as to bow down and worship them," Deuteronomy 4:19. It is as if he had said: Jehovah is the one and only God the Creator; to Him alone you must offer worship, and not to the images created by Him—that is, to the Lord who creates, and not to the servant or minister who is created. "The Lord is he who made the Sun," says the wise man, "in whose words it hastened its journey." And elsewhere this is expressly explained in this manner: "God created the sun, moon, stars and others to be in service to all nations under heaven," therefore he forbade them to be adored and worshiped. It is as if he said: I am the creator, therefore the things I created are not to be adored, but I alone the creator. But how ridiculous would it be to a wise man to revere a servant with honor and not think of the Lord, or to bestow the smallest praises while rejecting and neglecting the greater? What, I ask, is the body, or the soul, or the thing informed, without its form imparting life and glory? Truly nothing, a void, and plainly a deformed and horrendous shadow, as if someone chose the shadow for the true God, but rejected the true subject as nothing. This indeed is the way of the worldly, overwhelmed by darkness and ignorance, who choose things that are seen and are least significant, instead of those things which truly are but are least seen, choosing in the manner of the blind. Open therefore, O blind mortals, those eyes which Adam closed because of his sins; and close your carnal eyes, which in a deceptive manner think they see those things which are not, but truly are not powerful enough to penetrate to those things which are.

### CHAPTER XV.

### On the Manifold Power and Utility of the Sun.

The primary power <note>original: *virtus*; in this context, it refers to an inherent capability or active influence rather than moral virtue.</note> of the Sun consists in its light, motion, and heat, just as its secondary power is usually derived from these same effects. Therefore, we shall speak a little more broadly about both the primary and secondary powers as they are mingled together; and first, concerning Light.

As it is certain, and confirmed by the preceding arguments, that GOD is the fountain of light, this primary light made its emanation the first act or motion. By this, the *primum mobile* <term>the first moved</term> <note>In the traditional geocentric model of the universe, this is the outermost sphere that imparts motion to all the lower celestial spheres.</note> of the world—that is, the highest circle of the world’s subtle spirit—was carried around; by its motion, all the enclosed spheres are also rotated along their circumference. The effect of this mobility or mobile act is heat, just as, conversely, the dull and insensible state of rest is the parent of coldness. Among these celestial matrices <note>original: *matrices*; in this context, a "matrix" refers to a cosmic womb or mold that receives spiritual influences and gives them physical form.</note>, however, the moon is that common one which receives the seeds <note>original: *feminaria*; refers to "seminal principles" or the spiritual "blueprints" of life.</note> both immediately from the sun and mediately—that is, immediately from the higher stars—and distributes them everywhere to the air as well as to the water and the earth; for she is the common matrix of all the stars in general. Therefore, Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the divine nature of the cosmos.</note> and many others conclude that in Phoebus <note>A classical name for Apollo, used here to represent the Sun.</note>, who shines with a golden mane and holds the scepter and helm of the world like a king, all the virtues of the celestial beings reside. And Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist who argued that the Sun acted as a unifying force for all planetary powers.</note> testifies that at the sight of the sun, all the powers of all celestial beings are gathered into one and, as it were, collected together; these powers we believe are finally disseminated into this lower world through fiery breathing-holes <note>original: *ignea spiracula*; these were thought to be invisible channels or "pores" in the atmosphere through which celestial energy reached the Earth.</note>. Does not annual experience also prove that when the sun turns toward us, the earth grows green and reaches its youth; when the sun stands perpendicularly above us, it greatly heats and matures; and when it hastens and departs toward the fourth winter quarter, the plants and herbs lose their flowers and languish day by day as if from a disease? <meta>This page continues the exploration of the Sun as a divine symbol, moving from its role as an image of the Holy Spirit to its moral qualities—specifically its obedience to the Creator—and its "passions" or eclipses, which the author links to the death of Christ.</meta>

186 **Section I, Portion IV, Part II. Book IV. Member I.**

Thus those three in the fiery furnace, glorifying God with one voice, said, *Bless the Lord, O Sun and Moon; praise and exalt him above all forever* <note>original: "Benedicite Sol & Luna domino, Laudate & superexaltate eum in secula"; a quote from the Song of the Three Holy Children, an addition to the Book of Daniel.</note>. So also it is said elsewhere, that *the Sun knows its going down, Psalm 104:19.* From these few examples, therefore, it is right to conclude how great is the obedience of this solar creature toward its Creator. This suggests that man—a vessel most excellent in his creation but most perverse by nature—should yearn to offer his own obedience and duty according to the will of his Creator, and strive with his greatest effort to shine in such glory as the solar creature flashes forth in its justice. For according to that saying of the Evangelist, *the righteous will shine like the Sun in the kingdom of their Father* <note>Matthew 13:43</note>. For we believe that the image of Adam living in Paradise before the Fall was everywhere glowing and splendid, flashing with the glory of the divine light dwelling within him, being a vessel shaped by the very finger of God the Father of Light. Do we not read that the stone tablets, inscribed by the finger of God and entrusted to Moses, flashed with a sapphirine brightness in the eyes of those who beheld them? So also we read that the face of Moses (though he was still stained by the mark of mortality) so excelled in light that the Israelites could not look upon his face without a veil or covering. How much more so Adam, who was not in the least contaminated by the stain and blot of mortality before his disobedience?

Finally, we come now to the passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to suffering or undergoing a change, specifically the darkening of the Sun.</note> of the sun, which we gather it has undergone many times in the history of this world, not only from the sacred scriptures but also from the authority of trustworthy authors. *The sun is darkened at its rising,* says the Prophet, *Isaiah 13.* And elsewhere, *Your sun shall set no more, for the Lord will be your light, O Jerusalem: Isaiah 60.* And in Joel we find that *the sun shall be turned into darkness before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, Joel 2.* And elsewhere, *The sun and the moon are darkened, Joel 3,* so that in its place the Sun of Justice may rise for those who fear the Lord, as we have in the Prophet Malachi, *Malachi 4.* And in Ecclesiastes we have that *the sun, the light of the stars, and the moon shall grow dark for man, Ecclesiastes 12.* And in Saint Matthew, *the sun will be darkened immediately after the tribulation of those days, Matthew 24.* Finally, at the passion of the primary Sun—or rather, at the death and passion of His very tabernacle <note>The "tabernacle" refers to the physical body of Christ.</note>—the secondary and celestial sun lost its light and was darkened. It was as if, when the life of His fleshy tabernacle failed, that celestial sun also suffered death, or the deprivation of its lucid form, for a great space of time through an inseparable consensus. Regarding this deprivation of solar form or life, Eusebius writes thus: *In the 4th year of the 202nd Olympiad, a great and excellent failure of the sun occurred among all those that happened before; at the sixth hour, the day was turned into such a dark night that stars were seen in the sky, and there was an earthquake in Bithynia.* Thus he wrote; similarly Lucian of Antioch, a Martyr, while in his torments, cried out this to the judges of the infidels and the executioners: *Search in your annals and you will find that in the times of Pilate, while Christ was suffering, the sun was obscured and the day interrupted by darkness.* Furthermore, it is most certain and confirmed by three reasons that this solar passion was **miraculous and marvelous**, and beyond the ordinary failures of the sun <note>Meaning natural solar eclipses.</note> in which the Sun does not truly fail, but the body of the moon is placed between its sight and our eyes.

The first reason is that this passion occurred against the order of natural solar eclipses, which never happen when the moon is full—that is, when it is in opposition to the Sun—yet this failure of the Sun, a kind of fainting <note>original: "syncope"; used here to describe the sudden loss of light as a medical "faint" of the cosmos.</note>, occurred immediately after the opposition of the luminaries. Second, that the part of the sun toward the east was veiled and overshadowed first, and the same part was later re-illuminated first, from which it is clear that it occurred against the common laws of nature. Third (and what would seem monstrous and incredible to all), that in the hour of the eclipse, the moon moved against its own natural course—namely, from east to west—when its natural motion is from west to east; and then, immediately after the passion ended, it was observed to travel in its natural motion. From these things we must conclude that even this passion and failure was real, according to the nature of the solar body itself, and not merely in respect to us (as is the case in a normal eclipse).

And for this reason, this passion or failure was universal, which cannot happen to those caused by the moon's interposition between the earth and the sun. We conclude from these things, therefore, that in the first place, when the life of the tabernacle of the uncreated Sun failed on earth, that sun in heaven was also affected by a kind of fainting, and seemed to be deprived of its trial and lucid form. It was as if that lucid spirit, establishing its temple and tabernacle in both subjects, hated such an inhuman and cruel act and turned its shining face away from both worlds for some space of time. We see also from these things that this solar body is a creature subject to the will of GOD, either for life or for the deprivation of its light. Consequently, we see that GOD by no means acts in this world in the ordinary course of nature out of necessity or as if compelled, as that foolish assertion of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, whom the author critiques for believing God/Nature acts by fixed, mechanical necessity rather than free divine will.</note> suggests.

Finally, that the sun will be transfigured from its state on the last day and rendered seven times more splendid in its light—that is, that stripping off its corruptible garments, it will put on its incorruptible and immortal nature and be transmuted—seems primarily confirmed by the words of the Prophet: *The light of the moon itself,* he says, *will be like that of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, Isaiah 62 <note>This likely refers to Isaiah 30:26.</note>.* And he teaches this more clearly when he says elsewhere, *Your sun shall set no more, your moon shall not wane, for the Lord will be your light, O Jerusalem, Isaiah 60.* John in the Apocalypse seems to agree with this discourse, saying, *The city has no need of the Sun nor the moon to shine in it, for the brightness of GOD will illuminate it, and its lamp will be the Lamb.* From this it is declared that the spirit of Wisdom will be far more excellent than any brightness of sun or star; by putting aside the solar creature which it wore when it placed its tabernacle in it, it will reveal itself in its own inaccessible splendor and light, the sight of which no mortal in this state of mortality can behold...

† ...when the righteous will shine like the sun (as Saint Matthew has it) in that kingdom of their father <note>Matthew 13:43</note>, then they will see him as he truly is, with their garments stripped away, and so Alpha will be converted into Omega; the beginning will meet with its end. Among these, the **Zohar** <note>original: "Zoar"; the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah</note> says that all things are nothing but one in respect to GOD, but in respect to us, they are many. **Plato** and **Parmenides** <note>Parmenides was a pre-Socratic philosopher known for the doctrine that "All is One."</note> say that that which exists, insofar as it is in GOD and proceeds from him, is nothing but one. **Hermes**, in his **Emerald Tablet**, says: *just as all things were through the mediation of the One, so all things were born from this one by adaptation* <note>original: "readoptione"; likely a variation of "adaptatione" used in the famous Hermetic text, the Tabula Smaragdina</note>. And these things will find all the greater peace and concord the more closely they approach that One and participate with it.

**Plato** also speaks thus in his Epistles: All things proceed from the most high, and they strive with their greatest effort to return to him again, as it is in him that their final rest and the protection of their essence consists; and so it is with the rest.

By these things we have it confirmed that all things are in reality nothing but one, but are many only in the imagination of common men, whose habit it is to look at those things which appear in an external manner, which seem to be and yet are nothing...

### CHAPTER XVIII.

*How the wisdom of God is the first author and actor of the winds, both in the*
*Microcosm and the Macrocosm.*

**I**n the preceding chapter, we said that angels are sometimes winds and occasionally burning flames; but truly, how that great angel—who is the emanation or brightness of almighty power—is the great lord over these angels and governs them to perform the will of the father in the form of winds, we shall declare more fully in the following member. Indeed, we read *that God or Divine wisdom bowed the heavens and descended, and darkness was under his feet, and he ascended upon the Cherubim, and flew or glided upon the wings of the wind. 2 Kings 22:10 and Psalm 104.* <note>The text cites 2 Reg. 22:8, but the passage describing God riding the cherub matches 2 Samuel 22:10-11 / Psalm 18:9-10.</note> From this speech it is clear that just as the Seraphim are ministers burning with the fire of love and administering before God, so indeed the Cherubim are airy ministers, by whose act or motion in the air the winds are produced. Whence it is said *that he ascended upon the Cherubim and flew upon the wings of the wind,* that is, upon the airy spirits existing under the power of the Cherubim and having power in the air, as will be discussed more freely in its proper place; for which reason the winds are said by the Prophet to do the commands of God. *Baruch 5:60.* <note>Likely referring to Baruch 6:60 in the Vulgate, where stars, sun, and moon are obedient to God's purpose.</note> We described this matter more fully before: how the "will of God" is included in the word *Let it be done* <note>original: "Fiat"</note>, and with the sending forth of the word, it migrates and is sent to any creature whatsoever; and with the spark of that word or spirit dwelling in that creature, both for its formation and preservation, it joins itself and seizes that creature entirely to fulfill the creator's will without any resistance. This indeed cannot be otherwise, because God is the sole actor in every creature. Hence it happens that a creature, whether it be spiritual like the angelic kind, or corporeal, is always ready at hand to fulfill the will of God—that is, to perform his word and consequently his pleasure—according to that verse cited above: *Angels of God most strong in strength, doing his word, listening to his voice, that is, by the word doing his pleasure. Psalm 103:20.* And therefore these are called "intellectual winds," insofar as by their breath and motion, by divine will, the air is disturbed and is said to move from that quarter of the world from which these angelic spirits carry the spirit of wisdom, at whose nod they are moved where or when it wills. Whence it is said: *In his will the South wind breathed. Ecclesiasticus 43:17.* <note>original: "In voluntate eius aspirauit Notus." Sirach 43:16-17 describes God's power over the winds and storms.</note> But also elsewhere it says in clearer speech: *He who assigns weight to the air or wind, and weighs the waters in measure, makes a law for the rain, and a path for the lightning of the thunders.* By this speech it is denoted that God by his wisdom adapts the air in its light nature, and by agitating it through his ministers, he produces winds; and by compressing it to a still denser degree, he procreates clouds, from which rain later arises. Also, by another adaptation and informing of the air, he produces lightning and thunder; for his flame-vomiting ministers are the formal causes of the inflamed air, just as they themselves in their invisible nature are called winds, which are heard but by no means seen. Whence it is certain that the internal act of the winds or angels disturbing the air is immediately from God—that is, the ray of the divine will joined with its own ray, which is of the same essence, as described more broadly below. For this reason, it is necessary that they be moved and incited with all effort to fulfill the divine will; and for this reason, the truly efficient cause of winds, thunders, rains, comets, and other such meteors is referred to God and not to creatures, since they do not know how to move unless they are moved by God. *For in God we live, in God we move, and are. How ridiculous, therefore, are the schools of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy who explained nature through physical qualities like heat and cold</term>, who devise so many imaginary efficient causes of the winds—namely, a hot exhalation seeking only to rise, the heat of the sun lifting and calling it forth from the earth, and the intense cold of the middle region of the air. I leave this for you to consider, you who are lifted up on the more precise wings of doctrine and the science of truth.

***A comparison regarding man, in which it is proven that GOD is also the sole and only author of the winds produced within the Microcosm.*** <term>Microcosm: the human being, viewed as a "little world" that mirrors the structure of the "Macrocosm," or the universe</term>

Not without reason was man called by the Philosopher "the microcosm" <note>original: "ὁ μικρόκοσμος"</note>, insofar as he holds the greatest likeness and analogy to the great world. For he enjoys the same elements as the world, which are accustomed to act and be acted upon among themselves through similar actions and passions, both in the one world and the other. Indeed, the "lesser world" (man) seems to have received the parts of his substance and essence from that "greater world," if we consider the matter a little more accurately; for in time and order, the latter preceded the former. Hence, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric wisdom known as Hermeticism.</note> did not hesitate to call man the "son of the world," just as he called the world the "son of GOD." 

And indeed, if we weigh the words of the Prophet carefully, we shall find them relevant to this philosophical proposition; for where he speaks of the resurrection of the bones, he says: *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live: Ezekiel 37.* By this he seems to imply that life comes from that spirit which God granted to the world for its existence and vivification. However, this much is certain and well-known: just as God created the one world by His breath of life, so He also created the other. That is, just as the Spirit of the Lord, which moved over the waters in the great world, provided them with fiery vigor and created and animated its moist spirit, so too at the creation of man, He breathed the breath of life <note>original: "vitae spiraculum"</note> into the created spirit of man, *whence man was made into a living soul. I, says God, creating the heavens and establishing the earth and those things which sprout from it, give breath to the people who are upon it, Isaiah 42:5.* From these things we gather that the life not only of the world, but also of man, took its beginning from the wind or divine inspiration.

Furthermore, just as we see the common spirit of the world divided into four elements, so not only the human spirit (which we also call air) but also the body participates in these elements. Indeed, we see the air of both worlds enjoying its own proper sun: for the heart performs its duty in the human spirit no differently than the Macrocosmic sun does in its own. But truly, we see with open eyes that just as man's primary power came from the inspiration of Him who "set his tabernacle in the sun," and man received the parts of his constitution from the air and elements of the world, it is necessary that there be a continuous relationship. This relationship exists both between the incorruptible spirit in the sun and that in the heart—since both are but one thing in essence—and also between the air of the world and that of man, which both come from one and the same source. Both enter into this same common duty: namely, that the luminous spirit of the Creator flies upon the wings of each wind or spirit, and is carried as if by a vehicle or chariot. 

And just as in the world that airy spirit is divided into three regions, one of which is placed before the others in dignity and purity, so indeed is this spirit in man. It is divided into the **animal and intellectual spirit** in the brain (or "highest heaven"), relating to the Empyrean <term>Empyrean: the highest part of heaven, associated with pure fire and light</term> or Angelic spirit of the world; the **vital spirit** in the heart, compared to the ethereal part of the world; and the **natural spirit** in the liver, having respect for the sublunary <term>sublunary: the region below the moon, where things are changeable and corruptible</term> region of the world. 

From this arises such a great proximity—indeed, a continuity—between these two spirits and luminous souls (which in effect are of one essence governing them), that the later-born Microcosm cannot exist without the assistance and presence of the earlier. For this reason, Heraclitus said quite sensibly: if you take the Sun out of the world, what is our little body? If the soul is missing, no pulsing vein is drawn there, no vital breath, no breathing at all. And hence it is that the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle.</note> maintained that man cannot be generated by man unless the sun is assisting, etc. Whence comes his axiom: *The Sun and man generate man.* 

For this reason, therefore, man is said to live as long as he breathes (for we are now discussing his sympathy with the mundane spirit). Therefore, antiquity rightly ascribed the spirits to the Sun—spirits which the more excellent physicians judge to be "innate heat," which move the body, excite the senses, and cherish thoughts and minds. The Sun moves all things like an instrument and is the organic cause of all living things through that incomparable spirit which inhabits its center. These spirits, according to the testimony of Homer, are said to be present in us daily, just as the mundane Sun, the Prince of Planets, breathes out, moves, radiates, and prepares, refines, and elaborates through the medium of the sublunary air. 

This one thing (I mean the air), according to the testimony of Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity.</note> and experience itself, we are compelled to breathe continually and necessarily, whether we want to or not. With the help of the lungs, we draw it through the mouth and the "rough artery" <note>The trachea or windpipe.</note>, and from there send it back into the left chamber of the heart, which is most full of the body of the spirits that give life and restore animal power. Hence it is that, according to the state of the air in the sky and the sun in the air, we find our own spirit disposed everywhere in the blood, the viscera, and wandering through the flesh; where, for the sake of example, depending on the motion and temperature of the air which hangs upon the sun and the whole face of heaven, on one day...

From this it is clear that the spirits of men are refreshed by the clarity of the world's light, and likewise the sublunary world itself seems to be refreshed and to rejoice at the clear sight of the sun. Hence it is that in sad, thick, and dark air, the lower world seems to mourn, to be disturbed, and to be saddened. On the Efficient Cause of Meteors. 201

...the Wise Man <note>original: "ſapiens"</note> says, that the upper clouds by wisdom distil the dew, *Proverbs 3:20.* <note>The text cites Proverbs 10, but the quote corresponds to Proverbs 3:20.</note> From which it is clear enough, contrary to the false assertion of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who sought to explain the weather through physical causes like rising vapors and the cooling of the "middle region" of the air.</note>, that neither vapors emerging from the earth or waters, nor the cold of the middle region of the air thickening and sustaining that imaginary vapor, is either the material or efficient cause of a cloud, but the air itself is positioned and thickened by the opposing or transverse breath of God: that is, by the ray of wisdom of the angels who are snatched up and stirred to carry out the will of their Creator.

The matter is the same in the generation of snow, hail, and frost, except that in such a creation the North Wind has dominion, whose nature it is to constrict the air into a cloud—air which was brought back by the South Wind (though blowing at a weaker degree) and to harden it; for as it is the nature of the South Wind to soften, liquefy, and dissolve, so it is the nature of the North Wind <note>original: "Aquilonis"</note> to harden and constrict. Moreover, that God alone is the producer and effector of such meteors, through the mediation of His angelic ministers, is proven by these testimonies brought forth from the sacred fountain: *Who has fathered the frost of heaven?* <note>original: "Pruinam cals [cæli] ... quis genuit?"</note> *Job 38:29.* As if by such a question He would prove that no one does so except Himself alone. And elsewhere, *God emits snow like wool, and scatters the frost like ashes; He casts down His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? Psalm 147:16.* By which He seems to imply that God, through His winds—and especially the North Wind—begets snow from the air gathered by the weaker breaths of the South; whence it is said: *The strong God by His breath produces snow and ice, Job 37:9-10.* <note>The text cites Job 27:9, but the passage is found in Job 37.</note> And elsewhere: *The North Wind produces cold.* Furthermore, ice and frost are created from the concretion of dewy air by the breath of God from the north; hence we read of *ice coming out of the womb of the dew, Job 38:28.* And elsewhere, *By the breath of God, frost is frozen like a stone of water, etc. Job 37:10.* In this discourse, the matter of ice, as well as its form and author along with His instrument, is explained: namely, the dewy matter, the watery stone-like form, and God the agent acting through His windy instrument. From these things, therefore, the error of the ethnic philosophers <note>The author refers to non-Christian or "pagan" Greek philosophers like Aristotle.</note> regarding the matter and efficient cause of these types of meteors is evident.

### CHAPTER XX.

### On the single efficient cause of flashes, lightning, thunderbolts, and thunders; likewise on the actor of sulfuric smokes and flames.

AS the Creator of all things makes His angels Winds, so also He makes His ministers a burning fire or flame, as the royal Prophet testifies, *Psalm 103 [104]:4.* Moreover, we call lightning and flashes the air animated by their presence and clothed in their fiery form, which indeed we also gather from the consequence of this speech: *God fits a weight to the air, and weighs the waters by measure, and He makes a way for the lightning of thunders,* where He is seen to fit the air in its weight, so that through it as a medium, His fiery spirits may make their way to fulfill the will of the Creator; Job seems to imply this in another place. *The clouds scatter His light by which they illuminate all things round about, wherever the will of the Creator drives them for everything He has commanded them upon the face of the world, whether for a scourge or for benevolence, Job 37:11-13.* <note>The text cites Job 28:25 and Job 37.</note> And *God extends His light over the clouds, and covers the roots of the sea, Job 36:30.* And elsewhere: *Will you send lightning, and will they return and say to you, "Here we are"? Job 38:35.* Are we not also made more certain of the efficient cause of lightning from these words: *Fire coming out from the presence of Jehovah consumed the sons of Aaron, Leviticus 10:2.* And elsewhere, *Fire going out from Jehovah consumed the 250 men who had offered incense, Numbers 16:35.* Finally, in the Apocalypse we have that lightnings, voices, and thunders proceeded from the throne of God: by which it is clearly denoted that flashes and lightnings proceed immediately from God, and that this speech is to be understood in this way: namely, that the Divine Essence, in its wisdom or emanation, stirs its like in the fiery spirits (by means of which a fiery angel exists and remains such as it appears in the air at the time of lightning: for the incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing, but more abundantly in the angels); He urges and moves a part of Himself (I say) to perform those things which are ordained by the moving Father, and these fiery spirits in their motion disturb the air, conglommerating and constricting it into thick clouds; and conversely, spirits of an opposite nature and breathing from a contrary quarter of the world, waging an impetuous war, violently break out from their damp embrace and the thick prison surrounding them; which indeed those fiery or watery spirits or demons do not do [of their own accord], but God is accustomed to effect it by a double ray emitted from His essence acting in them. And this is the reason that many thunders are heard at the same time, rising from different corners of the world: whence Daniel says, *the four winds of heaven fought upon the great sea, Daniel 7:2.* That is, in the open air: where by the winds the Prophet understands the angelic intelligences which preside over the four corners of the world. But of these things we shall discourse more clearly in the second book of this member, God willing. — By which discourse it clearly appears that God performs all these things; and although we say in our common speech that the lightnings and thunders act, or in a more mystical sense, that angels inflame the air by their fiery presence, yet in truth it is God in the fiery angels, and God in the thick clouds or watery spirits, who brings all these things to their conclusion to fulfill His commands. Whence the holy page rightly said, *that in God all things live, move, and have their being. Acts 17:28.* <note>The original text cites Acts 17:9, but the quote is from Acts 17:28.</note> *And elsewhere: God works all in all. 1 Cor. 12.* And again, *God the Father from whom are all things. 1 Cor. 8.* Therefore, I leave it to be judged by you, looking into this matter with upright eyes and weighing it in the scales of justice, how foolish, tasteless, and over-subtly delivered is that opinion and assertion of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who emphasized physical causes over divine ones.</note>—both of the Heathen and the Christian orders—(presuming to assert that lightnings are hot and dry exhalations, leaping from the earth, which are raised by the solar power into the middle region of the air, and there enclosed in a cloud, and ignited by the force of the cold of that place, etc.). Consider whether this thing—namely, lightning and thunder—is a matter of such small moment (as those Aristotelians think) or of a far deeper profundity and inscrutability, since the fires of God leaping from His mouth and throne are called the voices and sounds of God everywhere in the sacred scriptures.

For this reason, it happened that certain of the Philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of the lightning-bolt, judged it to be not a work of nature, but an immediate effect of the supreme God. Indeed, this work seemed so marvelous to the Heathens that they doubted greatly concerning its origin and disputed among themselves. For Empedocles thought that the lightning and the flash were a fire generated by the rays of the sun descending downward, intercepted by the clouds; Anaxagoras maintained that this fire was a portion of the ether, which he says is sent down from on high and struck into that place where the clouds consist. Although Aristotle himself and Seneca attempted to refute these opinions, they nevertheless seem far more probable and pertinent to the matter than those of Aristotle and his sects, which is also declared clearly enough by arguments drawn from experience itself.

For, good God! how destitute of reason are those who are accustomed to rightly refer or attribute the wonderful effects of thunders to the power of a terrestrial exhalation, or to the weak faculty of terrestrial fire, whether it be actual or only in potential? For by the act of a lightning-bolt, we see wine drawn out of a jar by a sudden force while the vessel is not touched at all; a sword melted in its scabbard, gold and silver in a purse, and bones broken within the fleshy dwelling of a man; sudden winds created in the air, forests burned, stones crushed, huge towers suddenly torn down, and infinite other wonders performed. It is most difficult to give a ready reason for these; indeed, there seems to be sense and reason within the lightning, by which they offer obedience to the Creator, and they are said to bless Him by the holy scriptures. This indicates to us Christians that there is within them a certain Angelic virtue very close to divinity, by which they are ruled, and *being sent forth, they go out violently, and returning they say to the Creator, "Behold, here we are." Job 38:35.* <note>The original text cites Job 39:35, but the verse is Job 38:35.</note> Indeed, its spirits are so subtle, and its life so agile, that we have it written by one skilled in these mysteries: "Angels are much clearer and more splendid than spiritual bodies, which a man can hardly admit or comprehend; for by reason of their subtlety they can pass through and penetrate all things without any hindrance and without their own corruption, like lightning. Likewise, the human soul can do this, inasmuch as God created it from the same [substance] from which the angels were created." Thus he says in the *Book on the Secrets of Creation.* By which he seems to hint that the angelic substance, that of lightning, and that of the human soul, are of the same matter, which he delights to call the "sixth essence" in many places. And in truth, just as the substance of an Angel is not seen except in its aerial garment, which it illuminates in the manner of the spirit of the sun, which is illuminated by its internal soul; so indeed the internal part of lightning is an angelic power and essence, veiled in aerial clothing.

Hence it is that so many wonders arise from lightning, far surpassing the dull nature and disposition of an exhalation. For experience has revealed here in England, in the county of <term>Devon</term> <note>original: "Devoniensi"</note>, that a thunder-clap coming from the North sent a "fire-stone" <note>A contemporary term for a meteorite or a localized lightning strike perceived as a physical object.</note> into the kitchen of a certain nobleman. Rolling from that place into the hall of that house and passing between the feet of a certain man of that house, it rendered him for a time demented and Raging; and passing from that place into a chamber, by its mere sight <note>or "presence"</note> all the glass of the windows on that side were perforated in infinite places, just as if they had been penetrated by needles; and so penetrating through a thick wall and leaping out of the house, it immersed itself in a wonderful way into a hard rock. 

Furthermore, in Ireland, two women seeking a forest and traveling through a field were delayed on the way by a certain horrific thunder. One of them was struck with fear and terror, and crying out to God, she hurried quickly toward a tree. The other appeared not at all disturbed, but behaved in an impious manner, holding the voices of the thunders in derision and contempt; striking her buttocks <note>original: "anum seu podicem"</note> with her hand, she turned them toward that place from which the sounds were issued. Whence it happened that the former, moved by the fear of God and His voice, escaped safe; but the buttocks and hindquarters of the other were immediately torn and mangled by the thunder, and so that blasphemous woman died miserably. 

But to come closer to the foolish assertions of these Peripatetics: one day certain merchants and others in the company of a certain Peripatetic (a young man of good character who lived in the city of <term>Shrewsbury</term> <note>original: "Salopiensem"</note> and devoted his labor there to literary matters, and was held in esteem by all of that place for his knowledge in philosophy) were traveling together through the wide, flat plain of Shrewsbury. They noticed thick clouds with sounds and thunder approaching them, and the greater part of them began to fear vehemently.
