...are said to be; furthermore, in the same scale <note>original: *scala*; likely referring to a "Scale of Four" or a diagram of the Great Chain of Being</note> it says there are 4 Prefects of the elements: namely, **Seraph** of fire, **Cherub** of air, **Tharsis** of water, and **Ariel** of earth. But to show our mind’s opinion on this matter, we say that it is more probable to consider that, since the wheel of the sublunary spirit <note>The region below the moon, where change, decay, and weather occur</note> is filled with both the goodness of God and the malice of the Devil, it seems likely that every element has its own good and likewise its evil Prince. Both are ministers of the divine property: the former used for doing good in clemency, and the latter for punishing and doing harm in severity. Therefore we say that, just as there are four good princes—Seraph, Cherub, Tharsis, and Ariel—so there are evil and vengeful ones—**Samael, Azazel, Azael, and Mahazael**—in those same elements. And since the Winds participate in the Elements—namely, the East wind in fire, the North wind in earth, the West wind in water, and the South wind in air—the elementary Spirits, both evil and good, receive their strengths from the Spirits of the winds, whether blowing for good or ill. From this, it is certain that the East wind <note>original: *Eurus*</note> participates as much in the heat as in the violence of Samael, and so it is with the others. We also affirm that the royal spirits on the side of Satan who have power over the winds—namely **Uriens, Paymon, Egyn, and Amaymon** <note>These are traditionally the four demon kings of the cardinal directions in Renaissance occultism</note>—are subjected to the commands of those good angels who preside over the corners of the world: namely **Michael, Raphael, Gabriel, and Uriel**. This is especially true of that imperial Angel of goodness and life, Michael, who has force and power over the Prince of darkness or the dark air, because of the victory reported over the Dragon. Therefore, under his supreme command are all demons, whether of the Winds or the elements, and whether they be good or evil.

Here it must also be considered in passing that, according to the position of the gates in the celestial city <note>The "New Jerusalem" described in the Book of Revelation</note> (three of which were situated toward the east, three toward the west, and just as many toward the north and the south), the same holds true for the winds. For in every region of the world there are three winds: namely the East wind <note>original: *subsolanus*</note> with its two wings, the South wind <note>original: *Auster*</note> toward the south, and the Northeast wind <note>original: *Caecias*</note> toward the north, and so on for the others, as you have clearly depicted in the previous demonstration. And since, following the likeness of the gates of the celestial Jerusalem, you have the Zodiac of the starry sky divided into four triplicities <note>term: *triplicity* - a group of three astrological signs belonging to the same element</note>—namely the Fiery and eastern, the Airy and southern, the Watery and western, and the Earthy and northern—three signs are assigned to each of these triplicities. Specifically: **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius** to fire; **Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius** to air; **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces** to water; and finally **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn** to earth. Similarly, because a proper prince of Angelic nature is assigned to each triplicity, and a peculiar angel is likewise assigned to each sign under him, it seems likely (as it appears to me) that not only is a Prince Angel ascribed to the cardinal point, but also to every windy gate in that region, which ought to have a relation to its sign, under whose power it falls. We have made mention of the demons of the triplicities and the peculiar spirits of each sign before, where we spoke of the demons of the Zodiac. We could indeed compile great volumes on this subject, but since we shall discourse more openly on these matters elsewhere, we will speak no more of them in this place.

You have here, benevolent Readers, how evidently described and as if painted to the life are two great Princes of intelligence, strictly different in property and nature. The first of these, who is the most powerful of all, is an **Angel of light**, clement, good, the author of health and life, the solace and rest of the world, the driver-away of death and diseases, who holds evil in hatred and fosters and nourishes good benevolently. We have declared him to be the dispenser of clemency, benevolence, and divine kindness—the guardian of souls, and indeed of bodies—from whose region come those good angels of men whom we call the holy and good geniuses <note>original: *genios*; protective guardian spirits</note>. He is the author and actor of the world’s salvation and human resurrection, as one who obtained victory against the Devil and Death. The other Prince, however, is most opposite to this one in condition and will; for as an **Angel of darkness**, he is accustomed to seethe with severity and impiety. He delights in evil actions, is the author of diseases, sorrows, and destruction, the scourge and restlessness of the world, the destroyer of life, and the introducer of death into the world. He holds good in hatred and fosters and nourishes evil strenuously. We have declared him to be the dispenser of severity and malevolence—indeed, of universal impiety—the destroyer of souls and indeed of bodies, under whose rule are those evil and wicked demons called the evil geniuses. He is the author of the world’s ruin and man’s damnation. And so you see these two Angels are entirely contrary to one another in quality. Concerning these, therefore, I have decided (by the favor of the Best and Greatest God) to treat specifically in the following volume, where we shall discourse copiously on health and disease, and that with a more polished and clearer thread of speech.

<margin>Reason and authority.</margin>...rule in these elements, a view in which even **Plato** <margin>Plato.</margin> concurred. Saint **Athanasius**, <margin>Athanasius.</margin> moreover, says: "The demons who are tossed about in the air are not among the number of those who fell <note>original: "ex eorum numero, qui ceciderunt"; referring to the fallen angels who followed Lucifer into rebellion</note>, but are among those who were sent into this world to govern it." Likewise, **Hegesippus** <margin>Hegesippus.</margin> affirms that there are demons who stir up storms, hail, lightning, and other phenomena of that kind. Furthermore, Saint **Augustine**, <margin>Augustine.</margin> **Gregory**, <margin>Gregory.</margin> and **Ambrose** <margin>Ambrose.</margin> agree on this point, using these words: "In this visible world nothing happens except through an invisible creature, which presides over every physical body according to the will of God, who governs all things."

<column-break/>

From these examples it seems to follow that not only good Angels, but also evil ones, rule over these sublunary <term>sublunary<gloss>The region "below the moon," which according to ancient science was the only part of the universe subject to change, decay, and weather.</gloss></term> matters and **meteors** <term>meteors<gloss>In the 17th century, a "meteor" was any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or clouds, not just "shooting stars."</gloss></term>. This is also evident from the sacred scriptures, where it is said: that the Angel of the Lord descended and moved the water <note>original: "aquam movisse"; a reference to the healing pool of Bethesda in the Gospel of John</note>. Likewise, that the Angel of the Lord struck down one hundred eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. Likewise, that the Angel of the Lord struck Herod, because he did not give honor to God. Regarding evil spirits, however, we read in Job that fire fell from heaven and devoured the sheep and the servants; and that a powerful wind came from the region of the desert and struck the house, so that the children of Job perished in the collapse. Scripture itself testifies that all of this was done by Satan. Thus, it is clear that both good and evil Angels rule in these meteors and elements, carrying out all things according to the will <note>original: "nutum"; literally a nod or command</note> of God.

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors. 271

Therefore, the ancient Magi vainly attributed the actions of the one God to demons—actions which are the works of the Lord God alone and are by no means to be considered gods. And this is the reason for the idolatry of the nations, which is mentioned in the fountain of truth <note>The author uses "fountain of truth" to refer to the Holy Scriptures.</note>, where it is read: *They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know* <margin>Deuteronomy 32:17</margin>. And this is why an express law was given against the adoration of demons at the beginning of the Mosaic Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>: and elsewhere we are warned that sacrifices are not to be offered to demons, as in *Leviticus* <margin>17:7</margin>.

Vainly also have astrologers attributed the movements, powers, and operations of influences to the stars, whether fixed or wandering, and especially to the Sun and Moon, which are the works of wisdom or the Divine Word; without His life-giving gift, they could not exist at all. For this error was also the occasion for notable idolatry among the heathens and gentiles <note>original: "gentiles & Ethnicos"</note>. For example, the Egyptians worshipped the Sun, whose houses and statues the King of Babylon is said to have shattered <margin>Jeremiah 43</margin>. Furthermore, the Jews also fell into this damnable error, where it is said: *The chariot and horses of the Sun before the temple of the Lord were taken away* <margin>4 Kings 23:11</margin> <note>In many modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 23.</note>. And in another place the Bible testifies that God created the Sun, Moon, and other things for service to all nations under heaven, and therefore He forbade them to be adored or worshipped: He commanded the Israelites that they should not look upon the Sun, Moon, or stars, or any part of the heavenly host, so as to bow down and worship them <margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin>.

By these things we are taught that just as God is the sole author and actor in this world, so praise, honor, adoration, and worship must be given to Him alone and not to any created thing. Whatever might happen to us or to the world should not be derived from the creature, but we should believe it proceeds from the power of the Creator and the act of His emanation within the creature—emitted from it as if from a vehicle—since the creature itself is utterly dead without His act, having no value or standing in itself.

But because it is the custom of the world to affirm that heavenly influences and their powers are derived from the stars according to the doctrine of the ancient astrologers—and consequently to speak with the heathens of Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Orion, Corvus, Cassiopeia, and the other fixed stars, as well as Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and the Sun, etc., among the planets, as being the causes of this or that change in the air, earth, and water—we, for the better understanding of our readers, will follow in their footsteps. We shall name and speak of the planets and fixed stars as being the causes of storms and **meteors** <term>meteors<gloss>In the 17th century, "meteor" was a general term for any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or clouds, not just falling stars.</gloss></term> in the air. We do this, however, with the provision that we always keep in our memories that it is not the star we have named, but the divine influx emitted from the Sephirotic <note>The Sephirot are the ten attributes or channels in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (En Soph) reveals Himself.</note> divine gates into the sphere and body of the planets. This influx, which is rained down upon the lower regions by its Angelic minister according to the will of the *En Soph* <note>original: "Enſoph"; the Infinite or Boundless God in Kabbalah.</note> or the Paternal Infinitude—whether for the punishment or the benefit of mortals—is the fountain and origin of effects of every kind produced in the air, water, and earth.

These things having been first considered by the true Christian, we shall hasten to the description and living explanation of the triangle in our meteorographic Mirror <note>original: "Catoptro meteorographico"; likely a specialized diagram or instrument for observing and predicting weather.</note>. In this, meteorological prognostication is clearly expressed through the aspects of the planets to one another—namely, the **conjunction** <note>When two planets appear in the same place in the sky.</note> figured thus $\sigma$ : the **opposition** <note>When two planets are on opposite sides of the earth.</note> or $\rho$: or the **square** <note>A 90-degree angle between planets.</note> or $\square$: in relation to the moon. The image of the Triangle will be depicted below.

## CHAP. II.

*On the changes of the air, on the origin of comets, and then thereafter, on the various changes of the air according to the aspects—conjunction, opposition, and square—of all the planets both toward the moon and among themselves.*

Astrologers say that the efficient cause of all species of **Comets** is the stars, both fixed and wandering, and they generally advise us that meteors of this sort imitate the natures of Mars and Mercury. Hence they say it happens that they signify war, heat, and tumult. Similarly, Ptolemy in the second book of his *Quadripartitum* <note>Ptolemy's 2nd-century foundational work on astrology, also known as the Tetrabiblos.</note> wishes for us to also consider the stars that are accustomed (as he puts it) to stir up matter, to draw it along by their motion, and he also teaches us to observe the place or sign of the Zodiac under which it is ignited.

Now, regarding the various changes of the air in winds, clouds, rains, snows, hail, thunder, lightnings, and other matters, and also regarding the exposition of the meteorological triangle depicted in our meteorographic Mirror, receive this.

CHAPTER III.

A detailed explanation of the wheel depicted in the empty right-hand section of our Meteorographic Mirror, as well as the opening of the gates, floodgates, and great valves.

We have depicted this wheel here for your better understanding, so that by looking at it, you may more easily understand what is contained within it. In this wheel, taken from our Meteorological Mirror <note>original: "Catoptro" or "Speculo," a term for a scientific diagram or representative "mirror" of a subject.</note> or Speculum, a double description can be seen: namely, the openings of the **great valves** of heaven, which are described in the upper sphere, and then later the openings of the **gates of heaven**, which are revealed in the parts revolving around the center of the sphere.

Regarding the openings of the great valves of heaven, it should be known that the floodgates and great valves of heaven are said to be opened when the Moon, receding from a conjunction, square aspect, or opposition with the Sun, Jupiter, or Mars, is led and passes directly to Saturn, Mercury, and Venus, or vice-versa. That is, if the Moon—receding from a ☌ (conjunction), □ (square), or ☍ (opposition) with Saturn, Mercury, or Venus—is moved toward the Sun, Jupiter, or Mars; for then, according to the opinions of all astrologers, rains in abundance and consequently great floods are to be expected.

Similarly, the openings of the gates are to be gathered from the observation of the lower sphere. For when you observe in the order of the sphere a square line marked with a □ between the Sun and Saturn, or the Moon and Saturn, or Venus and Mars, or finally Mercury and Jupiter; or similarly a diametrical line or line of opposition marked with a ☍ between the Moon and Saturn, or between the Sun and Saturn, or between Jupiter and Mercury, or finally between Mars and Venus. Finally, where you see the ☾ (Moon) with ♄ (Saturn), or ☿ (Mercury) with ♀ (Venus), or Venus with Mars with this sign ☌ (conjunction)... in these cases, they say the gates of heaven are open or about to be opened immediately, so that copious rains and showers are to be expected.

For this is a secret observation among astrologers, a science not widely published by them. But indeed, Aomar <note>Likely referring to Abū Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer known in Latin as Albumasar, or perhaps Umar ibn al-Farrukhan al-Tabari (Aomar).</note> states in his observations that if the Moon recedes from Venus and, after its departure, applies its rays to Mars, or if it recedes from Mars and applies itself to Venus, then it opens the floodgates of heaven. If it recedes from Jupiter and applies to Mercury, or rather, having separated from Mercury, proceeds to Jupiter, it opens the gate here again.

But that which was previously condensed and reduced by us into the aforementioned sphere (as proven by long experience), we hold in the highest esteem, and consequently, we think it is far to be preferred by us over the precepts of others; however, use your own judgment, and I advise you to follow what seems more probable to you in this matter. Concerning the remaining celestial signs in the change of the air, we have spoken more fully in our **Astrological treatise** described in our **technical history**, wherefore I think you should be referred to that place.

->CHAPTER IV.<-

**On the celestial efficient cause of the Winds, wherein our own opinion concerning the Winds is incidentally introduced and supported by strong arguments.**

After Fregius <note>Thomas Freigius (1543–1583) was a German scholar and follower of Peter Ramus; he often sought to reconcile classical philosophy with practical observation.</note> made mention of the causes of the winds, he himself—led by better judgment and departing from the opinion of Aristotle—immediately speaks thus: *Although the entire dispute concerning winds, as with other meteors, is full of the wonderful works of God, for which no firm and sufficient efficient causes can be produced in nature; nevertheless, it is profitable to see how far human reason can progress. Indeed, Sacred Scripture says that GOD produces winds from His treasures <note>Original: "de thesauris suis," a reference to Psalm 135:7, "He bringeth the wind out of his treasuries."</note>, from whence we hear their blowing, but we know not from whence they come or where they go.* Thus he speaks. 

And indeed, both the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> themselves and **Pliny**, that most accurate seeker of causes, are so enveloped in clouds of obscurity and ignorance that when they perceive themselves caught in the mire of ignorance, they attempt to excuse themselves in part through subtle and vain distinctions. They say that some winds are **miraculous**—namely, those for which no cause can be rendered in nature. Of this sort is the one described by Pliny, who says there is a certain cave on the coast of **Dalmatia** <note>Modern-day Croatia.</note> with a vast, sheer opening; if a light weight is cast into it, even on an otherwise calm day, a stormy wind like a whirlwind is observed to arise immediately. 

They also judge in this way those winds that burst forth from the rocks of the **Cyrenaic province** <note>A region in modern-day Libya.</note>; for this reason, they hold those rocks to be so sacred that they believe them to be profaned by too much handling. For if they are touched by human hands even once, the **South Wind** <note>Original: "Auster."</note> is immediately stirred up, churning the sands; hence, they consecrated these rocks to the South Wind. 

But truly, regarding those winds for which they could devise some cause within the possibility of nature, they called these **natural**, and judged their efficient cause according to their own custom. From this, anyone may see how uncertain is the opinion of men engaged in vain philosophy concerning such profound matters, and how inconstant is the judgment of human wisdom. 

Furthermore, even among the fathers of the **Astrologers**, there appears to be great hesitation and instability in their opinion regarding the efficient cause of the winds. For just as the Peripatetics divide their natural winds into **fixed** and **sudden**—and the fixed winds again (which they define as those that begin and cease to blow at set times) into **general** or **principal** winds (namely, those that blow from the four cardinal points) and **particular** and **lesser principal** winds (which are observed to blow in certain provinces)—so indeed the Astrologers, looking deeper into...

Those ascending in the investigation of these causes have claimed that impetuous winds—whether they be sudden or general, and especially those which tend from the North toward the West—belong to the domain of **Mars**, and they say such winds are subject to him. Yet others make the winds the children of **Titan**, **Astraea**, and **Aurora**, <note>In Greek mythology, the winds (Anemoi) were the offspring of Astraeus (god of dusk) and Eos (Aurora/Dawn).</note> insofar as they are generated by the heat of the sun, which renders the air subtle and thin, particularly at dawn; indeed, even **Aristotle** admits that winds are produced by the heat of the Sun. However, all winds are said to receive the commands of **Juno**, because they do not blow except in the air, which is called Juno. <note>In the common allegorical physics of the Renaissance, Juno represents the element of Air, just as Jupiter represents Fire or Ether.</note> Others say that of the fixed winds, those they call *Prodromoi* (the "forerunners" who precede the *Etesiae*) <note>term: <term>Etesiae</term> (original Latin: *Etesias*). These are the strong, cool, annual Mediterranean winds that blow from the north in mid-to-late summer.</note> arrive during the most burning time of summer, around the time the Dog Star rises; they precede the Sun as it enters the first part of Leo by about 8 days. Furthermore, the *Etesiae* themselves, which are Northern winds, are observed to blow constantly for 40 days, and the *Prodromoi* run before them. **Ptolemy** is inclined to attribute these winds to **Jupiter**, saying that Jupiter stirs them up, which is why he claims they are more fertile and healthful than the others. They begin to blow immediately after the solstice and the rising of the Dog Star, as Aristotle says, but **Pliny** says the *Etesiae* blow for two days after the rising of the Dog Star, while the sun stays in Leo, and so on for the rest.

From these things you see that there is such great difficulty in finding the causes of the winds that the Philosophers themselves have been unable to judge anything certain or firm regarding them; instead, whatever they do, they gather from the event and from long experience and practice, seeing everything *a posteriori* <note>original: "à posteriori," meaning reasoning from observed effects back to causes.</note> and not *a priori* <note>original: "à priori," meaning reasoning from first principles or known causes to their effects.</note>.

But we, as befits a Christian, do not cease to scrutinize the mystery of the winds and other meteors in a more profound manner. We do this neither from Aristotle, nor from any other book of the pagan authors, who were ignorant of the acts of the Divine Word (through which, according to the Bible, the true source of truth, all things were made)—especially the greater part of them (for the Divine **Plato** must always be excepted). Instead, we have immersed ourselves in the most internal cause of these creatures (not without exceptional joy), guided by the instruction of the Sacred Page and the infallible reasoning and demonstration of philosophical probability. With all effort, we have sought out the opinion of the **Hebrew Doctors** in this matter, as they were more practiced in the mysteries of the Jews and especially in the exposition and interpretation of the Holy Bible. Truly, from **Rabbi Tedacus Levi** <note>This likely refers to a Kabbalistic source or a specific Jewish scholar cited by Renaissance occultists like Fludd or Reuchlin; possibly Rabbi Isaac the Levite.</note> who wrote on the ten numerations [Sephirot], he says: *Speaking of the four Cardinal Winds: From those four Winds, God made four Angels placed over them by day and by night. Michael, who is on the side of mercy, is placed over the Eastern Wind; and Raphael rules the Western wind. Then Gabriel, in the power of judgment and severity, is placed over the Northern or Boreal wind; and Noriel or Uriel presides over the South.* <note>original: "Michael... Raphael... Gabriel... Noriel vel Vriel." These are the four traditional archangels governing the directions in Judeo-Christian tradition.</note> Thus he says. And in the Book of Secrets [Sefer HaRazim] we find that each of these has many legions under him, which they employ in their business to obey the will of the Creator.

We, however, are forced to disagree with that Doctor in certain respects, considering the matter to its very core. For it is certain and beyond all doubt—as proven by the experience of navigators—that the **Frigid Zone** of the Antarctic region of the world is no less stiff with cold and cold effects than the Boreal [Northern] one; namely, with constant ice, snow, and frost. These effects are created by the wind blowing from the Antarctic pole in no different a way than the cold effects from the Boreal or Northern winds. Thus, it seems least probable that a burning spirit such as **Uriel** (which name means "Fire of God") or **Meriris** (which signifies a demon burning at midday) should have dominion or power in that region—namely, where the pole star of the Antarctic hemisphere has its seat. For this is certain and to be denied by no one: that just as the Northern hemisphere is divided into its temperate and frigid land zones, which extend all the way to the pole star, so also it is apparent that the opposite hemisphere is distinguished by just as many regions of similar condition. That is, the space of the **Torrid Zone** is that which is situated between the equinoctial line and the Tropic of Capricorn; and the temperate zone extends in latitude from the Tropic of Capricorn to the Antarctic Circle. Finally, the Frigid Zone is measured from the Antarctic Circle to its own pole star.

By these facts it is clearly established that the wind blowing from the Antarctic pole is governed neither by Meriris nor by Uriel or Noriel, since by nature and condition it is contrary to fire, being instead most cold. Therefore, we must consider, and seriously so, that a more suitable seat for the aforementioned angels would be in the Torrid Zon...

### PART III.

## BOOK TWO.

### On the elementary Efficient cause.

#### CHAPTER I.

#### How the regions of the world are compared to the visions of human sense, and that the more divinity immerses itself into the multitude, the more its rays are covered and hidden from human sense.

Just as three visions are observed to exist in man—of which one is **corporeal** and deals with corporeal objects, in which the exterior sense is most often deceived by judging those things as true which are in reality feigned and false likenesses, so that this is the most uncertain of all human visions. 

The **second** is in the **imagination** or phantasy, which is the first step of spiritual vision, in which the likenesses and, as it were, shadows of bodies are perceived: for to the phantastic spirit, corporeal objects sometimes appear no differently than an image in a mirror. This vision, being the medium between external sense and the intellect, sometimes sees false things and is deceived; but when looking toward the intellect, it can by no means be deceived; therefore, this species of human vision is more certain than the corporeal one. 

The **third** and final species of vision is the **intellectual**, which is accustomed to gazing upon things that are neither corporeal nor have the forms of bodies; and the objects of this kind of human vision are the mind itself, **GOD**, justice, wisdom, and every good affection of the soul. 

In a similar way, the matter holds true for men in the inspection of the "efficient cause" <note>term: <term>Efficient Cause</term>. The primary source of change or rest; the agent that brings something into being.</note> of meteors <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>. For those to whom it is given to look into and gaze upon the marrow of meteors by the vision of the intellect, see indeed that **God** himself—the supreme mind, the Word, or divine Wisdom—is the sole and infallible agent in their production; and that vision is truly intellectual. 

There is also another vision, which is the **phantastic**, by which men see and gaze upon the cause of meteors: and by this vision, man determines that the **Angels** or demons themselves are the causes of meteors. In this kind of inspection, man sometimes errs—namely, by having respect for the created nature or human spirit (which has the closest proximity to corporeal things)—for in attributing the efficient cause of the meteor to a created thing, he errs and seems to fall into the crime of Idolatry. But truly, if he looks to the Angel's internal part, which is light or divine emanation received immediately from the source ***Ensoph*** <note>term: <term>Ensoph</term>. Derived from the Hebrew *Ein Sof*, meaning "without end" or "infinite," representing God prior to any self-manifestation.</note>, he is not deceived in his vision to that extent, insofar as it is intellectual. 

Finally, if we look back at the celestial bodies through the corporeal vision of the first order along with the **Astrologers**, or look at the bodies of the elements and elemental things of the first degree with the **Peripatetic Philosophers** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who focused primarily on physical and material causes rather than spiritual ones.</note>, it is necessary that we fall into great error and immerse ourselves in the deep sea of Idolatry, namely...

Namely, by attributing that admirable work to gross and sensible creatures—which are in truth dead in themselves and of no importance—such as the sun, the rest of the stars, the elements of fire and air, the heat of the earth, the cold of the middle region of the air, exhalations, vapors, and so on. Therefore, I advise all who are curious about philosophy to attribute the work and act of such great and miraculous procreation, and consequently the honor and glory, neither to the elements or things made of elements, nor to the stars, nor even indeed to the **Angels** (insofar as they are considered creatures), but to God the Creator alone. It is He who produces all these things—and indeed far greater things—in the world, in and through the angelic creatures. These angels are in the closest state of proximity and nearness to the divinity, insofar as they immediately receive the impressions of light or divine emanations, which they then, led by divine command, desire to impart to creatures mixed both perfectly and imperfectly. Let a most fitting comparison be placed before your considerations regarding this matter. A certain man wounds another with a sword; the question is then asked: Which of these wounded the man? One person answers (in the manner of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who focused on physical and material causes.</note> who attribute the efficient cause of meteors to fire or air) that "the sword did this." Another truly (after the fashion of the **Astrologers** who attribute the acting cause to meteors or stars) will say that "the hand of the striker is the effecter of that deed." A third, coming closer to the truth (along with the **Magi** <note>Practitioners of "High Magic" or natural magic who believed spirits or "daemons" directed the forces of nature.</note> who say that the authors of meteors are spirits) will say it is "the spirit in the man" who did it. Finally, one skilled in theographic mysteries <note>Theography refers to the study of God's "writing" or signatures within the created world.</note>, looking with eyes a little sharper into the very center of both things, will say that **God** did both this and that. By this example, the error of the world is clearly explained. We, however, in this place, will make mention of the winds only in the common manner, under which name we nonetheless understand the Angels of GOD, who are accustomed to animate them. But since in this book of the third member we intend to act in a physical manner and occupy ourselves with the elements, we shall therefore deal with the winds in this place in the manner of ordinary philosophers.

**CAP. II.**

*On the correct division of the winds, and that they are the efficient causes (speaking in common speech or after the common philosophical manner) of any meteor whether in the Air, Water, or Earth.*

We make the **Winds** (whose souls we have said above are angels, either openly and manifestly or occultly bright) to be either invisible and subject only to hearing, or visible and bright. Of the latter kind are lightnings, fiery whirlwinds, flashes, and similar visible meteors which are driven through the air by violent motion, no differently than those winds that are visible. From these kinds of winds, therefore, as the first movers in the elementary world, are produced and procreated all other meteors, both bright and dark: namely, Comets, "chasms" <note>term: <term>Chasmata</term>. An atmospheric phenomenon appearing as an opening or "gap" in the sky, often associated with the Aurora Borealis.</note>, "beams," lightnings, flashes, fiery whirlwinds, "leaping goats" <note>term: <term>Capra Saltans</term>. An old meteorological term for a flickering, jumping appearance of lightning or ignited vapors.</note>, will-o'-the-wisps, and sulfurous flames which the earth vomits up. These and others like them come from the bright winds and clearly from fire, which in its nature is nothing but a most subtle air, animated and agitated by a fiery soul. But truly, clouds, mists, vapors, snow, hail, stones, frost, and ice are from the hidden and least manifest Winds as if from efficient causes, and from hidden and dark air contracted into such dark forms. Regarding the hidden and least visible winds, we shall speak a few words in this place, and that in the common manner.

**CAP. III.**

*On the East Wind (Subsolanus) and its two collateral winds.*

The hidden wind blowing directly from that place of the east, where the equinoctial line intersects the Eastern horizon, is called **Subsolanus** <note>original: *Subsolanus*. Literally "Under the Sun." The Greek name is *Apeliotes*.</note>, inasmuch as it rises under the Sun in the Torrid Zone, namely in that direct place where the equator passes; furthermore, it is also called *Apeliotes* by the Greeks. This wind, along with its two other collateral winds, is said to be hot and dry. But this wind, as the Prince of the eastern winds between the two aforesaid, standing like a Virtue in the middle, is most temperate in its fiery disposition like the celestial sun; whence it is a bringer of serenity to the **Macrocosm** <note>term: <term>Macrocosm</term>. The "Great World" or the universe as a whole.</note> and healthful to the **Microcosm** <note>term: <term>Microcosm</term>. The "Little World," specifically the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>. Its right wing, which blows from that point of the Eastern horizon which the Tropic of Cancer intersects (that is, from the summer sunrise), is called **Caecias** <note>The Northeast wind.</note> for its malice, and the **Hellespontic** from the place from which it blows. This Wind is very inconsistent in its disposition: sometimes it is cold with the disposition of the North, and sometimes burning with the nature of the east; but for the most part, it excels all winds in dryness, and that from the nature of the place, insofar as it partakes of Northern or earthly dryness, and that of the east or fire.

Partaking of fire. However, by accident, it is also observed at times to be imbued with a certain moisture. The reason for this is that it is not its property, in the manner of the North wind, to push clouds away, but rather to greedily attract them to itself. This occurs, if I am not mistaken, because of its intense dryness, which is attractive to moisture. He is therefore a "bringer of clouds."

The left wing, or the collateral wind of the East wind <note>The *Subsolanus* or "under the sun" wind</note> toward the south, which blows from that point where the Tropic of Capricorn cuts the eastern Horizon—that is, from the winter sunrise—is called *Eurus* in Greek. Whence also sometimes—indeed quite often—it is observed to gather clouds, just as, in respect to its dryness and heat, it is sometimes observed to dissipate gathered clouds through the air and fill it everywhere with smoky mists and thick vapors. For this reason, it is also known to deceive the sight, making visible objects appear larger than they truly are.

For a fuller explanation of the qualities of these winds, I refer and remit you to the following volume which, God willing, will deal with the nature of health and diseases.

### CHAP. IV.

### On the description of the West wind with its wings or collateral winds, and the meteors which they are accustomed to produce in the air.

That general wind blowing from the western angle, whose midpoint is intersected by the equinoctial line, is called *Favonius* in Latin and *Zephyrus* in Greek <note>original: "Zephyrus"; meaning "life-bearing"</note>—that is, "bearing life and vigor." This is the prince of those winds that blow from the west. In its nature, this wind is cold and moist in a most temperate degree. It has *Africus* on its right as its wing or collateral wind, and *Corus* on its left.

The collateral wind *Africus* <note>The Southwest wind</note> is that which blows from that point of the western Horizon intersected by the Tropic of Capricorn, namely from the winter solstice. Its disposition is to incline somewhat toward Southern heat, but primarily Western coldness abounds in it. This wind is accustomed to blow impetuously in turns, whence it is both stormy and sometimes accompanied by clouds.

The other wing of *Favonius* turning toward the North is that wind which blows from that point in the west which the Tropic of Cancer cuts, namely from the summer solstice. This is called *Corus* in Latin and *Argestes* in Greek <note>original: "Argestes"; implying a clearing or brightening, yet here described as impetuous</note>—that is, impetuous and stormy. In its condition, it inclines somewhat from the moisture of *Favonius* toward the dryness of the North. Whence it happens that it is naturally prone to hail, snow, and cold, and is moist by turns. During its blowing, the clouds in the sky are observed to be dark, although for a part of the day it may be serene, dry, and finally moist. Furthermore, sometimes because of more intense moisture, it brings hailstorms and snow; and occasionally—more frequently in summer—it brings the most vehement thunder, lightning, and horrendous tempests.

Regarding the production of these qualities for either disease or health in "both worlds," <note>Referring to the Macrocosm (the universe) and the Microcosm (man), a central theme in Fludd's philosophy.</note> we shall speak copiously in the following volume, God assisting.

### CHAP. V.

### On the North wind with its two companions and their effects in the air.

The North wind, called *Boreas* in Greek, is the principal wind in the North, and it usually blows directly from the pole star. This wind is, in its condition, exceedingly cold and dry. Its role is to cleanse and purify the air of the gross humors which the South wind produced. According to the testimony of Holy Scripture, it is accustomed to drive away rain; yet sometimes it produces hail and snow, specifically at that time when the South wind blows strongly against it. This usually happens when a louder noise is heard, for then it condenses the air into clouds; sometimes, especially in the summer time, it is observed to produce thunder.

Its left wing is called *Aquilo*, which blows from that point of the eastern region where the polar or arctic circle cuts the Horizon. This wind in its condition is very cold and dry, but truly some-

### CHAPTER VI.

**On the three Southern Winds, along with their conditions**
**in the production of meteors.**

Finally, the Cardinal wind reigning principally in the south, which is said to breathe from the Antarctic pole, is called *Auster* <note>The South wind</note>, named from "drawing up waters" <note>original: "ab hauriendo aquas"</note>, as some would have it. This wind is by its nature hot and moist, whence it is accustomed not only to gather thick and constant clouds, but also to pour out heavy rains. It is prone to produce lightning, to make the air thick and dense, to nourish mists, and also quite often to flash with lightning and give forth great peals of thunder. Furthermore, just as the North wind is a hard wind that hardens the humors, so the South wind is soft and softening.
     Its right wing blows from the place of intersection made by the antarctic circle on the Eastern Horizon, and it is called *Euro-Auster* <note>The South-Southeast wind</note>. In its quality, it is hot and moist, but because of its aspect toward the Eastern corner, it is somewhat hotter and not quite so moist as the main South wind. This is a cloud-bearing wind and occasionally a producer of thunder.
     Its left wing is the *Austro-Africus* <note>The South-Southwest wind</note>, which blows from the point of the western Horizon where the antarctic circle cuts it. This produces stormy winds, which are sometimes accompanied by clouds and thunder.
     From this, therefore, you see what those learned in common perception and experience perceive: that almost all meteors proceed from the winds. But truly, what the internal nature of these winds might be, the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> seemed to us to be surely ignorant of; for they, quite unadvisedly, made their internal agent to be merely exhalations springing from the earth and animated by solar heat. **But by Saint John we are taught that it is not known whence the winds arise or where they go, and that the spirit tends to breathe where it wills; and the Prophet says that Jehovah made His Angels winds, and His ministers a burning flame.** <note>The author is citing John 3:8 and Psalm 104:4 to argue that winds are actually angelic or spiritual forces.</note> By this discourse, he clearly seems to explain that there are two species of winds after the manner of Angels: namely, those which are heard and not at all seen, and are hidden; and those which are seen and are radiant, and are not at all heard, except through their effect, as in thunder there are lightning bolts and flashes. And so, worn out and as if fatigued by the weariness of such great labor, we gladly place an end to this volume (not without perpetual grace and blessing to God our Creator for such great favor and illumination).

**L. M.** is the neck of the <term>matrass<gloss>a long-necked glass bulb used in early chemistry and physics</gloss></term> whose opening is submerged in the water.

We believe it is worth proceeding quickly to the properties and use of this same instrument. First, therefore, it must be observed that when the body of the matrass **O** is heated, the air contained within it is thinned <note>original: *subtiliatur*, meaning to become less dense or more refined</note> by the external heat; and once thinned, it requires a more spacious place to contain its existence. Whence it happens that a larger portion of the air, which had been gathered and contracted in the hollow of that body by the cold, now thinned and dilated more or less by the heat, requires a broader place for its existence. For this reason, a portion of it is forced to exit into the open air while the vessel or body of the matrass is heating. 

Thus it follows that once the opening of the matrass neck is placed into the water (while the vessel is still warm), as that body gradually cools, the water is raised into the neck of the matrass step by step—namely from degree 1 to 2, and then later from 2 to 3. The reason for this is as follows: since the action of cold is in every way contrary to that of heat, it follows that if it is the nature of heat to thin and to require a broader or more spacious place for the thing it has thinned or attenuated, then conversely it is the nature of cold to thicken <note>original: *inspissare*</note>, gather together, and drive into a tighter space that which was dispersed and rarefied by heat. 

Therefore, as the vigor of the heat gradually fades and the power of the cold consequently strengthens, because a larger portion of the air was expelled from the cavity of the vessel by its thinning, and new air sufficient for the proportion of the strengthening spirit cannot be drawn into the belly of the vessel because of the obstruction of the water, it is necessary that a portion of water supply the deficiency of air. The water is raised into the neck of the matrass in place of the air, because the thinned air—which once filled the entire cavity of the body—is now contracted into a narrower place by the <term>styptic<gloss>contracting or astringent</gloss></term> and freezing faculty of the cold. Without the water supplying and filling that space, it would leave a vacuum in the vessel, which is in no way permitted by nature <note>This refers to the classical Aristotelian principle of *horror vacui*, or "nature abhors a vacuum," which was a standard explanation for suction before the discovery of atmospheric pressure.</note>; as has been explained more widely elsewhere.

Therefore, with the watery body having been drawn in and thus raised due to the successive creeping in and abundance of cold, it will be necessary that every successive increase of cold or heat be discerned by the naked eye. For if either the air surrounding that vessel, or something more solid applied or adhering to the vessel, becomes warm, then the more intense the heat of the surrounding air or the object applied to the vessel, the further the water will decline downward toward the box. For example, if during a state of cold the water stood at degree 6 or 7, and then the heat increases (whether in the surrounding air or by applying a hand or some other object to the body), the water will descend by as many degrees as the proportion of heat has increased in the enclosed air.

The reason for this is readily apparent: because (as has been said) the greater the proportion of heat, the greater the thinning or rarefaction of the enclosed air. And the thinner a thing becomes, the more it seeks a broader and more free place for its existence. For one handful of water expanded into air requires ten times as much space to be contained as it would claim in its watery consistency. The same ratio or proportion exists between air and fire; for air ignited by heat migrates step by step into the thinness of fire. Hence it is that the air enclosed in the body of the vessel, which was once contracted by cold and driven into a tighter space, is now dilated by the approach of heat and thrusts the water that was raised in the neck downward, so that it may acquire a broader or narrower place for itself according to the degree of its rarefaction. 

Are we not taught by experience that water reduced to vapor by the violence of fire requires a vaster place for its freedom? Whoever, therefore, prepares himself for a more exact inquiry into this matter, we wish him to be referred to the experiments produced by us in Chapter 2, Experiment 12, Experiment 13, and Experiment 16, Tract 2, Part 7, Book 3, Chapter 1, Rules 6 and 7, where we have clearly expressed nature's infinite faculty of expanding itself. Furthermore, this same thing is explained even more clearly to the unlearned in the case of <term>gunpowder<gloss>original: *pulvere Bombardali*</gloss></term>, where a small portion of its earthy substance is converted into a great smoke like a huge cloud, snatching and shattering everything in its path if its spacious freedom is obstructed. Likewise, in the extraction of <term>aqua fortis<gloss>nitric acid</gloss></term> distilled from saltpeter and vitriol, we observe that the receiver must contain the great spirits leaping out from the neck of the retort. 

We conclude, therefore, that heat, by dilating, causes the air enclosed in the body to repel the water raised in the neck, so that the dilated air may acquire a broader place for itself, according to the greater or lesser dominance of the heat’s effect on the enclosed air. But truly, as the effect of heat decreases and fades, and the cold gradually revives and predominates, it is necessary that all the power and operation of the preceding heat be removed, and that, on the contrary, the property and act of cold—which is contrary to heat—be produced. Hence it is that, just as the water raised in the neck was pushed downward by the act of heat, so now the contrary effect is produced by the contrary affection of cold.

Just as it is the role of heat to refine, so conversely it is the duty of cold to thicken and make dense that which heat has thinned. In this capacity, cold contracts into a smaller space and quantity that which heat has dilated; and the more the effects of cold press upon it, the more the air is constricted and compressed into a narrower place. 

From this it follows (lest a vacuum be committed <note>original: *ne vacuum committeretur*—the author refers to the traditional Aristotelian belief that nature "abhors a vacuum" and will move matter to fill empty space</note>) that all that water, which the action of heat was thrusting downward, the action of cold draws upward by contracting the air. It carries that water upward by as many degrees as the cold is exalted in its dominion over the power of heat.

## CAP. III.

## On the various uses of this experimental instrument.

Although the chief goal in demonstrating this kind of instrument is so that the most suitable study of meteors may be drawn from its dual action of contrary motion, it is nevertheless my purpose in this place to speak, not at all irrelevantly, of its common use for our subsequent contemplation.

By its general action of constriction—that is, the rising of water through the contraction of air—we perceive the logic of the **Dense** or the thickness of any thing; this action of nature proceeds from cold (as you have recorded above). Truly, by the mediating action of dilation, by which water is propelled downward because of the dissipation and resolution of the enclosed air, we perceive the cause of the **Rare** or of thinness in nature, which property is derived from heat. Whence it is certain, and we are made more sure beyond all doubt, that nothing in the entire kingdom of nature can be rarefied or thinned except by the mediation of light or fire (whether it be visible or invisible), the effect of which is heat. Conversely, nothing can be condensed, constricted, or thickened where darkness does not have dominion, as its effect is cold, as was clearly explained in the place cited before.

Its more specific use is manifold: for first and most evidently, it is accustomed to indicate the natural state and temperament of the external air in heat and cold. For the more the water tends upward through the degrees of the neck, the greater is the dominion of cold in the air. Thus, in any quarter of the year, as well as in any day of the week, we can judge the degrees of cold by the elevation of the water. Indeed, in the same day, we shall perceive the conflict between solar heat and cold, and many other things worthy of observation. Furthermore, by the same reasoning, we shall discern the dominion of heat in any quarter, day, or hour of the year through the contrary motion; these observations are matters of no small importance in the explanation of nature and her mysteries.

Besides these, those same effects are usually provided by "adventitious" <note>external or added</note> heat or cold. Thus it happens that if we apply only a hand over the bottom of the glass <term>matrass<gloss>a long-necked glass bulb</gloss></term>, the enclosed air, thinned by the heat of the applied limb, urges the water to incline downward in the blink of an eye; and once the hand is removed from the vessel, the water immediately yearns to breathe back into its former place assigned to it by natural cold.

Finally, by proper observation of this kind of instrument and vigilant attention to the movement of the water, we can measure the heat of chemical furnaces. For if we have two such instruments at hand, one of which is exposed to the mercy of naturally affected air, while the other is applied to a vent-hole breathing from the furnace, they will provide a ratio for adapting the artificial heat of the one to the natural heat of the other. At last, the one applied to the artificial heat will be rectified in its degree by this natural one. Whence it will be very easy to derive a unity of proportion in artificial heat in this way: namely, by adapting the degree of heat in the natural air to the artificial one. For example, if the heat in the naturally disposed instrument has pushed the water only to the 7th degree, but the heat of the instrument applied to the furnace has depressed it to the 4th degree, then I may observe that the artificial fire exceeds the natural one by only three degrees. Therefore, if the natural heat in the air is decreased later, and the water rises to the 8th or 9th degree, I will expect the water in the artificially applied instrument to rise by the same proportion to the 5th or 6th degree. Thus, it always observes in its distance a triple proportion, which is to be ascribed to the artificial heat, and so on for the rest.

Now indeed, I shall proceed to the second part of this book, where, God willing, we shall discuss the strict contemplation of the generation of meteors, having held regard for the action or property of this <term>spiritual instrument<gloss>so called because it operates using the "spirit" or air trapped inside</gloss></term>.

This is what the wise man intended through the words brought forth before, which in Jerome's translation <note>The Vulgate.</note> are as follows: *The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place: and there rising again, maketh his round by the south, and turneth again to the north: the spirit goeth forward surveying all places round about, and returneth to his circuits.* Or, as Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Hebraist.</note> prefers: *In its conversion, the air hastens about in a circuit.* Or, as Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino, an Italian Dominican and philologist.</note> prefers: *The wind proceeds by circling immediately, and the wind returns to its circuits.* 
      From these things, one may gather how great the obedience and aptitude of the air, or spirit, or wind is for receiving the impressions of the sun. Finally, the earthly principles of clouds are the winds, which by their various blasts gather and accumulate mountains of air, and this is done by way of compression and condensation. And yet all these principles have a sincere relation to that unique "Principle of Principles," the Uncreated, who placed His tabernacle in the sun; for without Him all things are nothing, and with Him everything that is exists exactly as it truly is, according to that saying of the Evangelist: *Christ is all and in all.* And elsewhere: *By that Word all things were made, and without Him was not any thing made that was made. John 1.* For what is a cloud but an object without wind? What is the wind if no consideration is given to the sun? What, finally, is the sun if its luminous soul were extinguished? Who, then, is the prime mover of this soul? What is its inner life in the absence of Him who placed His tabernacle in the solar spirit? From Him, this divine and central Apollo—the lovely and gracious desire of the entire world—disperses life and being everywhere to His creatures. This uncreated light of the world, the Son of the invisible God, obtaining His seat in the visible Son of God (as Plato has it), to whom be praise, honor, and glory. Amen.

->Correlation.<-

We have seen in our experimental instrument that the air itself, enclosed in a <term>matrass<gloss>a round-bottomed glass flask used in alchemy and chemistry</gloss></term>, dilates itself by the contact of heat. In its dilation, it requires a larger and more spacious place, whence it tends downward against the quarter of the heat dilating it, with a motion so strong—even against the nature of its own bodily lightness—that it compels and urges even a dense mass of water before it. By these things we are taught that air dilated by solar heat moves for the most part either to the right or to the left in the world, and recedes from the seat of heat (namely, the solar place) toward other light things. This happens many degrees faster than in the glass, both because of the immense motion of the sun in the open air and because dilated air is not as strongly opposed or repelled by thickened air as it is by thick and dense water. 
      It follows, therefore, that if air applied or joined to air usually procreates a denser air, it is necessary that such a thickening of the air creates a "middle" composition, of a moderate substance between water and earth. For there must be a medium between two extremes—namely, water and air. Indeed, those more skilled in natural philosophy have freely acknowledged the condensation of air into water, and again the rarefaction of water into air. Therefore, the medium between such a starting point and destination is vapor; and a denser or thinner vapor usually procreates such a cloud as itself is, which cloud is finally resolved into drops of water. Therefore, thinned air, mixed with thick air, passes into a cloudy vapor, which is finally seen to distill into rain. 
      But even if some were ignorant of the opposite, we can prove this by ocular experience, moving from the lesser to the greater in this way: If a part of the subtlety of air is usually transmuted into a watery substance, how much more so when that air is joined to thicker air? That a part of the thinned air usually migrates into a watery substance is evident in the greater sense, but the lesser is explained by the following experiment.
      Take a glass that is sufficiently round, filled only with air, and hermetically sealed; place it almost entirely in ashes...

Thus, it will first change into a white smoke, and then gradually into drops, a fact which I have tested quite often. By a clearly similar logic, in the dissolution of water into air, which occurs through its strong boiling, we first observe a wind being stirred up, and that wind accompanies the vapor, which then afterwards vanishes into the air. So also (since the logic of contraries or opposites is the same), air heated by the sun’s warmth is easily condensed into a cloud in the presence of cold along with dense air; this happens much more readily because of the abundance of material to be condensed, since the aforementioned experiment shows that this same thing is usually achieved by the simple condensation of air. From this it is clear how absurd that opinion of the <term>Peripatetics<gloss>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</gloss></term> is, who affirm that the cause of clouds is the freezing of vapors from the earth and water in the middle region of the air due to the quality of that place. Similarly, we are taught by experience that clouds and rains are so rare in the summer time because of the strong mastery that the solar rays have in our air; for the more subtle and <term>rarefied<gloss>thinned out</gloss></term> the air is, the further it is from thickening into a cloud. But if by chance the thinned air is gathered together by opposing blasts and migrates into the existence of a cloud, it is then mixed with such great fiery spirits for the most part that thunder and lightnings arise therefrom.

### CHAPTER III.

#### On the origin of springs and consequently of rivers.

From the preceding arguments, resting both upon philosophical speculation and experimental practice, we consider it demonstrated more than sufficiently that the air filling all things in this world is dilated in its regions by the power of heat (the common source of which we have said is the sun itself). By this dilation, the air requires a larger space—above and below, right and left, before and behind—to receive its expanded substance. But conversely, we have explained that this same air, universally spread out, is condensed by the presence of cold (more or less according to the greater or lesser predominance of said quality), and is gathered and contracted into one. We have also noted that just as dilated air requires a larger space for itself, so indeed, when its members are contracted, it is content with a narrower space. Since this is the case, it follows that the reason for the diminishing and drying up of springs and rivers in the summer time is not because of the evaporation of their water into the air, as is the opinion of the Peripatetics. For if this were so, it would follow that solar heat was not the cause of the thinning of the air, but rather its thickening; for if the aquatic substance of the springs and rivers were evaporated into the air, then it would be necessary for the air to be thicker in the summer time. Consequently, the sun, by its proximity and the direction of its rays, would not rarefy the air, but rather make it thick. Yet we are taught that the property of heat is to rarefy and not to thicken, which we also gather from the property of our aforementioned experiment: for in the presence of heat, the air contained in the <term>matrass<gloss>A glass flask with a long neck used in laboratory experiments</gloss></term> is dilated, whereas on the contrary, by the assault of cold, it is again thickened. But to pursue this inquiry further, let us see, I pray: if the substance of rivers and springs is converted into air during the summer, what finally becomes of that superfluous air, since the extreme heat of the sun always tends toward the thinning of the air? Certainly it is not converted into clouds, because in the summer time—and especially when the sun is most extremely hot—clouds are not so frequent, nor are rains in such abundance. Indeed, as it says in the <term>Sacred Page<gloss>The Bible</gloss></term>, "the heavens are as brass and dry" <note>original: *caeli sint aenei & sicci*. A reference to Deuteronomy 28:23: "And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass."</note>, and if any clouds are present, they are sterile. From this it follows that, contrary to the doctrine of the ancient philosophers, there is another cause for this outflow of rivers, springs, and pools, and another path for them, albeit invisible and quite hidden. Namely, the air of the hemisphere, being greatly thinned and requiring a wider and more vast place for its existence, thrusts the waters of the springs downward into their whirlpools and causes the moisture to descend into the innermost parts of the earth. Is this not indicated by the ocular demonstration of our machine? In it we see that in the presence of heat, the air contained in the matrass requires a larger place for itself by dilation. There, the heat in its dilation does not convert the nature of the lower vessel of water (sublimated through the neck) into dense air—since such a sublimation would be entirely against the laws of the nature of heat—but visibly thrusts it downward toward its innermost deep hiding places (from which it had first been raised upward by the effort of the cold). But perhaps someone will question the location: where is that water moved when it is così depressed among us in the summer time, while its waves are hidden from us? For without doubt it is necessary that the waters of springs are always in motion. To this we respond with the Holy Bible: "they return to the sea from whence they first came" <note>original: *ad mare reuertantur à quo prius decesserunt*. A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:7.</note>. Nor yet does the sea seem to grow, because the sea distributes that portion of water which the more summery quarter of the world refused to the winter quarter of the world. For beyond any controversy, by as many degrees as the Northern hemisphere of the world excels in heat and dryness, by so many does the Southern hemisphere prevail in cold and moisture.

And this is the reason why the sea always seems to claim the same portion for itself in quantity, according to that saying of the wise man: *All rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again. Ecclesiastes 1, verse 7.* <note>original: "Omnia flumina properant ad mare, nec tamen mare impletur, quocunque loci flumina properant, eodem reuertuntur propere."</note> How foolish, then, is that opinion of the Pagan philosophers which you can easily see from these things, whose opinion is that the material of springs and rivers is vapor resolved and liquefied into water by heat and cold simultaneously within the earth, just like clouds, snow, and rain. Either the Holy Scriptures are false, or this <term>Peripatetic<gloss>referring to the followers of Aristotle</gloss></term> opinion is plainly imaginary. And yet nonetheless, their Christian followers or disciples are so intoxicated by the magical cups of those Pagan philosophers that they strive to prefer their false opinions over the true and infallible spirit of all truth. Let me bring one living example to light. Velcurio, <note>Johannes Velcurio (1490–1534), a German author whose commentaries on Aristotle’s physics were widely taught in universities.</note> a Doctor of Philosophy among Christians and held in no small esteem in the Academies of Europe, speaks thus in that place where he treats the nature of springs and rivers: *The Sacred Scriptures clearly do not agree with the Philosophers regarding the origin of springs and rivers; for Ecclesiastes chapter 1 says they flow from the sea through various channels and passages and flow back to their sources: All rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from where the rivers go out, they return so that they may flow again. But the natural philosophers (he says) say their material is vapor resolved into water and liquefied by cold and heat together within the earth.* Thus he speaks, and yet he retreats from this fountain of truth in his own doctrine, and taking his philosophy or instruction from the Pagan philosopher Aristotle while neglecting Solomon, he causes so many contradictions to be found in all the sciences depending on natural philosophy—indeed, even in theology as it is commonly handled—that truth itself seems to be imprisoned in deceptive clouds and darkness for us Christians. **But** let us return to the matter. It is most certain, contrary to the doctrine of the Peripatetics and as the Sacred Page asserts, that the nourishment of springs comes from the sea, and not from vapor or air enclosed in the earth, condensed there into vapor by the cold as they would have it. For what need is there for many operations when a thing is usually perfected by nature through fewer? Especially since this is an invincible axiom published by them to the world, namely: *that it is done in vain through more things which can be done through fewer.* <note>original: "quod frustra fiat per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora" – This is a version of the principle of parsimony, often called Occam's Razor.</note> For without the conversion of air into vapor and vapor into water, water by its own simple nature is carried upward through the pores and veins of the earth, from the deep whirlpool of the sea through the hidden passages and secret veins of its bowels, being solely <term>styptic<gloss>having a contracting or binding quality</gloss></term> and congregative of air in its cold nature. This is indicated exactly both by philosophical reasons and by this practical experiment of ours. For unless there were such a close contiguity between the elements of water and air that one could not be separated from the other, that monster in the nature of things—namely, the **Vacuum** <note>The idea of a "vacuum" or empty space was considered "monstrous" or impossible by many Renaissance thinkers, who believed nature would move any matter to prevent it.</note>—would be admitted. From this it necessarily follows that where air recedes through vessels closed on all sides, there water also follows, because of the natural embrace of the one with the other. This, moreover, has been exactly demonstrated by us through the conclusion of *Rule 7, Tract 2, Part 7, Book 3, On the Technical History of the Macrocosm*, where elementary motion is discussed. The Rule is as follows: *The substance of the element of water is contiguous to air by a tenacious mixture, so that there is no distance between them.* From this, therefore, it happens that water is raised upward with the air. And at the end of that rule, an experimental demonstration follows, which we have expressed in this place.

But on the contrary, it is the nature of heat to thin and dilate the air, as is shown by the preceding demonstration. The air, seeking a wider space during this thinning process, is seen not to draw waters upward from the center of the earth, but rather to press them further downward from that region, so that they might find a broader scope for their existence. Now, we have said that the universal source of these waters is the sea, which also seems to be suggested by the Holy Bible in these words: *Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so. Genesis 1:9.* <note>original: "Congregentur aquæ quæ sunt infra cælum in locum vnum vt conspiciatur arida & fuit ita, Gen.1.9."</note> Moreover, God called the dry land "Earth," and the gathering together of the waters He called "Seas."

But in passing, some might object to these things we are writing: that if this were true, then the winds would be accustomed to blow more abundantly and fruitfully at that time when the cold in our Zone is most intense. Indeed, in the time of frost and rime, the air is found to be at its coldest; therefore, in these times, the air should be more centrally contracted, and consequently, the rivers should be more abundant and the springs more overflowing and full.

To these people we respond that the cause of the outflow and the more copious flux of springs is not solely from the cold of the region in which they flow (which contracts the air of the place and consequently draws up the waters hidden in the earth due to the proximity and connection of water with air), but also the heat of the opposite region, which thins the air, is quite suited to the task. 

For example, in our winter <gloss>original: "brumali"</gloss> season, when the sun occupies the spaces beyond the equinoctial region—namely, toward the Antarctic pole—traveling through Scorpio, Sagittarius, and especially Capricorn; the air of that place or space of the earth is thinned due to the directness of the solar rays. It seeks a more spacious place everywhere (that is, circularly) for its expanded existence. Whence it happens that the springs of that place are thrust down toward the bowels or center of the earth. For this reason, that hot action very easily provides "hot matter" <note>Fludd uses "matter" here in a philosophical sense, referring to the displaced air/vapor.</note> for the multiplication of Northern springs. This matter, having been so offered, is then carried upward by the dominance of the cold which contracts the air—due to the sun's absence or the weakness of the solar heat in Northern parts (that is, because of the slant and feebleness of the rays striking there)—and it fills the springs copiously. 

However, it is certain that no more water can be raised by the Northern cold than in that proportion which the Southern heat has pressed down into the earth. If it were to happen otherwise, a vacuum would be left in the nature of things, which would be most absurd and abominable to Nature herself. And this is why, although the rivers (according to the saying of the wise man) flow into the sea, yet the sea does not overflow, nor is it fuller at one time than another. For there is a circular motion in nature, but it admits no increase or decrease in itself. <note>Fludd is referencing Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full."</note>

And although we see that floods occur and rivers overflow their banks in their Northern parts, we are taught that this usually happens more abundantly because of rains. These rains occur due to the extreme thinning of the air in Southern places, in which a great portion of that thinned air is led into Northern parts by means of the Southern wind. There, it is reduced into clouds by the cold of the place, and finally, by its own heat (which it receives from the solar rays by way of thickening), it is immediately dissolved into rains; for enclosed heat naturally **seeks the open**
