### Corollary.
What need is there for more words? Do we not see in the observation of our present machine <note>Fludd refers to his weather-glass or thermoscope, an early instrument for measuring temperature through the expansion and contraction of air.</note> that upon the approach of heat to the flask, the air is dilated, and that in its dilation it requires a larger space for its existence? This is proven by the fact that we notice with our own eyes that the water—which had been raised many degrees into the neck of the flask by the presence of cold—is gradually driven downward by the dilation of the air. 

This experience has been very dear and laborious, and indeed even quite dangerous, for certain common chemists. For in the making of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid; literally "strong water," used by alchemists for dissolving metals.</note> from saltpeter and vitriol, the spirits leaping forth from the small mass contained in the retort <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note> are not contained by the vast glass vessel or receiver because of the dilation of the nitrous air. Instead—and I speak from experience—they miserably tear that vessel into infinite particles, accompanied by a horrendous sound like a gunshot, so that they might acquire a wider field in the air for their existence. 

Hence, therefore, is the reason for the diminishing of springs in the summertime: namely, because the air in our Zone is thinned by the presence of solar heat, as can be seen by a diligent gaze at the properties of our machine. Therefore, the dilated air does not pull the water upward toward itself, but on the contrary, thrusts the earthly waters downward. Thus we see in paralytics that the nerves, relaxed by thinning, do not stretch and pull the limbs to perform their functions, but conversely, we note them falling or being pressed downward toward the earth. Do we not observe this same thing in the action of our instrument, whose water, raised by the cold, is driven downward by the presence of heat and the rarefaction of the air? 

By the same reasoning, in the wintertime, we see the air contracted by the cold, and in its contraction, we see the springs overflowing with water and the rivers swelling. We have said this happens because of the constriction of the air, which moves the water itself as if it were its servant and handmaid; it moves it, I say, either by driving it away from the center toward the circumference (in its hot and dilated condition), or by contracting it from the circumference to the center (in its cold or contractive and gathering nature). Behold the sign in our machine, where the air contained in the flask is so condensed by the contact of cold that it raises the water many degrees high into the neck of the flask, through which the cold is intensified in its nature. From this, it is clear that this is the reason why waters are raised high from the central depths of the earth: namely, by the presence of winter cold.

### CHAPTER IV.
### On the origin of Luminous Meteors, and how they are brought forth in rarefied air.
Since ocular experience teaches us that the more the air is heated, the rarer and thinner it becomes, it follows conversely that the rarer and purer the air is, the closer it approaches the nature of the element of fire, or the luminous and fiery spirit. On the other hand, it is clear that the more the air cools, the denser it is rendered. Therefore, the first degree of condensing air is into the consistency of vapor; the second into the consistency of mist; the third of a cloud; the fourth of rain; the fifth of snow; and the last of hail and ice. 

Such also is the relationship of degrees in the thinning of air from its middling state up to the very sphere of fire: namely, wind, <term>ignis fatuus</term> <note>Literally "foolish fire"; the phosphorescent light seen over marshland, also known as a will-o'-the-wisp.</note>, a falling star, lightning, a flash, a pillar of fire, and other kinds of comets. All these fiery <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon (rain, wind, lightning), not just space rocks.</note> have air rarefied by fiery heat for their existence. 

Here, however, we think it must be diligently observed by us that the hidden—that is, the greatest spiritual part of the air—is light. It gives life to the air itself no differently than the soul gives life to an animal, agitating it everywhere according to its will. Therefore, the hidden or internal part of the air which dwells in its center is pure fire, just as its manifest or external part is a certain moist substance, covering and enclosing that hidden light no differently than a body encloses a soul. A dense cloud of lightning is this: for the fiery or central substance of the air is pure fire, which God, in the first creation, when He said "Let there be light" <note>original: "Fiat lux"</note>, breathed into the universal spirit of the world. Therefore, by stripping off its moist garment or by making the hidden manifest and hiding the manifest, the moist invisible air is changed into invisible fire. 

But just as we see the external and manifest (yet invisible) air itself take on first the appearance of visible vapor and then a dense cloud through contraction, so also we will perceive the hidden or fiery invisible air change first into the substance of a flash and lightning, and then, in a tighter contraction, into a visibly fiery meteor, namely a comet, a falling star, a will-o'-the-wisp, and other things of this kind. Therefore, the limit toward which the air tends from its middling nature by thinning is a fiery existence; but that toward which it is accustomed to migrate from its middling nature is the nature of a dense cloud. From this, it is clear that in middling air there is an aptitude either toward a dark nature by virtue of thickening, or toward a luminous existence by way of rarefaction. In this way, both dark and luminous meteors are produced in the world, from which afterward both the internal and external—that is, both the soul and body of any thing, whether simple or composite—is derived.

### On the Generation of Meteors. 303

Hence it is that on account of ignorance of this world, many, not knowing the true author of these evils <note>original: *verum horum malorum authorem* — Fludd refers here to the divine source of natural disasters, which he believes are sent as judgments or trials rather than being merely random physical accidents.</note>, unknowingly cease to cry out to Him for His mercy and help and to solicit Him with due prayers; and thus they are destroyed by **Jehovah the Destroyer** or by His wrathful Angels, who disturb the air, seas, and earth in a stupendous manner, and are exterminated in various ways. 

However, it is the role of the philosophy brought forth by us to attribute all these things justly to God, as they are; led by the authority of the **Sacred Page** <note>The Bible, specifically the Old Testament in this context.</note>, we acknowledge that He acts by means of Angels—that is, in the angels and through the angels as the instruments <term>organa</term> <note>From the Greek *organon*, meaning a tool or instrument used to accomplish a specific task.</note> and vehicles of His will. 

And we say without hesitation, supported by His testimony, that the air is moved, led, and governed through the **Word of God**, insofar as it swims in the all-encompassing Word of God, and is led by the Angels of God appointed for this purpose (whose role it is, according to the witness of **David** <note>A reference to Psalm 103:20: "Bless the Lord, you his angels... that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word."</note>, to carry out the Word of God) whenever, wherever, and however God wills. 

And although this itself may seem absurd and trivial to some disciples of **Aristotle**, nevertheless Christians, weighing all these things in the **scales of truth**, and beholding the mysteries of divinity with sharper eyes...
